questions.meaning: the joint between your hand and arm

questions.prompt: The pharmacist recommended this ___ for allergies. (you squirt it into your nose)
questions.explanation: A "spray" is the medicine you squirt into your nose. A syrup and a tablet are swallowed, and a plaster goes on a cut.
questions.meaning: liquid that comes out in a fine mist

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: I should see a doctor about my cough
questions.explanation: Correct order: "I should see a doctor about my cough."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: He's got a nasty bruise on his knee.
choices: He's got a nasty bruise on his hand.
He's got a nasty bruise on his knee.
He's got a nasty bruise on his arm.
He's got a nasty bruise on his leg.
questions.answer: He's got a nasty bruise on his knee.
questions.explanation: The audio says "He's got a nasty bruise on his knee."

questions.prompt: Say that you should drink more water.
acceptableAnswers: I should drink more water.
I ought to drink more water.
I need to drink more water.
I should be drinking more water.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I should drink more water."

units.title: Superlatives
units.description: Adjective → superlative — Short adjectives take -est; long ones take "most".

questions.prompt: Superlative of "big":
questions.explanation: "Big" is a short adjective ending in one vowel and one consonant, so we double the g and add -est: "biggest".
questions.meaning: larger than all the others
questions.example: This is the biggest room in the house.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "hot": ___
questions.explanation: "Hot" is a short adjective ending in one vowel and one consonant, so we double the t and add -est: "hottest".
questions.meaning: with the highest temperature
questions.example: July is the hottest month here.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "happy":
questions.explanation: "Happy" ends in consonant + -y, so change the y to i and add -est: "happiest".
questions.meaning: feeling the most joy
questions.example: It was the happiest day of my life.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "easy": ___
questions.explanation: "Easy" ends in consonant + -y, so change the y to i and add -est: "easiest".
questions.meaning: the least difficult
questions.example: This is the easiest question.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "good":
questions.explanation: "Good" is irregular: its superlative is "best", not "goodest" or "most good".
questions.meaning: better than all the others
questions.example: She is the best player on the team.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: It was the happiest day of my life
questions.explanation: The superlative "the happiest" goes before the noun "day", and "of my life" comes at the end: "It was the happiest day of my life".

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: July is the hottest month here.
choices: August is the hottest month here.
July is the coldest month here.
July is the hottest month here.
July is the longest month here.
questions.answer: July is the hottest month here.
questions.explanation: The audio says "July is the hottest month here."

questions.prompt: Say that this is the tallest building in town.
acceptableAnswers: This is the tallest building in town.
This is the tallest building in the town.
This is the tallest building in the city.
This is the tallest building in this town.
This building is the tallest in town.
This is the highest building in town.
This is the tallest building in the whole town.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "This is the tallest building in town."

questions.prompt: Superlative of "bad": ___
questions.explanation: "Bad" is irregular: its superlative is "worst", not "baddest" or "most bad" ("worse" is the comparative).
questions.meaning: worse than all the others
questions.example: That was the worst film I've ever seen.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "far":
questions.explanation: "Far" is irregular, so its superlative is "furthest" (also "farthest"), not "farrest" or "most far". "Further" is only the comparative.
questions.meaning: at the greatest distance
questions.example: Our house is the furthest from school.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "expensive": ___
questions.explanation: expensive → most expensive. Short adjectives take -est; long ones take "most".
questions.meaning: costing more than all the others
questions.example: That is the most expensive watch here.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "beautiful":
questions.explanation: beautiful → most beautiful. Short adjectives take -est; long ones take "most".
questions.meaning: the nicest to look at
questions.example: She wore the most beautiful dress.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "thin": ___
questions.explanation: "thin" ends in one vowel plus one consonant, so we double the n before -est: "thinnest".
questions.meaning: the least thick
questions.example: This is the thinnest book here.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence that starts with "This is".
questions.answer: This is the thinnest book here
questions.explanation: Correct order: "This is the thinnest book here."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: That is the most expensive watch here.
choices: That is the most expensive bag here.
That is the most expensive watch here.
That is the most expensive phone here.
That is the most expensive clock here.
questions.answer: That is the most expensive watch here.
questions.explanation: The audio says "That is the most expensive watch here."

questions.prompt: Say that she is the youngest in her class.
acceptableAnswers: She is the youngest in her class.
She is the youngest student in her class.
Nobody in her class is younger than her.
She is the youngest in the class.
She is the youngest one in her class.
She is the youngest person in her class.
In her class she is the youngest.
She is the youngest child in her class.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "She is the youngest in her class."

questions.prompt: Superlative of "early": ___
questions.explanation: "early" ends in a consonant plus y, so the y changes to i before -est: "earliest".
questions.meaning: before all the others
questions.example: The earliest train leaves at five.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "busy":
questions.explanation: "busy" ends in a consonant plus y, so the y changes to i before -est: "busiest".
questions.meaning: with the most things to do
questions.example: Friday is the busiest day at work.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "safe": ___
questions.explanation: "safe" is a short adjective, so it takes -est; because it already ends in -e, you add only -st: "safest".
questions.meaning: the least dangerous
questions.example: This is the safest road in town.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "large":
questions.explanation: "large" is a short adjective, so it takes -est; because it already ends in -e, you add only -st: "largest".
questions.meaning: the biggest in size
questions.example: Russia is the largest country in the world.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "simple": ___
questions.explanation: Two-syllable adjectives ending in -le, like "simple", take -est, and since it already ends in -e you add only -st: "simplest".
questions.meaning: the easiest to understand
questions.example: This is the simplest game to learn.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence that starts with "This is".
questions.answer: This is the simplest game to learn
questions.explanation: Correct order: "This is the simplest game to learn."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: Friday is the busiest day at work.
choices: Friday is the quietest day at work.
Friday is the busiest day at work.
Friday is the longest day at work.
Monday is the busiest day at work.
questions.answer: Friday is the busiest day at work.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Friday is the busiest day at work."

questions.prompt: Say that this is the cheapest hotel.
acceptableAnswers: This is the cheapest hotel.
This hotel is the cheapest.
This is the cheapest hotel here.
This hotel is the cheapest one.
It is the cheapest hotel.
That is the cheapest hotel.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "This is the cheapest hotel."

questions.prompt: Superlative of "careful":
questions.explanation: "Careful" has two syllables and does not end in -y, so it takes "most": "most careful".
questions.meaning: taking the most care
questions.example: He is the most careful driver here.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "tired": ___
questions.explanation: Adjectives formed from -ed participles, like "tired", take "most" even when they are short, so the superlative is "most tired".
questions.meaning: more tired than all the others
questions.example: Of the three of us, I'm the most tired.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "funny":
questions.explanation: "Funny" ends in consonant + -y, so change the y to i and add -est: "funniest".
questions.meaning: making you laugh the most
questions.example: He is the funniest boy in our class.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "heavy": ___
questions.explanation: "Heavy" ends in a consonant + y, so change y to i and add -est: "heaviest".
questions.meaning: weighing the most
questions.example: This is the heaviest box.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "modern":
questions.explanation: "Modern" does not take -est, so we put "most" in front of it to make the superlative: "most modern".
questions.meaning: the newest in style
questions.example: It is the most modern school in town.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "This is the heaviest box."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: He is the most careful driver here.
choices: He is the most careful teacher here.
He is the most careful pilot here.
He is the most careful cook here.
He is the most careful driver here.
questions.answer: He is the most careful driver here.
questions.explanation: The audio says "He is the most careful driver here."

questions.prompt: Say that today is the coldest day of the year.
acceptableAnswers: Today is the coldest day of the year.
Today is the coldest day this year.
It's the coldest day of the year today.
It is the coldest day of the year.
Today is the coldest day of this year.
This is the coldest day of the year.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Today is the coldest day of the year."

questions.prompt: Superlative of "narrow":
questions.explanation: "Narrow" ends in -ow, so we just add -est without doubling any letter: "narrowest".
questions.meaning: the least wide
questions.example: This is the narrowest street in the city.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "polite": ___
questions.explanation: "polite" has two syllables, and its usual superlative is "most polite".
questions.meaning: with the best manners
questions.example: She is the most polite student.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "quiet":
questions.explanation: "Quiet" is a common two-syllable adjective that takes -est, so we add -est with no other change: "quietest".
questions.meaning: making the least noise
questions.example: The library is the quietest place here.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "strange": ___
questions.explanation: "Strange" already ends in -e, so we only add -st: "strangest".
questions.meaning: the most unusual
questions.example: That is the strangest story I know.

questions.prompt: Superlative of "useful":
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -ful, like "useful", take "most" instead of -est, so the superlative is "most useful".
questions.meaning: helping the most
questions.example: A phone is the most useful thing I own.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: That is the strangest story I know
questions.explanation: Correct order: "That is the strangest story I know."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: This is the narrowest street in the city.
choices: This is the narrowest street in the city.
This is the narrowest bridge in the city.
This is the longest street in the city.
This is the widest street in the city.
questions.answer: This is the narrowest street in the city.
questions.explanation: The audio says "This is the narrowest street in the city."

questions.prompt: Say that he is the fastest runner in the club.
acceptableAnswers: He is the fastest runner in the club.
He runs the fastest in the club.
Nobody in the club runs faster than him.
He is the fastest runner at the club.
He is the club's fastest runner.
He is the fastest in the club.
He is the fastest runner in our club.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "He is the fastest runner in the club."

units.title: At the Restaurant
units.description: Ordering and dining out — Common phrases for eating out.

questions.prompt: Could I see the ___, please? (the list of dishes)
questions.explanation: The list of dishes in a restaurant is the "menu". The bill is what you pay and the tip is extra money for the waiter.
questions.meaning: a list of food at a restaurant

questions.prompt: I'd like to ___ a table for two.
questions.explanation: After "I'd like to" you need the base form of the verb, so "book" is correct. -ing, -ed and -s forms don't fit here.
questions.meaning: to reserve a table in advance

questions.prompt: Are you ready to ___? (tell the waiter what you want)
questions.explanation: Telling the waiter what food you want is to "order". Pay and leave come later, and sit comes before.
questions.meaning: to ask for food and drink

questions.prompt: I'll ___ the chicken, please.
questions.explanation: "I'll" means "I will", and after "will" you use the base verb, so "have" is correct. "I'll have the chicken" is the usual way to order food.
questions.meaning: to choose food; used in "I'll have"

questions.prompt: Could we have the ___ when you're ready? (we want to pay)
questions.explanation: When you want to pay in a restaurant, you ask for the "bill", the paper that shows what you owe. Ketchup and cards aren't what you ask for, and you order before the meal.
questions.meaning: the paper that shows what you owe

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "Are you ready to order?"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: I'll have the chicken, please.
questions.explanation: The audio says "I'll have the chicken, please."

questions.prompt: Say that you would like a table for two.
acceptableAnswers: I'd like a table for two.
Could we have a table for two?
A table for two, please.
Could I have a table for two, please?
Can we have a table for two, please?
We'd like a table for two.
I'd like a table for two, please.
Could I have a table for two?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I'd like a table for two."

questions.prompt: Is service ___ in the price?
questions.explanation: The question is passive (service is counted in the price), so it needs the past participle, "included". The other forms don't make a passive.
questions.meaning: counted as part of the price

questions.prompt: Do you have any ___ dishes for people who don't eat meat?
questions.explanation: Dishes for people who don't eat meat are "vegetarian" dishes. Menu, water and ketchup can't describe dishes in this way.
questions.meaning: without meat, or not eating meat
questions.example: Do you have any vegetarian dishes?

questions.prompt: I'm allergic to ___, so no peanuts please. (they grow in a shell)
questions.explanation: "nuts" completes the sentence "I'm allergic to nuts, so no peanuts please."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: hard-shelled seeds you eat

questions.prompt: Could I get some tap ___ as well? (you drink it)
questions.explanation: Tap "water" is the free drinking water from the tap. Ketchup, bread and dish don't go with "tap" or with "you drink it".
questions.meaning: a clear drink with no color
questions.example: Could I have some tap water as well?

questions.prompt: The ___ recommended the fish today. (he brings your food to the table)
questions.explanation: The person who brings food to your table and recommends dishes is the "waiter". A chef or cook works in the kitchen, and a manager runs the restaurant.
questions.meaning: a man who brings food to tables

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: Do you have any vegetarian dishes
questions.explanation: Correct order: "Do you have any vegetarian dishes?"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: Is service included in the price?
choices: Is service included in the price?
Is service included in the bill?
Is breakfast included in the price?
Is service including in the price?
questions.answer: Is service included in the price?
questions.explanation: The audio says "Is service included in the price?"

questions.prompt: Say that you do not eat meat.
acceptableAnswers: I don't eat meat.
I'm a vegetarian.
I never eat meat.
I don't eat any meat.
I am vegetarian.
I eat no meat.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I don't eat meat."

questions.prompt: We're just ___ at the menu for now, not ready to order. (reading it)
questions.explanation: "looking" completes the sentence "We're just looking a table for now, not ready to order."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: reading or checking
questions.example: We're still looking at the menu.

questions.prompt: Could you bring some more ___, please? (we want to eat it with butter)
questions.explanation: The clue says you eat it with butter, which is true of "bread" and not of water, soup or wine.
questions.meaning: food baked from flour

questions.prompt: I'd like my steak ___, not too well done.
questions.explanation: "medium" completes the sentence "I'd like my steak medium, not too well done."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: cooked between rare and well done
questions.example: I'd like my steak medium, please.

questions.prompt: Is there a ___ menu for the children?
questions.explanation: A menu made for children is called a "kids" menu; credit, water and window menus are not things a restaurant offers.
questions.meaning: an informal word for children
questions.example: Is there a kids' menu, please?

questions.prompt: Can I pay by ___ card? (you pay the bank later)
questions.explanation: A "credit" card lets you pay the bank later, which matches the clue; a debit card takes the money straight away.
questions.meaning: money you borrow now and pay back later

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: Is there a kids menu for the children
questions.explanation: Correct order: "Is there a kids menu for the children?"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: Could you bring some more bread, please?
choices: Could you bring some more wine, please?
Could you bring some more bread, please?
Could you bring some more water, please?
Could you bring some more soup, please?
questions.answer: Could you bring some more bread, please?
questions.explanation: The audio says "Could you bring some more bread, please?"

questions.prompt: Ask for a glass of water.
acceptableAnswers: Could I have a glass of water, please?
Can I have a glass of water, please?
A glass of water, please.
May I have a glass of water, please?
Could I get a glass of water, please?
Can I get a glass of water, please?
Could you bring me a glass of water, please?
I'd like a glass of water, please.
Can I have some water, please?
Could we have a glass of water, please?
Could I have a glass of water?
Can I have a glass of water?
A glass of water.
May I have a glass of water?
Could I get a glass of water?
Can I get a glass of water?
Could you bring me a glass of water?
I'd like a glass of water.
Can I have some water?
Could we have a glass of water?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Could I have a glass of water, please?"

questions.prompt: We would like to sit by the ___, please. (so we can see the street)
questions.explanation: You can see the street through a "window", so that is the place to ask to sit by.
questions.meaning: an opening in a wall with glass

questions.prompt: This soup is ___ hot, be careful. (it could burn you)
questions.explanation: The warning 'be careful' and the clue that it could burn you need a strong word, so "very" fits; barely, hardly and slightly mean it is not very hot.
questions.meaning: extremely; to a high degree

questions.prompt: Could we get some extra ___ for the fries? (a red sauce)
questions.explanation: The clue says a red sauce, and "ketchup" is the red tomato sauce served with fries; mustard, mayonnaise and vinegar are not red.
questions.meaning: a red sauce made from tomatoes
questions.example: Could we have some extra ketchup with our chips, please?

questions.prompt: The ___ was excellent tonight, please thank the chef. (everything we ate)
questions.explanation: The clue says everything we ate, which is the whole "meal"; a dish is only one item of food, and a menu or bill cannot be excellent food.
questions.meaning: the food you eat at one time
questions.example: The meal was excellent. Please thank the chef.

questions.prompt: I will have the same ___ as my friend. (what is on the plate)
questions.explanation: The clue says what is on the plate, and that is the "dish" you order; a menu, bill or table is not what you eat.
questions.meaning: food cooked and served in one way

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The waiter brings the bill"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: This soup is very hot, be careful.
choices: This soup is very hot, be careful.
This soup is slightly hot, be careful.
This soup is barely hot, be careful.
This soup is hardly hot, be careful.
questions.answer: This soup is very hot, be careful.
questions.explanation: The audio says "This soup is very hot, be careful."

questions.prompt: Say that the pasta is too salty.
acceptableAnswers: The pasta is too salty.
This pasta is too salty.
The pasta is much too salty.
The pasta has too much salt.
My pasta is too salty.
There is too much salt in the pasta.
That pasta is too salty.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The pasta is too salty."

questions.prompt: Do you take ___ or only cash?
questions.explanation: 'Cash' is contrasted with another way to pay, and "cards" is the only option that is a payment method.
questions.meaning: plastic things used for paying

questions.prompt: Could you box this up, we'd like a ___ bag? (the nickname for a bag of leftovers)
questions.explanation: A bag for taking leftover food home is called a "doggy" bag; gift, party and kitchen bags have a different meaning.
questions.meaning: used in "doggy bag" for leftover food
questions.example: Could we have a doggy bag for the rest, please?

questions.prompt: The restaurant was fully ___, so we waited outside.
questions.explanation: If a restaurant is fully "booked", every table has already been reserved, so you cannot get in without a booking.
questions.meaning: reserved ahead of time
questions.example: We booked a table for eight o'clock.

questions.prompt: Please leave a ___ for the staff if service was good. (extra money)
questions.explanation: A "tip" is the extra money you leave for the staff when the service was good, which matches the clue.
questions.meaning: extra money for good service
questions.example: Leave a tip if the service was good.

questions.prompt: Enjoy your ___!
questions.explanation: "dinner" completes the sentence "Enjoy your dinner!"; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: the main meal in the evening

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "Enjoy your dinner!"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: Leave a tip if the service was good.
choices: Leave a receipt if the service was good.
Leave a deposit if the service was good.
Leave a tip if the service was good.
Leave a discount if the service was good.
questions.answer: Leave a tip if the service was good.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Leave a tip if the service was good."

questions.prompt: Say thank you to the waiter and ask for the bill.
acceptableAnswers: Thank you. Could we have the bill, please?
Thanks. Can we have the bill, please?
Thank you. The bill, please.
Thank you. Could I have the bill, please?
Thank you. Can I have the bill, please?
Thank you. Could we get the bill, please?
Thanks. Could we have the bill, please?
Thank you very much. Could we have the bill, please?
Thank you. May I have the bill, please?
Thank you. Could I get the bill, please?
Thanks. Can I have the bill, please?
Thank you. Could we have the bill?
Thank you. Can we have the bill?
Thank you. Could we have the check, please?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Thank you. Could we have the bill, please?"

units.title: Adverbs of Frequency
units.description: How often things happen — Match each frequency adverb to how often it means something happens.

questions.prompt: How often does "always" happen?
questions.explanation: "Always" means "every single time, without exception". The other options all describe something that happens rarely or never.
questions.meaning: every time, without exception
questions.example: I always brush my teeth at night.

questions.prompt: How often does "usually" happen? ___
bank: the great majority of the time
questions.answer: the great majority of the time
questions.explanation: "Usually" means it happens "the great majority of the time", so most of the time but not always. The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: most of the time
questions.example: I usually walk to work.

questions.prompt: How often does "normally" happen?
choices: as a rule, under typical conditions
questions.explanation: "Normally" means "as a rule, under typical conditions", so what happens most of the time. The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: usually; in the usual way
questions.example: We normally eat dinner at seven.

questions.prompt: How often does "generally" happen? ___
questions.explanation: "Generally" means "in most cases", so most of the time. The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: in most cases
questions.example: It is generally quiet here at night.

questions.prompt: How often does "frequently" happen?
questions.explanation: "Frequently" means "on many separate occasions", so very often. The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: very often; many times
questions.example: He frequently visits his grandmother.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: How often do you brush your teeth
questions.explanation: Correct order: "How often do you brush your teeth"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: I always brush my teeth at night.
choices: I often brush my teeth at night.
I always brush my teeth at night.
I never brush my teeth at night.
I always brush my hair at night.
questions.answer: I always brush my teeth at night.
questions.explanation: The audio says "I always brush my teeth at night."

questions.prompt: Say that you never eat breakfast.
acceptableAnswers: I never eat breakfast.
I never have breakfast.
I don't ever eat breakfast.
I never eat my breakfast.
I don't eat breakfast.
I never have my breakfast.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I never eat breakfast."

questions.prompt: How often does "often" happen? ___
questions.explanation: "Often" means "quite a lot, many times". The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: many times; not rarely
questions.example: She often calls her mother.

questions.prompt: How often does "regularly" happen?
questions.explanation: "Regularly" means "at fixed, repeated intervals", such as every week. The other options all mean rarely or never.
questions.meaning: again and again, at fixed times
questions.example: I regularly go to the gym.

questions.prompt: How often does "sometimes" happen? ___
bank: on certain occasions but not most
questions.answer: on certain occasions but not most
questions.explanation: "Sometimes" means it happens on some occasions but not most of the time, so the answer is "on certain occasions but not most".
questions.meaning: on some occasions, but not always
questions.example: Sometimes we eat out on Fridays.

questions.prompt: How often does "occasionally" happen?
choices: now and then, but not often
questions.explanation: "Occasionally" means something happens now and then but not often, so the answer is "now and then, but not often".
questions.meaning: now and then; not often
questions.example: We occasionally go to the cinema.

questions.prompt: How often does "periodically" happen? ___
questions.explanation: periodically → at intervals, coming and going. Frequency adverbs matched to how often they mean.
questions.meaning: from time to time, at intervals
questions.example: I check my email periodically.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: How often does she call her mother
questions.explanation: Correct order: "How often does she call her mother"

questions.prompt: Would you like to ___ out for dinner tonight?

questions.explanation: "I'm" needs an -ing form, and the present continuous is used for a plan already arranged, so "going" is correct. "Go", "went" and "goes" don't follow "I'm".

questions.meaning: to come together with someone
questions.example: Let's meet at the cinema at seven.

units.title: Prepositions of Place
units.description: Where things are — A2-level prepositions describing location.

questions.prompt: The cat is sitting ___ the table. (below it)
questions.explanation: The clue says the cat is below the table, and "under" means in a lower position directly beneath something. "Above" means higher than it.
questions.meaning: in a lower place than

questions.prompt: The vase stands ___ the shelf. (the shelf holds it up)
questions.explanation: The shelf holds the vase up, so the vase rests on its top surface, and "on" means touching and supported by a surface. "In", "under" and "behind" would put it somewhere else.
questions.meaning: touching the top of

questions.prompt: She is standing ___ the door. (hidden on the other side of it)
questions.explanation: The clue says she is hidden on the other side of the door, and "behind" means at the back of something, out of sight. "In front of" would put her on the visible side.
questions.meaning: at the back of

questions.prompt: The keys are ___ the drawer. (inside it)
questions.explanation: The clue "inside it" means the keys are within the drawer, and "in" is the preposition for being inside something. "Near", "above" and "under" do not mean inside.
questions.meaning: inside a room or place

questions.prompt: The park is ___ the school and the shop. (in the middle of the two)
questions.explanation: The clue says the park is in the middle of two places, and "between" is used for something with one thing on each side. "Opposite" means facing, not in the middle.
questions.meaning: in the middle of two things

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: The keys are in the drawer
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The keys are in the drawer."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: The cat is sitting under the table.
choices: The cat is sitting above the table.
The cat is sitting behind the table.
The cat is sitting under the table.
The cat is sitting beside the table.
questions.answer: The cat is sitting under the table.
questions.explanation: The audio says "The cat is sitting under the table."

questions.prompt: Say that the book is on the desk.
acceptableAnswers: The book is on the desk.
The book is on top of the desk.
The book is lying on the desk.
The book is on my desk.
The book is sitting on the desk.
The book lies on the desk.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The book is on the desk."

questions.prompt: He is sitting ___ to his sister.
questions.explanation: The words after the blank are "to his sister", and only "next" makes the fixed phrase "next to" meaning 'at his side'. "Beside" never takes "to" and "far" needs "from".
questions.meaning: beside; used in "next to"

questions.prompt: The picture is hanging ___ the wall. (touching it)
questions.explanation: The clue says the picture is touching the wall, and "against" means in contact with a surface. "Near", "behind" and "in front of" do not require touching.
questions.meaning: touching and leaning on something
questions.example: The ladder is leaning against the wall.

questions.prompt: The dog is running ___ the garden. (in circles)
questions.explanation: The clue "in circles" describes a circular path, which is what "around" expresses. "Through" and "across" mean going from one side to the other, and "into" means entering.
questions.meaning: moving in a circle or on all sides

questions.prompt: The shop is right ___ the corner. (just past the bend)
questions.explanation: "round" fits here. Rule to remember: A2-level prepositions describing location.
questions.meaning: another word for "around"

questions.prompt: She parked the car ___ the building. (not inside it)
questions.explanation: The clue says the car is not inside, so "outside" is right. "Inside" and "in" mean the opposite, and "between" needs two things.
questions.meaning: not inside

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: The shop is right round the corner
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The shop is right round the corner."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: The ladder is leaning against the wall.
choices: The ladder is leaning against the wall.
The ladder is leaning near the wall.
The ladder is leaning against the door.
The ladder is leaning behind the wall.
questions.answer: The ladder is leaning against the wall.
questions.explanation: The audio says "The ladder is leaning against the wall."

questions.prompt: Say that the ball is between the chairs.
acceptableAnswers: The ball is between the chairs.
The ball is in between the chairs.
The ball is between the two chairs.
questions.explanation: Use "between" when something has one thing on each side of it: "The ball is between the chairs."

questions.prompt: The ball rolled ___ the stairs. (from the top to the bottom)
questions.explanation: The ball moves from the top of the stairs to the bottom, and "down" means moving to a lower place. "Up" goes the other way, while "over" and "across" do not describe moving along stairs.
questions.meaning: from a high place to a low place

questions.prompt: The balloon floated ___ the village. (higher than the houses)
questions.explanation: The clue says the balloon is higher than the houses, and "above" means at a higher level. "Below" means lower, and "among" and "in" do not describe being higher.
questions.meaning: higher than

questions.prompt: The cat hid ___ the sofa cushions. (underneath them)
questions.explanation: The clue says the cat is underneath the cushions, and "beneath" means under. "Above", "behind" and "beside" give different positions.
questions.meaning: under or below

questions.prompt: The children are playing ___ the swings. (next to them)
questions.explanation: The clue "next to them" means at the side of the swings, which is what "by" means. "Among" means in the middle of them, and "under" and "inside" give other positions.
questions.meaning: close to the side of

questions.prompt: The bridge goes ___ the river.
questions.explanation: A bridge crosses above the water from one bank to the other, and "over" means above and across. "Through", "down" and "into" do not describe crossing from above.
questions.meaning: above and across

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: The children are playing by the swings
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The children are playing by the swings."

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: The bridge goes over the river.
choices: The bridge goes through the river.
The bridge goes down the river.
The bridge goes over the river.
The bridge goes into the river.
questions.answer: The bridge goes over the river.
questions.explanation: The audio says "The bridge goes over the river."

questions.prompt: Say that the lamp is above the sofa.

questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The lamp is above the sofa."

questions.prompt: The bank is ___ the café. (on the other side of the street, facing it)
questions.explanation: The clue says the bank is on the other side of the street, facing the café, which is what "opposite" means. "Next to" and "near" mean beside or close, and "behind" means at the back.
questions.meaning: across from

questions.prompt: He walked ___ the room and sat down. (entered it)
questions.explanation: The clue "entered it" and sitting down show he went from outside to inside, which "into" expresses. "Through" and "across" mean passing over or out the other side, and "onto" means moving on top of a surface.
questions.meaning: moving to the inside of

questions.prompt: The lamp is ___ the desk. (right next to it)
questions.explanation: The clue "right next to it" means at the side of the desk, so "beside" fits; "under" and "behind" give other positions, and "opposite" means facing it.
questions.meaning: at the side of

questions.prompt: She placed the vase ___ the window. (close to it, not touching)
questions.explanation: The clue "close to it, not touching" describes a short distance away, which is what "near" means. "On", "against" and "in" (on the windowsill) all put the vase at or touching the window.
questions.meaning: not far from

questions.prompt: The tunnel goes ___ the mountain. (from one side to the other, inside it)
questions.explanation: The tunnel goes inside the mountain from one side to the other, and "through" describes movement from one end to the other inside something; "over" and "around" stay outside it.
questions.meaning: from one end to the other

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The children walk to school"

questions.prompt: Say that the school is next to the church.

questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The school is next to the church."

questions.prompt: The cinema is ___ the shopping center. (within the building)
questions.explanation: The clue "within the building" means in the inner part of the shopping center, so "inside" is right; "outside" is the opposite, and "behind" and "opposite" describe positions around it.
questions.meaning: in the inner part of
questions.example: The cinema is inside the shopping center.

questions.prompt: He stood ___ the crowd, watching. (in the middle of the people)
questions.explanation: The clue "in the middle of the people" shows he is surrounded by the group, which is what "among" means; "behind", "beside" and "in front of" place him outside the crowd.
questions.meaning: in the middle of a group

questions.prompt: The car is parked ___ the garage. (next to it, not inside)
questions.explanation: The clue "next to it, not inside" means the car is parked at the side of the garage, so "alongside" fits; "in" and "inside" put it in the garage, and "behind" is at the back.
questions.meaning: next to and in line with

questions.prompt: The plane flew ___ the city. (it went by without stopping)
questions.explanation: The clue "it went by without stopping" means the plane moved by the city, and "past" means going by something; "into" and "onto" mean entering or landing, and "towards" gives only the direction.
questions.meaning: by and beyond something
questions.example: We walked past the school on our way home.

questions.prompt: The path leads ___ the forest. (it stops before the first trees)
questions.explanation: The clue "it stops before the first trees" means the path only goes in the direction of the forest without entering, so "towards" fits; "into" and "through" mean entering, and "onto" means reaching a surface.
questions.meaning: in the direction of

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.answer: The car is parked alongside the garage
questions.explanation: Correct order: "The car is parked alongside the garage."

acceptableAnswers: The dog is lying under the tree.
The dog is under the tree.
The dog lies under the tree.
The dog is lying beneath the tree.
The dog is lying down under the tree.
The dog is resting under the tree.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The dog is lying under the tree."

units.title: Past Continuous

lessons.title: Past Continuous 1

questions.prompt: I was ___ TV when the phone rang.
questions.explanation: "watching" completes the sentence "I was watching TV when the phone rang."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: looking at something moving

questions.prompt: They were ___ soccer when it started to rain.
questions.explanation: After "were" the past continuous needs the -ing form, so "playing" fits the action in progress when it started to rain; "play", "played" and "plays" cannot follow "were" here.
questions.meaning: taking part in a game
questions.example: They were playing soccer when it started to rain.

questions.prompt: She was ___ dinner when I arrived home.
questions.explanation: "cooking" completes the sentence "She was cooking dinner when I arrived home."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: preparing food by heating it

questions.prompt: We were ___ when the teacher walked in.
questions.explanation: The past continuous uses "were" + verb-ing for an action in progress when the teacher walked in, so "talking" is right; "talk", "talked" and "talks" cannot follow "were".
questions.meaning: speaking with someone

questions.prompt: He was ___ when the alarm went off.
questions.explanation: The past continuous is "was" + verb-ing, so after "He was" you need "sleeping". The alarm interrupted an action that was already in progress.
questions.meaning: resting your body and mind, not awake

questions.prompt: We were ___ in the park when it began to snow.
questions.explanation: After "We were" you need the -ing form, so "walking" is right. The snow began in the middle of the walk.
questions.meaning: going on foot

questions.prompt: He was ___ when the power went out.
questions.explanation: "was" + verb-ing forms the past continuous, so "working" fits. The power cut interrupted his work in progress.
questions.meaning: doing a job

questions.explanation: Correct order: "She was studying English"

lessons.title: Past Continuous 3

questions.prompt: I was ___ for the bus when it started to rain.
questions.explanation: The past continuous is "was" + verb-ing, so "waiting" is correct. The rain started while the waiting was already going on.
questions.meaning: staying until something comes
questions.example: I was waiting for the bus in the rain.

questions.prompt: They were ___ dinner when the doorbell rang.
questions.explanation: After "were" the past continuous needs the -ing form, so "having" is right ("having dinner" means eating dinner). The doorbell interrupted the meal.
questions.meaning: eating; used in "having dinner"

questions.prompt: She was ___ to music when I knocked.
questions.explanation: "was" + verb-ing makes the past continuous, so "listening" is correct. Your knock interrupted her listening to music.
questions.meaning: paying attention to a sound

questions.prompt: We were ___ when we bumped into an old friend.
questions.explanation: After "We were" you need the -ing form, so "shopping" fits. The meeting with the friend happened during the shopping.
questions.meaning: buying things in shops

questions.prompt: He was ___ when he twisted his ankle.
questions.explanation: The past continuous is "was" + verb-ing, and "jog" doubles its g, giving "jogging". The ankle injury happened during the run.
questions.meaning: running slowly for exercise

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "They were having dinner"

questions.meaning: putting words on paper or a screen

questions.prompt: They were ___ when the storm began.
questions.explanation: After "were" the past continuous needs the -ing form, and "were swimming" shows the action in progress when the storm began, so "swimming" is right.
questions.meaning: moving through water

questions.prompt: She was ___ when the microphone stopped working.
questions.explanation: The past continuous is "was" plus the -ing verb, and the microphone failing interrupted her singing in progress, so "singing" is right.
questions.meaning: making music with your voice

questions.prompt: We were ___ when the tent collapsed.
questions.explanation: "Were" must be followed by an -ing verb to show the action in progress when the tent collapsed, so "camping" is right.
questions.meaning: sleeping outside in a tent

questions.prompt: He was ___ the fence when it started to rain.
questions.explanation: The past continuous ("was" + -ing) describes the painting that was in progress when the rain started, so "painting" is right.
questions.meaning: covering a surface with color

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "We were camping"

lessons.title: Past Continuous 5

questions.explanation: The past continuous is "was" plus -ing, describing what she was doing when she slipped, so "dancing" is right.
questions.meaning: moving to music

questions.prompt: We were ___ when the lights suddenly went out.
questions.explanation: "Were" is followed by an -ing verb to show the chat was in progress when the lights went out, so "chatting" is right.
questions.meaning: talking in a friendly way

questions.prompt: He was ___ his bike when he saw the accident.
questions.explanation: "Was" needs an -ing verb to show he was in the middle of cycling when he saw the accident, so "riding" is right.

units.title: Modal Verbs — Ability & Permission
units.description: Can, could, may — A2-level modal verbs for ability and permission.

questions.prompt: I ___ swim very well when I was younger.
questions.explanation: "When I was younger" refers to the past, and "could" is the past form of "can" for general ability, so "could" is right.
questions.meaning: the past of "can"; was able to

questions.prompt: ___ I open the window, please? (asking for permission)
questions.explanation: "May I...?" is the polite way to ask permission, while "will", "would" and "must" do not make a permission question here, so "may" is right.
questions.meaning: used to ask permission politely

questions.prompt: She ___ speak three languages fluently. (she has the skill)
questions.explanation: The clue "she has the skill" points to present ability, which is expressed with "can"; "must", "might" and "would" do not state ability, so "can" is right.
questions.meaning: is able to

questions.prompt: ___ you help me carry this bag? (a polite request)
questions.explanation: "could" is the polite way to ask someone to do something for you; "must" gives an order, and "shall" and "might" do not form a request with "you".

questions.prompt: We ___ leave early if we finish the work. (it is possible)
questions.explanation: "can" expresses that something is possible or allowed; "must" and "mustn't" express obligation or prohibition, and "would" does not fit this present, real condition.

questions.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence.
questions.explanation: Correct order: "I can ride a bike"

questions.prompt: Which sentence did you hear?
questions.audioText: She can speak three languages fluently.
choices: She can speak three languages fluently.
She must speak three languages fluently.
She would speak three languages fluently.
She might speak three languages fluently.
questions.answer: She can speak three languages fluently.
questions.explanation: The audio says "She can speak three languages fluently."

questions.prompt: Say that you can play the piano.
acceptableAnswers: I can play the piano.
I am able to play the piano.
I know how to play the piano.
I can play piano.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I can play the piano."

questions.prompt: ___ I use your phone for a moment? (asking for permission)
questions.explanation: "may" is the polite modal for asking permission with "I"; "will" and "would" don't ask permission with "I", and "must" expresses obligation.
questions.meaning: used to ask permission politely

questions.prompt: He ___ ride a bike when he was five.
questions.explanation: "could" is the past of "can" for ability, and "when he was five" shows the past, so "can" doesn't fit.
questions.meaning: the past of "can"

questions.prompt: You ___ park here because it's not allowed.
questions.explanation: "can't" means something is not allowed or not possible, which matches "it's not allowed"; "can" and "may" would say the opposite.
questions.meaning: short for cannot

questions.prompt: ___ I ask you a question? (asking for permission)
questions.explanation: "may" is the polite modal for asking permission with "I"; "will" and "would" don't ask permission with "I", and "must" expresses obligation.

questions.prompt: They ___ not attend the meeting yesterday.
questions.explanation: "could" fits here. Rule to remember: A2-level modal verbs for ability and permission.

questions.answer: She moved here ten years ago.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "She moved here ten years ago." Use the past simple with "ago" to say how long before now something happened.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We are meeting at the cafe later.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We are meeting at the cafe later." The present continuous with "later" talks about a plan you have already arranged.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I forgot to bring my umbrella.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I forgot to bring my umbrella." Use "forgot to" plus a verb to say you didn't do something you meant to do.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Do you know when the shop opens?
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Do you know when the shop opens?" After "Do you know", use statement word order ("the shop opens"), not "when does the shop open".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: My flight was delayed by an hour.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "My flight was delayed by an hour." "Was delayed" is passive, and "by an hour" says how late the flight was.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would rather stay at home tonight.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I would rather stay at home tonight." Use "would rather" plus the base verb ("stay") to say what you prefer to do.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "He finished his homework already." Everyday phrases for asking, arranging and explaining.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Can I pay by card here?
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Can I pay by card here?" Use "Can I...?" to ask if something is allowed, and "by card" to say how you pay ("by" also goes with cash and phone).

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The film was better than I expected.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "The film was better than I expected." "Better" is the comparative of "good", and "than I expected" compares the film with what you thought before.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am trying to eat less sugar.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I am trying to eat less sugar." Use "trying to" + verb for something you are working at, and "less" with uncountable nouns like sugar.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We walked all the way to the river.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We walked all the way to the river." "All the way to" shows you went the whole distance, often further than expected.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: She is studying to be a nurse.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "She is studying to be a nurse." "Studying to be" + a job says what someone is training for.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I have never been to Italy.
questions.explanation: "I have never been to Italy." uses the present perfect with "never" to talk about life experience; we say "been to" a place, not "gone to".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Would you like to join us?
questions.explanation: "Would you like to join us?" is a polite way to invite someone; "Would you like to" is followed by the base verb.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.explanation: "The train was completely full." uses "completely" to stress that there was no space left at all.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I need to book a room for one night.
questions.explanation: "I need to book a room for one night." uses "book" to mean reserve, and "for" to give the length of the stay.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: He works from home on Fridays.
questions.explanation: "He works from home on Fridays." uses the present simple for a regular routine; note "on Fridays" for days and "from home" with no article.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We should leave before it gets dark.
questions.explanation: "We should leave before it gets dark." uses "should" to give advice, and the present "gets" after "before" even though it refers to the future.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I left my bag on the bus.
questions.explanation: "I left my bag on the bus." uses "left" (past of leave) to mean forgot it somewhere; we say "on the bus", not "in the bus".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: This jacket is a little too small.
questions.explanation: "This jacket is a little too small." uses "a little" to soften "too small", which makes it a polite way to complain in a shop.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: They are building a new library.
questions.explanation: "They are building a new library." uses the present continuous for a project that is happening around now.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I will call you when I arrive.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I will call you when I arrive." After "when" we use the present simple ("arrive"), not "will", even though we are talking about the future.

units.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done
units.description: Write the idea in English — Everyday errands and arrangements, with more than one right way to say it.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done 1
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Ask what time a shop opens.
acceptableAnswers: What time does the shop open?
When does the shop open?
Could you tell me what time the shop opens?
questions.explanation: "What time does the shop open?" uses "does" with the base verb "open"; in the polite "Could you tell me..." version, the word order changes to "the shop opens".

questions.prompt: Say you went to the market yesterday.
acceptableAnswers: I went to the market yesterday.
Yesterday I went to the market.
I was at the market yesterday.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I went to the market yesterday." "Yesterday" is a finished time, so use the past simple "went" (the past of "go").

questions.prompt: Ask a neighbor to water your plants while you are away.
acceptableAnswers: Could you water my plants while I am away?
Would you mind watering my plants while I'm away?
Can you look after my plants while I am away?
questions.explanation: "Could you water my plants while I am away?" is a polite request; you can also say "Would you mind" followed by the -ing form, "watering".

questions.prompt: Say you have never been to Italy.
acceptableAnswers: I have never been to Italy.
I have never visited Italy.
I have not been to Italy before.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I have never been to Italy." Use the present perfect with "never" for something that has not happened at any time in your life.

questions.prompt: Ask whether you can pay by card.
acceptableAnswers: Can I pay by card?
Do you take cards?
Is it possible to pay by card?
questions.explanation: "Can I pay by card?" asks for permission with "Can I"; note the preposition "by card", not "with card".

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done 2
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say your train was delayed.
acceptableAnswers: My train was delayed.
The train was late.
My train ran late.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "My train was delayed." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Offer to help someone with their bags.
acceptableAnswers: Can I help you with your bags?
Would you like some help with your bags?
Let me help you with those bags.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Can I help you with your bags?" Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say you would rather stay at home tonight.
acceptableAnswers: I would rather stay at home tonight.
I'd rather stay in tonight.
I would prefer to stay home tonight.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would rather stay at home tonight." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Ask where you can find a pharmacy.
acceptableAnswers: Where can I find a pharmacy?
Is there a pharmacy near here?
Could you tell me where the pharmacy is?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Where can I find a pharmacy?" Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say you forgot your umbrella.
acceptableAnswers: I forgot my umbrella.
I left my umbrella behind.
I have forgotten my umbrella.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I forgot my umbrella." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done 3
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Ask someone to call you later.
acceptableAnswers: Could you call me later?
Can you ring me later?
Please call me later.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Could you call me later?" Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say the film was better than you expected.
acceptableAnswers: The film was better than I expected.
The film was better than I thought.
I enjoyed the film more than I expected.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The film was better than I expected." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say you are looking for the post office.
acceptableAnswers: I am looking for the post office.
I am trying to find the post office.
Could you point me to the post office?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am looking for the post office." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Ask how long the journey takes.
acceptableAnswers: How long does the journey take?
How long is the journey?
How much time does the trip take?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "How long does the journey take?" Use "How long...?" to ask about time, with "does...take" because "the journey" is singular.

questions.prompt: Say you booked a room for one night.
acceptableAnswers: I booked a room for one night.
I have booked a room for one night.
I reserved a room for one night.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I booked a room for one night." "Book" means arrange a room in advance, and "for one night" says how long you will stay.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done 4
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Apologize for missing the meeting.
acceptableAnswers: I am sorry I missed the meeting.
Sorry for missing the meeting.
My apologies for not making the meeting.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am sorry I missed the meeting." Use "I am sorry" plus what happened in the past simple ("missed") to apologize for something you did not do.

questions.prompt: Ask whether the seat is free.
acceptableAnswers: Is this seat free?
Is anyone sitting here?
May I sit here?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Is this seat free?" Use "this seat" for the one next to you, and "free" here means no one is using it.

questions.prompt: Say you are trying to eat less sugar.
acceptableAnswers: I am trying to eat less sugar.
I'm trying to cut down on sugar.
I am eating less sugar these days.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am trying to eat less sugar." "Trying to" shows an effort that is still going on, and "less" goes with uncountable nouns like "sugar".

questions.prompt: Ask someone what they did on the weekend.
acceptableAnswers: What did you do on the weekend?
How was your weekend?
What did you get up to on the weekend?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "What did you do on the weekend?" Use the past simple question "What did you do...?" for a finished time.

questions.prompt: Say the jacket is a little too small.
acceptableAnswers: This jacket is a little too small.
The jacket is slightly too small.
This jacket is a bit small for me.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "This jacket is a little too small." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Getting Things Done 5
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say you will call when you arrive.
acceptableAnswers: I will call you when I arrive.
I'll call when I get there.
I am going to call you when I arrive.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I will call you when I arrive." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Ask whether breakfast is included.
acceptableAnswers: Is breakfast included?
Does the price include breakfast?
Is breakfast part of the price?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Is breakfast included?" Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say that you went on foot from the start of the journey right to the river.
acceptableAnswers: We walked all the way to the river.
We walked the whole way to the river.
We went all the way to the river on foot.
questions.explanation: "We walked all the way to the river." uses "all the way" to show you went on foot for the whole journey, from start to finish.

questions.prompt: Ask someone to repeat the address.
acceptableAnswers: Could you repeat the address?
Can you say the address again?
Please repeat the address.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Could you repeat the address?" Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

questions.prompt: Say you are studying to be a nurse.
acceptableAnswers: I am studying to be a nurse.
I'm training to be a nurse.
I am studying nursing.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am studying to be a nurse." Everyday errands and arrangements, more than one wording.

units.title: Phrasal Verbs
units.description: Meaning match — Phrasal verbs rarely mean the sum of their parts.

questions.prompt: "give up" means:
questions.explanation: "give up" means "stop trying": when you give up, you stop making an effort, usually because something feels too hard.
questions.meaning: stop trying to do something
questions.example: I never give up on my dreams.

questions.prompt: "look after" means: ___
questions.explanation: "Look after" someone or something means you "take care of" them, for example a child, a pet or a house.
questions.meaning: to take care of someone or something
questions.example: She looks after her little brother.

questions.prompt: "put off" means:
questions.explanation: "put off" means "postpone": you move something to a later time, as in 'We put off the meeting until Friday.'
questions.meaning: to move something to a later time
questions.example: We had to put off the meeting.

questions.prompt: "run out of" means: ___
questions.explanation: "run out of" means "have none left": you have used all of something, as in 'We've run out of milk.'
questions.meaning: to use all of something
questions.example: We run out of milk every week.

questions.prompt: "turn down" means:
questions.explanation: "turn down" an offer means "reject" it, as in 'He turned down the job.'
questions.meaning: to say no to an offer
questions.example: He turned down the job offer.

questions.prompt: "find out" means: ___
questions.explanation: "find out" means "discover": you learn a fact you did not know, as in 'I found out the truth.'
questions.meaning: to learn a fact you did not know
questions.example: Please find out the answer.

questions.prompt: "get on with" means:
questions.explanation: "get on with" a person means "have a good relationship with" them, as in 'I get on with my colleagues.'
questions.meaning: to be friendly with someone
questions.example: I get on with my new colleagues.

questions.prompt: "bring up" means: ___
questions.explanation: When you "bring up" a subject, you start talking about it, so it means "raise a topic".
questions.meaning: to start talking about a subject
questions.example: Don't bring up that subject again.

questions.prompt: "call off" means:
questions.explanation: If you "call off" an event such as a match or meeting, you decide it will not happen, so it means "cancel".
questions.meaning: to decide an event will not happen
questions.example: They called off the match because of rain.

questions.prompt: "come across" means: ___
questions.explanation: If you "come across" something, you find it without looking for it, so it means "find by chance".
questions.meaning: to meet or find by chance
questions.example: You may come across old photos there.

questions.prompt: "carry on" means: ___
questions.explanation: "carry on" means "continue": you keep doing something, as in 'Carry on with your work.'
questions.meaning: to keep doing something without stopping
questions.example: Please carry on with your work.

questions.prompt: "break down" means:
questions.explanation: "break down" means "stop working": when a machine or car breaks down, it stops working, as in 'My car broke down on the highway.'
questions.meaning: to stop working, like a machine
questions.example: I hope the car won't break down.

questions.prompt: "look into" means: ___
questions.explanation: "look into" means "investigate": you study a problem to find the cause, as in 'Police will look into the crime.'
questions.meaning: to study a problem to learn the cause
questions.example: The police will look into the crime.

questions.prompt: "take over" means:
questions.explanation: "take over" means "assume control": you start to be in charge, as in 'She will take over the company.'
questions.meaning: to begin to be in charge
questions.example: She will take over the company next year.

questions.prompt: "put up with" means: ___
questions.explanation: "put up with" means "tolerate": you accept something unpleasant without complaining, as in 'I can't put up with this noise.'
questions.meaning: to accept something bad without complaining
questions.example: I can't put up with this noise.

questions.prompt: "set up" means:
questions.explanation: "set up" means "establish": you set up a business or a system when you start it, as in 'They set up a small shop.'
questions.meaning: to start a business or a system
questions.example: They set up a small shop.

questions.prompt: "work out" means: ___
questions.explanation: "work out" can mean "solve or exercise": you work out a puzzle (solve it), or you work out at the gym (exercise).
questions.meaning: to find the answer to a problem
questions.example: I can't work out this puzzle.

questions.prompt: "turn up" means:
questions.explanation: "turn up" here means "arrive", often late or unexpectedly, as in 'He turned up an hour late.'
questions.meaning: to come to a place, often late
questions.example: He turned up an hour late.

questions.prompt: "let down" means: ___
questions.explanation: If you let someone down, you fail to do what they hoped, so "let down" means "disappoint", as in 'Please don't let me down.'
questions.meaning: to make someone feel disappointed
questions.example: Please don't let me down.

questions.prompt: "pick up" means:
questions.explanation: "pick up" means "collect" when you go and get someone or something, as in 'I'll pick up the children at four.'
questions.meaning: to go and get someone or something
questions.example: I'll pick up the children at four.

questions.prompt: "go over" means:
questions.explanation: To go over something is to check it carefully again, so "go over" means "review", as in 'Let's go over the plan once more.'
questions.meaning: to check something carefully again
questions.example: Let's go over the plan once more.

questions.prompt: "hold on" means: ___
questions.explanation: "Hold on" is an everyday way to ask someone to "wait" for a short time, as in 'Hold on, I'll be right back.'
questions.meaning: to wait for a short time
questions.example: Hold on, I'll be right back.

questions.prompt: "sort out" means:
questions.explanation: To sort out a problem is to deal with it and fix it, so "sort out" means "resolve", as in 'We must sort out this mistake.'
questions.meaning: to deal with a problem and fix it
questions.example: We must sort out this mistake.

questions.prompt: "cut down on" means: ___
questions.explanation: To cut down on something is to use or do less of it, so "cut down on" means "reduce", as in 'I'm trying to cut down on sugar.'
questions.meaning: to use or do less of something
questions.example: I'm trying to cut down on sugar.

questions.prompt: "look forward to" means:
questions.explanation: "look forward to" means "anticipate happily": you wait for something with pleasure, as in 'I look forward to the holidays.'
questions.meaning: to wait for something with pleasure
questions.example: I look forward to the holidays.

units.title: Conditionals
units.description: If-clauses — First conditional: if + present, will. Second: if + past, would.

questions.prompt: If it rains, we ___ stay home.
questions.explanation: 'If it rains' uses the present simple for a likely future event, so the result clause takes "will". 'Would' is for unreal situations, and 'am' and 'worked' do not fit before 'stay'.
questions.meaning: shows a likely result in the future
questions.example: If it rains, we will stay at home.

questions.prompt: If we ___ closer, I'd visit more often.
questions.explanation: The result clause 'I'd visit' (would) shows this is an unreal, imagined situation, so the 'if' clause needs the past form "were". 'Would' and 'will' cannot follow 'if' here, and 'is' does not match 'we'.
questions.meaning: a form of be for unreal situations
questions.example: If the weather were better, we'd go out more.

questions.prompt: She'd help if she ___ time.
questions.explanation: The result clause "She'd help" (would) signals an unreal present situation, so the if-clause takes the past form "had".
questions.meaning: the past of have, used in unreal ifs
questions.example: She'd help if she had time.

questions.prompt: If you heat ice, it ___.
questions.explanation: Ice melting is a general fact, so both clauses use the present simple: "melts" follows "If you heat ice".
questions.meaning: changes from solid to liquid with heat
questions.example: If you heat ice, it melts.

questions.prompt: I'll call you if I ___ late.
questions.explanation: "I'll call you" is a real future possibility, so the if-clause uses the present simple, and "am" is the form that goes with "I".
questions.meaning: a form of be used with I
questions.example: I'll call you if I am late.

questions.prompt: If he studied, he ___ pass.
questions.explanation: "If he studied" is a past form used for an unreal present situation, so the result clause needs "would".
questions.meaning: shows an unreal result in the present
questions.example: If he studied, he would pass.

questions.prompt: Unless you hurry, you ___ miss it.
questions.explanation: The "unless" clause uses the present ("hurry"), so this is a first conditional and the result needs "will" plus the bare verb: "will miss".
questions.meaning: shows a future result that depends on something
questions.example: Unless you hurry, you will miss it.

questions.prompt: If I ___ you, I'd apologize.
questions.explanation: "were" fits here. Rule to remember: First conditional: if + present, will. Second: if + past, would.
questions.meaning: a form of be used for advice
questions.example: If I were you, I'd apologize.

questions.prompt: What would you do if you ___ the lottery?
questions.explanation: "What would you do" shows an imagined situation, so the if-clause takes the past simple "won".
questions.meaning: came first in a game or contest
questions.example: What would you do if you won the lottery?

questions.prompt: If they leave now, they ___ arrive by six.
questions.explanation: "If they leave now" uses the present simple for a real possibility, so the likely result takes "will".
questions.meaning: shows a likely future result
questions.example: If they leave now, they will arrive by six.

questions.prompt: I wouldn't do that if I ___ you.
questions.explanation: "were" fits here. Rule to remember: First conditional: if + present, will. Second: if + past, would.
questions.meaning: a way to give advice
questions.example: I wouldn't do that if I were you.

questions.prompt: If she ___ harder, she'd succeed.
questions.explanation: "she'd succeed" (would) shows an unreal present situation, so the if-clause uses the past simple "tried".
questions.meaning: made an effort to do something
questions.example: If she tried harder, she'd succeed.

questions.prompt: We'll go out if the weather ___ good.
questions.explanation: "We'll go out" is a real future possibility, so the if-clause uses the present simple "is".
questions.meaning: the form of be with he, she, it
questions.example: We'll go out if the weather is good.

questions.prompt: If I had known, I ___ have come.
questions.explanation: "If I had known" is a past unreal condition, so the result takes "would" plus "have come".
questions.meaning: shows an imagined result, not a real one
questions.example: If I had known, I would have come.

questions.prompt: He would be happier if he ___ less and relaxed more.
questions.explanation: The "would be" in the result clause signals a second conditional, so the if-clause takes the past simple: "worked" less. It describes an unreal, imagined situation.
questions.meaning: spent time doing a job
questions.example: He would be happier if he worked less.

questions.prompt: If you don't water plants, they ___ .
questions.explanation: This states a general fact, so both clauses use the present simple: if you don't water plants, they "die". "will" would need 'will die'.
questions.meaning: stop living; the opposite of live
questions.example: If you don't water plants, they die.

questions.prompt: I'd tell you if I ___ the answer.
questions.explanation: The result clause "I'd tell" is a second conditional, so the if-clause needs the past simple: if I "knew" the answer. "would" and "will" cannot follow "if" here.
questions.meaning: had information in your mind
questions.example: I'd tell you if I knew.

questions.prompt: If the shop ___ open, buy milk.
questions.explanation: An instruction like 'buy milk' goes with a real, possible condition, so the if-clause uses the present simple: if the shop "is" open. We don't use "will be" after "if" here, and "were" would make the situation unreal.
questions.meaning: the form of be with he, she, it
questions.example: If the shop is open, buy milk.

questions.prompt: She'll be angry if you ___ her.
questions.explanation: "She'll be angry" is a first conditional result, so the if-clause uses the present simple: if you "tell" her. We don't use "will tell" after "if" here, and "told" or "would tell" belong to unreal conditionals.
questions.meaning: to give information to someone
questions.example: She'll be angry if you tell her.

questions.prompt: If we ___ earlier, we'd have seen it.
questions.explanation: "we'd have seen" is a third conditional result about the past, so the if-clause needs the past perfect: if we "had left" earlier.
questions.meaning: the past perfect of leave
questions.example: If we had left earlier, we'd have seen it.

questions.prompt: Provided you pay, we ___ deliver.
questions.explanation: "Provided" works like 'if' in a first conditional, so the result clause uses "will": provided you pay, we "will" deliver.
questions.meaning: shows a result that depends on a condition
questions.example: Provided you pay, we will deliver.

questions.prompt: If only I ___ speak Spanish.
questions.explanation: "If only" expresses a wish about the present, so it takes a past form: "could" + 'speak'. "can" and "will" are not past forms, and "were" cannot be followed by a bare verb.
questions.meaning: shows an ability you wish you had
questions.example: If only I could speak Spanish.

questions.prompt: Even if it rains, we ___ go.
questions.explanation: "will" fits here. Rule to remember: First conditional: if + present, will. Second: if + past, would.
questions.meaning: shows a result that happens in any case
questions.example: Even if it rains, we will go.

questions.prompt: If I ___ time, I'd learn piano.
questions.explanation: "I'd learn" is a second conditional result, so the if-clause takes the past simple: if I "had" time. "could" and "were" cannot be followed directly by a noun like 'time'.
questions.meaning: the past of have, for an unreal situation
questions.example: If I had time, I'd learn piano.

questions.prompt: Should you need help, ___ me.
questions.explanation: "Should you need help" is a formal way of saying "if you need help", and the main clause gives an instruction, so it needs the imperative "call".
questions.meaning: to phone someone
questions.example: Should you need help, call me.

units.title: Modal Verbs
units.description: Obligation, advice, possibility — Modals express degree of certainty, permission, or obligation.

questions.prompt: You look ill. You ___ see a doctor.
questions.explanation: To give advice before a bare verb we use "should"; "ought" and "have" would need "to", and "had" would need "better".
questions.meaning: used to give advice
questions.example: You should see a doctor.

questions.prompt: I ___ speak three languages.
questions.explanation: "can" says you are able to do something, so it fits 'I ___ speak three languages'. 'Needn't', 'should' and 'had' do not express ability.
questions.meaning: shows that you are able to do something
questions.example: I can speak three languages.

questions.prompt: Visitors ___ wear a badge. (= they are required to)
questions.explanation: The clue says visitors are required to wear a badge, and a rule or obligation is expressed with "must" + base verb.
questions.meaning: shows that a rule says you have to
questions.example: Visitors must wear a badge.

questions.prompt: You ___ not smoke here. (= it is not allowed)
questions.explanation: The clue says smoking is not allowed, and we express a prohibition with "must" not + base verb.
questions.meaning: shows that something is not allowed
questions.example: You must not smoke here.

questions.prompt: She ___ be at work now.
