questions.prompt: Please find my ___ attached to this email.
questions.explanation: A "CV" is the document you attach to a job application email. The other options are not things you can attach.
questions.meaning: a short document listing your work and studies
questions.example: My CV is attached to this email.

questions.prompt: I have three years of ___ in customer service.
questions.explanation: "experience" completes the sentence "I have three years of experience in customer service."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: skill you gain by doing a job
questions.example: I have three years of experience.

questions.prompt: I'm looking for a role with more ___.
questions.explanation: "responsibility" completes the sentence "I'm looking for a role with more responsibility."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: a duty to take care of something
questions.example: I want a role with more responsibility.

questions.prompt: Could you tell me about your ___ strengths?
questions.explanation: We need an adjective before the noun "strengths", and "main" means most important. "Mainly" is an adverb, and "most" and "much" cannot go straight before "strengths" here.
questions.meaning: most important
questions.example: My main strength is teamwork.

questions.prompt: I'm a very ___ team player.
questions.explanation: After "very" and before the noun "team player" we need an adjective, so "reliable" is right. "Reliably" is an adverb, "reliance" is a noun and "rely" is a verb.
questions.meaning: able to be trusted to do things
questions.example: I am a reliable team player.

questions.prompt: The interviewer asked about my greatest ___.
questions.explanation: Interviewers commonly ask candidates about their greatest "weakness", meaning a flaw or area to improve. A degree, interview or contract is not something you can have as a 'greatest' trait.
questions.meaning: something you are not good at
questions.example: He asked about my greatest weakness.

questions.prompt: I believe I would be a great ___ for this role.
questions.explanation: "fit" is used in the phrase 'a great fit for', meaning someone who suits the role well. The other nouns do not combine with 'a great ... for this role'.
questions.meaning: a person or thing that suits something well
questions.example: I think I'm a good fit for this role.

questions.prompt: I'm available for an ___ any day next week.
questions.explanation: You are available for an "interview", a meeting to discuss the job, on a particular day. A degree or a fit is not something you schedule, and 'an' needs a vowel-start noun.
questions.meaning: a meeting to talk about a job
questions.example: I'm free for an interview next week.

questions.prompt: My current ___ ends next month.
questions.explanation: A work "contract" is an agreement that runs for a set time, so it can end next month. A salary, weakness or responsibility does not end on a date in this way.
questions.meaning: a written agreement to do work
questions.example: My contract ends next month.

questions.prompt: I'm hoping to ___ my career to the next level.
questions.explanation: The set phrase is "take your career to the next level", meaning to move it forward, so "take" is right. "Demonstrate", "consider" and "hear" do not go with "to the next level".
questions.meaning: to raise to a higher stage
questions.example: I want to take my career to the next level.

questions.prompt: The job ___ mentions strong communication skills.
questions.explanation: A job "description" is the document listing a post's duties and required skills, so it can 'mention strong communication skills'. A salary, interview or degree does not mention skills in this way.
questions.meaning: words that say what something is like
questions.example: The job description lists the duties.

questions.prompt: I have a ___ in business administration.
questions.explanation: You have a "degree" in a subject, meaning a university qualification. 'Information' is uncountable so cannot follow 'a', and touch and responsibility do not take 'in business administration'.
questions.meaning: a qualification you get from university
questions.example: I have a degree in business.

questions.prompt: I worked as an ___ for a local company last summer.
questions.explanation: After 'worked as an' you need a job title starting with a vowel sound, and an "intern" is a temporary trainee, typical of a summer job. The other words are not roles.
questions.meaning: a trainee who works to learn
questions.example: She worked as an intern last summer.

questions.prompt: Could you describe your ___ working style, the way you usually work?
questions.explanation: "typical" means usual or normal, matching the clue 'the way you usually work'. 'Fit', 'reliable' and 'tight' do not mean 'usual'.
questions.meaning: usual; normal
questions.example: Describe your typical working day.

questions.prompt: I'm confident I can meet ___ deadlines.
questions.explanation: 'Tight deadlines' are deadlines that leave very little time, and 'meet tight deadlines' is the standard phrase in interviews, so "tight" fits; 'strong', 'fit' and 'typical' do not collocate with 'deadlines' this way.
questions.meaning: leaving very little time
questions.example: I can meet tight deadlines.

questions.prompt: The company offers a competitive ___ package.
questions.explanation: A 'salary package' is the pay and benefits a company offers, and "salary" is the only option that fits 'competitive ___ package'. Weakness, intern and touch make no sense here.
questions.meaning: money paid regularly for work
questions.example: The company offers a good salary.

questions.prompt: I would appreciate the chance to ___ my skills.
questions.explanation: "demonstrate" means to show clearly, so "the chance to demonstrate my skills" fits an interview; "apply", "hearing" and "take" do not work after "chance to" with "my skills".
questions.meaning: to show clearly that you can do something
questions.example: I can demonstrate my skills.

questions.prompt: Please let me know if you need any further ___.
questions.explanation: "information" is the uncountable noun that follows "any further" when you offer to give more details; "interview" and "degree" don't fit this polite closing line.
questions.meaning: facts about something
questions.example: Please send me more information.

questions.prompt: I'm currently ___ for new opportunities.
questions.explanation: "searching" fits after "I'm currently" (present continuous) and takes "for" to mean looking for new job opportunities.
questions.meaning: looking carefully for something
questions.example: I am searching for a new job.

questions.prompt: I have excellent ___ skills, both written and spoken.
questions.explanation: "communication" is the skill that can be "written and spoken", so it is the only word that fits "excellent ___ skills" here.
questions.meaning: sharing ideas and information with other people
questions.example: I have good communication skills.

questions.prompt: The recruiter will be in ___ shortly.
questions.explanation: "be in touch" is a fixed phrase meaning to contact you, so "touch" is the only option that completes "will be in ___ shortly".
questions.meaning: in contact
questions.example: The recruiter will be in touch soon.

questions.prompt: I'm keen to ___ more about the role.
questions.explanation: "learn" fits "keen to ___ more about the role" because you learn more about something; "take", "apply" and "demonstrate" don't collocate with "more about".
questions.meaning: to gain knowledge of something
questions.example: I'd love to learn more about the role.

questions.prompt: Thank you for ___ my application.
questions.explanation: After the preposition "for" a verb takes the -ing form, and "considering" makes sense: you thank someone for thinking about your application.
questions.meaning: thinking about something carefully
questions.example: Thank you for considering my application.

questions.prompt: I look forward to ___ from you soon.
questions.explanation: "look forward to" is followed by an -ing form, and "hearing from you" means receiving news from them, so "hearing" is right.
questions.meaning: to get news from someone
questions.example: I look forward to hearing from you.

units.title: Describing People's Character
units.description: Personality traits — Personality adjectives matched to typical behavior.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "generous" tends to…
choices: share what they have with others
work hard to achieve big goals
questions.explanation: Generous people are happy to give, so they "share what they have with others"; envy, ambition and tidiness describe other personality traits.
questions.meaning: happy to give and share
questions.example: She is generous with her time.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "stubborn" tends to… ___
bank: say things without thinking of others' feelings
questions.explanation: A "stubborn" person keeps the same opinion even when others give good reasons, so they "refuse to change their mind".
questions.meaning: unwilling to change your mind
questions.example: My dad is very stubborn.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "honest" tends to…
choices: put a lot of effort into tasks
questions.explanation: An "honest" person does not lie or hide things, so they "always tell the truth".
questions.meaning: always telling the truth
questions.example: He is an honest man.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "reliable" tends to… ___
questions.explanation: You can trust a "reliable" person to keep their word, so they "always do what they promise".
questions.meaning: able to be trusted to do things
questions.example: She is a reliable friend.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "ambitious" tends to…
choices: work hard to achieve big goals
say things without thinking of others' feelings
questions.explanation: An ambitious person wants to achieve a lot, so the typical behavior is to "work hard to achieve big goals".
questions.meaning: wanting very much to succeed
questions.example: He is an ambitious student.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "patient" tends to ___.
bank: put a lot of effort into tasks
questions.explanation: A patient person can wait without getting annoyed, so they "stay calm while waiting".
questions.meaning: able to wait calmly
questions.example: Be patient – the bus is coming.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "curious" tends to…
questions.explanation: A "curious" person wants to learn and find things out, so they "ask a lot of questions".
questions.meaning: wanting to learn and know things
questions.example: My son is very curious.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "confident" tends to ___.
questions.explanation: A confident person feels sure of themselves, so they "believe in their own abilities" rather than feeling nervous.
questions.meaning: sure of your own ability
questions.example: She feels confident before exams.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "shy" tends to…
choices: work hard to achieve big goals
questions.explanation: A "shy" person is uncomfortable with people they don't know, so they "feel nervous meeting new people".
questions.meaning: nervous with new people
questions.example: He is shy at parties.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "outgoing" tends to… ___
bank: share what they have with others
questions.explanation: An "outgoing" person is sociable and confident with others, so they "enjoy meeting new people".
questions.meaning: friendly and fond of meeting people
questions.example: She is outgoing and friendly.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "careless" tends to… ___
questions.explanation: A "careless" person doesn't pay enough attention, so they "make mistakes without noticing".
questions.meaning: not paying enough attention
questions.example: A careless driver caused the crash.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "organized" tends to…
questions.explanation: An "organized" person plans ahead and keeps things tidy, so they "keep everything neat and planned".
questions.meaning: good at planning and keeping things in order
questions.example: She is very organized.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "lazy" tends to… ___
bank: think they are better than others
questions.explanation: A "lazy" person doesn't want to make an effort, so they "avoid doing work".
questions.meaning: not wanting to work
questions.example: He is too lazy to cook.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "hardworking" tends to…
choices: put a lot of effort into tasks
feel jealous of what others have
questions.explanation: A hardworking person works hard and does not give up easily, so they "put a lot of effort into tasks"; the other options describe jealousy, tidiness and moodiness.
questions.meaning: putting a lot of effort in
questions.example: She is a hardworking student.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "selfish" tends to… ___
bank: share what they have with others
questions.explanation: A "selfish" person cares about their own needs and not other people's, so they "think mainly of themselves".
questions.meaning: caring only about yourself
questions.example: Don't be so selfish!

questions.prompt: Someone who is "kind" tends to…
choices: put a lot of effort into tasks
questions.explanation: A "kind" person is gentle and helpful towards people, so they "treat others with care".
questions.meaning: caring and good to others
questions.example: He is kind to animals.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "arrogant" tends to… ___
bank: think they are better than others
questions.answer: think they are better than others
questions.explanation: An "arrogant" person is too proud of themselves, so they "think they are better than others".
questions.meaning: too proud of yourself
questions.example: An arrogant boss is hard to like.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "modest" tends to…
questions.explanation: A "modest" person doesn't talk proudly about their own success, so they tend to "not boast about achievements".
questions.meaning: not boasting about yourself
questions.example: He is modest about his success.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "cheerful" tends to… ___
bank: work hard to achieve big goals
questions.explanation: "Cheerful" means happy and in a good mood, so a cheerful person tends to "stay happy and positive".
questions.meaning: happy and positive
questions.example: She is cheerful every morning.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "moody" tends to…
choices: share what they have with others
questions.explanation: A "moody" person's feelings go up and down without warning, so they tend to "change mood suddenly and often".
questions.meaning: having feelings that change quickly, often bad-tempered
questions.example: My brother is moody and often sulks.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "loyal" tends to…
choices: work hard to achieve big goals
questions.explanation: A "loyal" person supports their friends and doesn't let them down, so they tend to "stay faithful to friends".
questions.meaning: faithful to friends
questions.example: A loyal friend never leaves you.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "jealous" tends to… ___
questions.explanation: A "jealous" person is unhappy when others have things they want, so they tend to "feel envious of others".
questions.meaning: unhappy because someone has what you want
questions.example: He gets jealous easily.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "sensitive" tends to…
choices: think they are better than others
say things without thinking of others' feelings
questions.explanation: A sensitive person feels things strongly, so the typical behavior is to "get upset easily".
questions.meaning: easily hurt or upset
questions.example: She is sensitive about her looks.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "creative" tends to… ___
questions.explanation: A "creative" person uses their imagination to make new things, so they tend to "come up with original ideas".
questions.meaning: good at making original things
questions.example: He is a creative designer.

questions.prompt: Someone who is "tactless" tends to…
choices: say things without thinking of others' feelings
share what they have with others
questions.explanation: "Tact" is the skill of not upsetting people, so a "tactless" person tends to "say things without thinking of others' feelings".
questions.meaning: careless about others' feelings
questions.example: His tactless joke upset her.

units.title: Used to & Would
units.description: Past habits and states — B1-level structures for talking about past habits.

questions.prompt: I ___ to walk to school every day when I was young.
questions.explanation: "used" completes "used to walk", which describes a past habit; "would" cannot be followed by "to" here.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: I used to walk to school.

questions.prompt: We ___ visit our grandparents every summer.
questions.explanation: "would" followed directly by "visit" describes a repeated past habit ("every summer"); "used" would need "to" after it.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: We would visit them every summer.

questions.prompt: She ___ to have long hair, but she cut it short.
questions.explanation: "used" fits here. Rule to remember: B1-level structures for talking about past habits.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: She used to have long hair.

questions.prompt: He ___ play soccer every weekend as a teenager.
questions.explanation: "would" followed directly by "play" describes a repeated past habit ("every weekend as a teenager"); "used" would need "to" after it.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: He would play soccer every weekend.

questions.prompt: I ___ to live in a small village.
questions.explanation: The blank is followed by "to", and only "used" forms the structure "used to"; "would to" does not exist.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: I used to live in a village.

questions.prompt: They ___ argue about everything when they were kids.
questions.explanation: There is no "to" after the blank, so the structure must be "would" + base verb, which describes a repeated habit in the past.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: They would argue about everything.

questions.prompt: She ___ to be afraid of the dark.
questions.explanation: "Be afraid" is a past state, not an action, so we use "used" (used to); "would" cannot describe states like this.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: She used to be afraid of the dark.

questions.prompt: We ___ spend hours playing outside after school.
questions.explanation: No "to" follows the blank, so we need "would" + base verb, which suits a repeated past habit like playing outside after school.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: We would play outside after school.

questions.prompt: He ___ to smoke, but he quit years ago.
questions.explanation: "used" fits here. Rule to remember: B1-level structures for talking about past habits.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: He used to smoke.

questions.prompt: I ___ eat candy every day when I was a child.
questions.explanation: There is no "to" after the blank, so "would" + base verb is needed to describe a repeated childhood habit.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: I would eat candy every day.

questions.prompt: She ___ to work as a teacher before she retired.
questions.explanation: The sentence has "to" after the blank, and working as a teacher was a past situation, so "used" (used to) is correct.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: She used to work as a teacher.

questions.prompt: We ___ to have a dog when I was young.
questions.explanation: "Have a dog" is a past state, and "to" follows the blank, so "used" (used to) is correct; "would" is not used for states.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: We used to have a dog.

questions.prompt: They ___ meet at the same café every Friday.
questions.explanation: No "to" follows the blank, so "would" + base verb is needed to describe a repeated habit, meeting every Friday.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: They would meet at the same café every Friday.

questions.prompt: He ___ to be much thinner than he is now.
questions.explanation: "Be thinner" is a past state, and "to" follows the blank, so "used" (used to) is correct; "would" cannot describe states.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: He used to be thinner.

questions.prompt: I ___ to hate vegetables when I was a kid.
questions.explanation: "Hate" describes a past feeling (a state), and "to" follows the blank, so "used" (used to) is correct.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: I used to hate vegetables.

questions.prompt: We ___ stay up late telling stories.
questions.explanation: There is no "to" after the blank, so "would" + base verb is needed; it describes a repeated past habit, staying up late to tell stories.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: We would stay up late telling stories.

questions.prompt: She ___ to own a bright red car.
questions.explanation: Owning a car is a past state, and 'would' can't describe states. The word 'to' also follows the blank, so "used" is the form that fits.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: She used to own a red car.

questions.prompt: He ___ complain about the weather every winter.
questions.explanation: The blank is followed directly by the bare verb "complain", and 'every winter' shows a repeated past habit, so "would" fits. 'Used' would need 'to' after it.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: He would complain about the weather.

questions.prompt: I ___ to study French at school.
questions.explanation: The word 'to' follows the blank, and 'would' is never followed by 'to', so "used" is the only form that fits. It describes a past situation that has ended.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: I used to study French.

questions.prompt: They ___ to travel a lot before they had children.
questions.explanation: The structure is 'used to' + verb for a past habit or situation that no longer happens, and 'to' follows the blank. 'Would' is never followed by 'to', so the answer is "used".
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: They used to travel a lot.

questions.prompt: We ___ sing songs on long car journeys.
questions.explanation: Singing on journeys is a repeated past action, and the bare verb "sing" follows the blank directly. That pattern needs "would"; 'used' would need 'to' after it.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: We would sing on long journeys.

questions.prompt: She ___ to be much more confident as a teenager.
questions.explanation: Being confident is a past state, not a repeated action, and 'would' can't describe states. 'To' follows the blank, so "used" is correct.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: She used to be more confident.

questions.prompt: He ___ to play the piano every evening.
questions.explanation: The word 'to' follows the blank, and the pattern 'used to' + verb describes a past habit. 'Would' is never followed by 'to', so the answer is "used".
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: He used to play the piano.

questions.prompt: I ___ collect stamps when I was younger.
questions.explanation: The bare verb "collect" follows the blank directly, and 'when I was younger' signals a past habit. 'Would' takes a bare verb, so "would" fits, while 'used' needs 'to'.
questions.meaning: describes something you did again and again
questions.example: I would collect stamps when younger.

questions.prompt: They ___ to live next door to us years ago.
questions.explanation: Living next door is a past state, and 'would' can't describe states. 'To' also follows the blank, so "used" is correct.
questions.meaning: describes a past habit or state that ended
questions.example: They used to live next door.

units.title: Question Tags
units.description: Confirming and checking information — B1-level question tag practice.

questions.prompt: You're coming to the party, ___ you?
questions.explanation: The main clause "You're coming" is positive and uses the verb 'be', so the tag is negative with the same verb. That gives "aren't" you?
questions.meaning: the short form of are not
questions.example: You're coming, aren't you?

questions.prompt: She's happy with the result, ___ she?
questions.explanation: "She's happy" is a positive statement with 'is', so the tag must be negative and use the same verb: "isn't" she?
questions.meaning: the short form of is not
questions.example: She's happy, isn't she?

questions.prompt: He can dance really well, ___ he?
questions.explanation: "He can dance" is positive and uses the modal 'can', so the tag repeats that modal in the negative: "can't" he?
questions.meaning: the short form of cannot
questions.example: He can dance well, can't he?

questions.prompt: He can't swim very far, ___ he?
questions.explanation: The statement "He can't swim very far" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the same auxiliary: "can" he?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: He can't swim far, can he?

questions.prompt: It was sunny yesterday, ___ it?
questions.explanation: The statement "It was sunny yesterday" is positive and uses "was", so the tag is negative with the same verb: "wasn't" it?
questions.meaning: the short form of was not
questions.example: It was sunny, wasn't it?

questions.prompt: It wasn't sunny yesterday, ___ it?
questions.explanation: The statement "It wasn't sunny yesterday" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the verb be: "was" it?
questions.meaning: the past of be, used to check
questions.example: It wasn't sunny, was it?

questions.prompt: They were at the party, ___ they?
questions.explanation: The statement "They were at the party" is positive and plural, so the tag is negative with the same verb: "weren't" they?
questions.meaning: the short form of were not
questions.example: They were there, weren't they?

questions.prompt: They weren't at home last night, ___ they?
questions.explanation: The statement "They weren't at home last night" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the verb be: "were" they?
questions.meaning: the past of be, used to check
questions.example: They weren't home, were they?

questions.prompt: She likes chocolate, ___ she?
questions.explanation: "She likes chocolate" is positive present simple with no auxiliary, so the tag uses negative "doesn't" for she.
questions.meaning: the short form of does not
questions.example: She likes chocolate, doesn't she?

questions.prompt: She doesn't like tea very much, ___ she?
questions.explanation: "She doesn't like tea very much" is negative present simple, so the tag is positive and uses "does" for she.
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: She doesn't like tea, does she?

questions.prompt: You smoke sometimes, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "You smoke sometimes" is positive present simple with no auxiliary, so the tag uses negative "don't" for you.
questions.meaning: the short form of do not
questions.example: You smoke sometimes, don't you?

questions.prompt: You don't smoke at all, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "You don't smoke at all" is negative present simple, so the tag is positive and uses "do" for you.
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: You don't smoke, do you?

questions.prompt: You've seen this film before, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "You've seen" is positive present perfect (you have), so the tag is negative with the same auxiliary: "haven't" you?
questions.meaning: the short form of have not
questions.example: You've seen it, haven't you?

questions.prompt: You haven't seen my keys, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "You haven't seen my keys" is negative present perfect, so the tag is positive and repeats the auxiliary: "have" you?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: You haven't seen it, have you?

questions.prompt: He's finished his homework, ___ he?
questions.explanation: "He's finished" means he has finished (present perfect), so the negative tag repeats "has": "hasn't" he?
questions.meaning: the short form of has not
questions.example: He's finished his homework, hasn't he?

questions.prompt: He hasn't finished the report yet, ___ he?
questions.explanation: The statement is negative ("hasn't finished"), so the tag is positive and repeats the auxiliary: "has" he?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: He hasn't finished, has he?

questions.prompt: She'll call us later, ___ she?
questions.explanation: "She'll" means "she will", a positive statement, so the tag is negative with the same auxiliary: "won't" she?
questions.meaning: the short form of will not
questions.example: She'll call us, won't she?

questions.prompt: She won't be late again, ___ she?
questions.explanation: "won't be late" is negative, so the tag is positive and reuses the auxiliary "will": she "will"?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: She won't be late, will she?

questions.prompt: You'd like some tea, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "You'd like" is short for "you would like", a positive statement, so the tag is negative with the same auxiliary: "wouldn't" you?
questions.meaning: the short form of would not
questions.example: You'd like tea, wouldn't you?

questions.prompt: You wouldn't mind helping, ___ you?
questions.explanation: "wouldn't mind" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the auxiliary: you "would"?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: You wouldn't mind, would you?

questions.prompt: He could swim as a child, ___ he?
questions.explanation: "could swim" is positive, so the tag is negative and repeats the modal "could": "couldn't" he?
questions.meaning: the short form of could not
questions.example: He could swim, couldn't he?

questions.prompt: He couldn't swim before lessons, ___ he?
questions.explanation: "couldn't swim" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the modal: he "could"?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: He couldn't swim, could he?

questions.prompt: We should leave soon, ___ we?
questions.explanation: "should leave" is positive, so the tag is negative and repeats the modal: "shouldn't" we?
questions.meaning: the short form of should not
questions.example: We should leave, shouldn't we?

questions.prompt: We shouldn't be late, ___ we?
questions.explanation: "shouldn't be late" is negative, so the tag is positive and repeats the modal: we "should"?
questions.meaning: used after a negative to check
questions.example: We shouldn't be late, should we?

questions.prompt: They didn't call you yesterday, ___ they?
questions.explanation: "didn't call" is negative and past simple, so the tag is positive with "did": they "did"?
questions.meaning: the past of do, used to check
questions.example: They didn't call, did they?

units.title: Giving Opinions & Agreeing
units.description: Sharing your point of view — B1-level phrases for discussion and debate.

questions.prompt: In my ___, this is the best option.
questions.explanation: "opinion" completes the sentence "In my opinion, this is the best option."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: what you think about something
questions.example: In my opinion, this is best.

questions.prompt: I ___ agree with what you're saying.
questions.explanation: "totally" is an adverb meaning completely, so it can strengthen the verb "agree". "total" is an adjective, "very" cannot modify "agree" on its own, and "not" would need "don't" before the verb.
questions.meaning: completely
questions.example: I totally agree with you.

questions.prompt: I'm not really ___ about that idea.
questions.explanation: "sure" is correct because "not really sure about" is the fixed phrase for expressing doubt; "view", "honest" and "kind" do not fit after "I'm not really" with "about".
questions.meaning: certain; without doubt
questions.example: I'm not really sure about that.

questions.prompt: That's a fair ___, but I see it differently.
questions.explanation: "point" is correct because "That's a fair point" is the set phrase for conceding that someone has said something reasonable before you disagree.
questions.meaning: an idea you give in a discussion
questions.example: That's a fair point.

questions.prompt: I couldn't ___ more with you.
questions.explanation: "agree" is correct because "I couldn't agree more" is the fixed idiom meaning you completely share the other person's opinion.
questions.meaning: to have the same opinion
questions.example: I couldn't agree more.

questions.prompt: Personally, I ___ that we should wait.
questions.explanation: "think" is correct because "I think that..." is how you introduce your own opinion; "mean", "hear" and "side" do not fit before "that we should wait".
questions.meaning: to have an opinion about something
questions.example: Personally, I think we should wait.

questions.prompt: I see what you ___, but I disagree.
questions.explanation: "mean" is correct because "I see what you mean, but..." is the set phrase for showing you understand someone's point before disagreeing.
questions.meaning: to want to say or express something
questions.example: I see what you mean.

questions.prompt: As ___ as I'm concerned, it's a bad idea.
questions.explanation: "far" is correct because "as far as I'm concerned" is a fixed phrase meaning 'in my opinion'.
questions.meaning: used to say how much something applies
questions.example: As far as I'm concerned, it's bad.

questions.prompt: I'm ___ sure that's correct.
questions.explanation: "not" is correct because "I'm not sure that's correct" is how you politely say you doubt something; the other words do not go before "sure" here.
questions.meaning: used to make a sentence negative
questions.example: I'm not sure that's right.

questions.prompt: I'd have to ___ with you on that one.
questions.explanation: "disagree" is correct because "I'd have to disagree with you" is a polite way to say you hold the opposite opinion. "think", "view" and "mean" don't make sense before "with you" here.
questions.meaning: to have a different opinion
questions.example: I'd have to disagree with you.

questions.prompt: From my point of ___, it's a good plan.
questions.explanation: "view" is correct because "from my point of view" is a fixed phrase meaning 'in my opinion'.
questions.meaning: an opinion or way of thinking about something
questions.example: In my view, it's a good idea.

questions.prompt: I ___ your point, but I still disagree.
questions.explanation: "understand" is correct because "I understand your point, but..." shows you follow the other person's argument before disagreeing. "feel" and "think" can't take "your point" as an object like this.
questions.meaning: to know what someone means
questions.example: I understand your point, but I disagree.

questions.prompt: Honestly, I don't ___ it that way.
questions.explanation: "see" is correct because "I don't see it that way" is the usual phrase for saying you view something differently.
questions.meaning: to think about something in a particular way
questions.example: I don't see it that way.

questions.prompt: I tend to ___ with the majority here.
questions.explanation: "side" is correct because "side with" means to support one group or person in a disagreement, as in "I tend to side with the majority".
questions.meaning: to support one group in an argument
questions.example: I tend to side with them.

questions.prompt: That's exactly what I was going to ___.
questions.explanation: "say" completes the phrase 'exactly what I was going to say', used when someone voices your own thought. The other options don't fit after 'going to'.
questions.meaning: to tell your thoughts in words
questions.example: That's what I was going to say.

questions.prompt: Honestly, I'm ___ convinced by that argument; it has too many gaps.
questions.explanation: "hardly" means 'almost not at all', so "I'm hardly convinced" matches the complaint that the argument has too many gaps. "totally" and "completely" would mean the opposite, and "view" is a noun that doesn't fit here.
questions.meaning: almost not at all
questions.example: I can hardly believe that's true.

questions.prompt: It seems to ___ that we have no choice.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'It seems to me that...', which introduces your opinion, so "me" is needed after 'to'.
questions.meaning: the person speaking, as the object
questions.example: It seems to me we have no choice.

questions.prompt: I have to ___ with you there.
questions.explanation: "concur" completes the sentence "I have to concur with you there."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: a formal way to say you agree
questions.example: I concur with your view.

questions.prompt: I'm afraid I ___ agree with that.
questions.explanation: "can't" completes the sentence "I'm afraid I can't agree with that."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: the short form of cannot
questions.example: I'm afraid I can't agree.

questions.prompt: That's a good ___, actually.
questions.explanation: A comment about something you noticed is an "observation". "Notice" is a verb here, so it does not fit after "good".
questions.meaning: a comment about something you noticed
questions.example: That's a good observation.

questions.prompt: I'm ___ of torn about this.
questions.explanation: "kind" completes the sentence "I'm kind of two minds about this."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: rather; a little
questions.example: I'm kind of unsure about it.

questions.prompt: I really don't think that's ___.
questions.explanation: After "that's" you need an adjective, so "true" gives the natural disagreement "I don't think that's true". "truth" and "trust" are nouns, and "truly" is an adverb.
questions.meaning: correct; not false
questions.example: I don't think that's true.

questions.prompt: Let's agree to ___ on this one.
questions.explanation: 'Agree to differ' is a fixed phrase meaning you accept you hold different opinions, so "differ" is needed.
questions.meaning: to hold different opinions
questions.example: Let's agree to differ.

questions.prompt: I ___ what you're saying, but I still think I'm right.
questions.explanation: "hear" completes the sentence "I hear what you're saying, but I still think I'm right."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to understand someone's point of view
questions.example: I hear you, but I disagree.

questions.prompt: To be ___, I hadn't thought of it that way.
questions.explanation: 'To be honest' is a fixed phrase for admitting something frankly, so "honest" fits before 'I hadn't thought of it that way'.
questions.meaning: truthful; used to admit something
questions.example: To be honest, I'm not sure.

units.title: Health & Fitness
units.description: Exercise and healthy living — B1-level vocabulary for talking about fitness and wellbeing.

questions.prompt: I try to ___ out at the gym three times a week.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb 'work out' means to do physical exercise, so "work" fits 'work out at the gym'. 'Cool out', 'warm out' and 'rest out' aren't used this way.
questions.meaning: to do physical exercise
questions.example: I work out three times a week.

questions.prompt: Eating a ___ diet keeps you healthy.
questions.explanation: A "balanced" diet includes the right mix of food groups, and it is the only option that describes a diet and keeps you healthy.
questions.meaning: including all the food groups you need
questions.example: Eat a balanced diet.

questions.prompt: I always ___ up before I start exercising.
questions.explanation: "warm" up is the phrasal verb for preparing your body before exercise; it needs a verb, and "warm" is the one that fits with "up".
questions.meaning: to prepare your body for exercise
questions.example: I warm up before running.

questions.prompt: Getting enough ___ is important for your health.
questions.explanation: "sleep" is the only noun that follows "enough" naturally here, because you need enough of it each night for good health.
questions.meaning: the natural rest you need every night
questions.example: Enough sleep is important.

questions.prompt: She ___ five kilometres every morning.
questions.explanation: "runs" is the third-person singular verb needed after "She", and you run kilometres on foot.
questions.meaning: moves fast on foot
questions.example: She runs five kilometres every day.

questions.prompt: Drinking plenty of ___ keeps you hydrated.
questions.explanation: You stay hydrated by drinking "water", the only drink among the options.
questions.meaning: a clear liquid we drink
questions.example: Drink plenty of water.

questions.prompt: He joined a ___ to get fit.
questions.explanation: You join a "gym" to get fit, and the article "a" needs a singular noun, which rules out "weights".
questions.meaning: a place with machines for exercise
questions.example: He joined a gym.

questions.prompt: Doing ___ exercise strengthens your heart.
questions.explanation: "cardio" exercise raises your heart rate and so strengthens your heart; the other words cannot describe a type of exercise.
questions.meaning: exercise that makes your heart work harder
questions.example: Cardio strengthens your heart.

questions.prompt: I need to ___ down after my workout.
questions.explanation: After a workout you "cool" down to let your heart rate and breathing return to normal gradually; "warm up" is what you do before exercise.
questions.meaning: to let your body relax after exercise
questions.example: I cool down after a workout.

questions.prompt: Lifting ___ builds muscle strength.
questions.explanation: You lift "weights" to build muscle strength; the other options cannot be lifted for that purpose.
questions.meaning: heavy objects you lift for strength
questions.example: Lifting weights builds muscle.

questions.prompt: Cutting down on ___ food is good for you.
questions.explanation: "junk" food is unhealthy food, so cutting down on it is good for you; the other words do not go before "food" this way.
questions.meaning: low-quality and unhealthy, as in junk food
questions.example: Cut down on junk food.

questions.prompt: Stretching helps prevent ___.
questions.explanation: Stretching protects your muscles, so it helps prevent "injuries"; you cannot prevent rest, a habit or alcohol in this sense.
questions.meaning: damage done to the body
questions.example: Stretching helps prevent injuries.

questions.prompt: I try to eat five portions of ___ a day.
questions.explanation: The "five a day" advice is about eating portions of "fruit" (and vegetables); you do not eat portions of water, air or stress.
questions.meaning: sweet food like apples and bananas
questions.example: Eat five portions of fruit a day.

questions.prompt: Getting regular exercise reduces ___.
questions.explanation: Exercise is known to reduce "stress", meaning worry and tension. Flexibility is something exercise improves, and a vitamin or a gym is not something that gets reduced.
questions.meaning: worry and tension
questions.example: Exercise reduces stress.

questions.prompt: She follows a strict fitness ___.
questions.explanation: We say someone follows a "routine", a regular plan of exercises. "Follows a strict ... " points to a set plan, not a habit, alcohol or injuries.
questions.meaning: a regular plan you follow
questions.example: She follows a strict fitness routine.

questions.prompt: He hired a personal ___ to help him train.
questions.explanation: "trainer" completes the sentence "He hired a personal trainer to help him train."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: a person who helps you exercise
questions.example: He hired a personal trainer.

questions.prompt: Drinking too much ___ isn't good for you.
questions.explanation: You drink "alcohol", and drinking too much of it is unhealthy. Flexibility, vitamin and weights are not things you drink.
questions.meaning: drinks such as beer and wine
questions.example: Too much alcohol is unhealthy.

questions.prompt: Stretching in yoga improves your ___, so you can bend and touch your toes.
questions.explanation: Being able to bend easily and touch your toes describes "flexibility", which is what yoga stretching improves.
questions.meaning: the ability to bend easily
questions.example: Yoga improves flexibility.

questions.prompt: I go ___ every weekend to stay active.
questions.explanation: "swimming" completes the sentence "I go swimming every weekend to stay active."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: moving through water as a sport
questions.example: I go swimming every weekend.

questions.prompt: Skipping breakfast isn't a healthy ___.
questions.explanation: A "habit" is something you do regularly, and "a healthy habit" is a common phrase. Skipping breakfast is described as a bad habit.
questions.meaning: something you do regularly
questions.example: Skipping breakfast is a bad habit.

questions.prompt: Getting fresh ___ is good for your lungs.
questions.explanation: We breathe "air", and "fresh air" is a fixed phrase that is good for your lungs. Calorie, routine and injuries cannot be fresh.
questions.meaning: the gas we breathe
questions.example: Fresh air is good for you.

questions.prompt: Cycling to work is good ___.
questions.explanation: "exercise" completes the sentence "Cycling to work is good exercise."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: physical activity that keeps you fit
questions.example: Cycling is good exercise.

questions.prompt: He tracks his ___ intake carefully.
questions.explanation: "calorie" completes the sentence "He tracks his calorie intake carefully."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: a unit of energy in food
questions.example: He counts calories to lose weight.

questions.prompt: A good night's ___ helps you recover.
questions.explanation: "rest" completes the sentence "A good night's rest helps you recover."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: time when you relax or sleep
questions.example: Good rest helps you recover.

questions.prompt: She takes a daily ___ for her health.
questions.explanation: You "take" a daily "vitamin", a pill with substances your body needs. You don't take flexibility, junk or cardio.
questions.meaning: a substance in food that keeps you healthy
questions.example: Oranges are full of vitamin C.

units.title: Weather & Natural Events
units.description: Extreme weather vocabulary — B1-level vocabulary for weather and natural events.

questions.prompt: A strong ___ knocked down several trees.
questions.explanation: Strong winds in a "storm" can knock trees down, but a heatwave or drought cannot.
questions.meaning: a violent wind with rain
questions.example: A strong storm knocked down trees.

questions.prompt: Days of heavy ___ caused severe flooding in the town.
questions.explanation: "Days of heavy" goes with "rain", and a lot of rain over several days fills rivers and floods towns.
questions.meaning: water that falls from clouds
questions.example: Heavy rain caused flooding.

questions.prompt: Scientists are monitoring the ___ forming over the warm Atlantic Ocean.
questions.explanation: A "hurricane" is a huge storm that forms over warm ocean water; a drought, an earthquake or ice does not form as a storm over a warm sea.
questions.meaning: a violent storm with strong winds
questions.example: Scientists are tracking the approaching hurricane.

questions.prompt: The ___ shook the entire building.
questions.explanation: An "earthquake" is a sudden shaking of the ground, so it is what shakes a whole building.
questions.meaning: a sudden shaking of the ground
questions.example: The earthquake shook the building.

questions.prompt: Heavy ___ blocked the roads for days.
questions.explanation: Only "snow" collects on the ground in deep piles that block roads for days, and as an uncountable noun it fits "Heavy ___" with no article.
questions.meaning: soft white flakes of frozen water
questions.example: Heavy snow blocked the roads.

questions.prompt: The region suffered a long ___ last summer, with no rain for months.
questions.explanation: A "drought" is a long period without rain, which matches "no rain for months"; a storm brings rain rather than a lack of it.
questions.meaning: a long time with no rain
questions.example: A long drought hit the region.

questions.prompt: The ___ swept away several homes near the coast.
questions.explanation: A "flood" is water covering the land, and moving water can sweep homes away; a drought, a hailstorm or a blackout cannot carry houses away.
questions.meaning: a large amount of water covering land
questions.example: The flood swept away several homes.

questions.prompt: A sudden ___ blew the boats onto the rocks.
questions.explanation: A "gale" is a very strong wind, so it can blow boats onto rocks; fog, a drought or a heatwave cannot push anything.
questions.meaning: a very strong wind
questions.example: A sudden gale hit the town.

questions.prompt: The ___ warning said it would be rainy and windy all weekend.
questions.explanation: A warning about rain and wind is a "weather" warning, the general word for conditions in the sky. A tsunami, heat or drought warning would be about something more specific.
questions.meaning: the conditions outside, like rain and sun
questions.example: The weather is lovely today.

questions.prompt: Thick ___ made driving dangerous because we couldn't see the cars ahead.
questions.explanation: "fog" is cloud near the ground, and "thick fog" is the usual phrase for weather that stops drivers seeing ahead.
questions.meaning: thick cloud near the ground
questions.example: Thick fog made driving dangerous.

questions.prompt: Ice the size of golf balls fell during the ___ and damaged the crops.
questions.explanation: A "hailstorm" is a storm in which balls of ice fall from the sky, which matches the falling ice in the sentence.
questions.meaning: a storm with falling balls of ice
questions.example: The hailstorm damaged the crops.

questions.prompt: Firefighters battled a huge ___ in the forest.
questions.explanation: Firefighters fight fires, and a big fire in a forest is a "wildfire". A blackout, a surge and fog are not things firefighters battle.
questions.meaning: a big fire in a forest
questions.example: Firefighters fought a huge wildfire.

questions.prompt: The city was covered in deep snow after a rare ___ this winter.
questions.explanation: A "blizzard" is a storm with heavy snow and strong wind, so it explains the deep snow; a tornado or a tsunami does not bring snow.
questions.meaning: a storm with heavy snow and wind
questions.example: A rare blizzard hit the city.

questions.prompt: The ___ touched down in the village overnight.
questions.explanation: We say a "tornado" "touches down" when the spinning wind reaches the ground; fires and rain do not touch down.
questions.meaning: a violent whirling wind
questions.example: The tornado swept through the village.

questions.prompt: Rising sea levels are linked to climate ___.
questions.explanation: "change" completes the sentence "Rising sea levels are linked to climate change."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to become different
questions.example: The weather can change very quickly here.

questions.prompt: The ___ lasted for nearly three hours, and lightning hit two trees.
questions.explanation: A "thunderstorm" is a storm with thunder and lightning, so it matches the lightning hitting the trees; a blizzard brings snow, not lightning.
questions.meaning: a storm with thunder and lightning
questions.example: The thunderstorm lasted three hours.

questions.prompt: The heatwave caused several ___-related illnesses.
questions.explanation: A heatwave means very high temperatures, so the illnesses it causes are "heat"-related. Rain, floods and eruptions are not part of a heatwave.
questions.meaning: the quality of being very hot
questions.example: The heat made several people ill.

questions.prompt: The storm caused a ___ that left thousands without electricity.
questions.explanation: A "blackout" is a loss of electric power, the thing a storm causes when homes are left without electricity; a gale or heatwave is the weather itself.
questions.meaning: a loss of electric power
questions.example: A blackout left thousands without power.

questions.prompt: Meteorologists predicted a severe ___ this weekend.
questions.explanation: Meteorologists forecast weather, and a sudden very heavy fall of rain is a "downpour"; a wildfire or an eruption is not forecast by weather experts.
questions.meaning: a very heavy fall of rain
questions.example: Forecasters predicted a severe downpour.

questions.prompt: The volcano's ___ affected air travel for days.
questions.explanation: A volcano's ash cloud comes from its "eruption", which disrupts flights; a blackout, storm or gale is not something a volcano produces.
questions.meaning: when a volcano throws out lava
questions.example: The eruption closed the airport.

questions.prompt: The ___ made the roads extremely slippery.
questions.explanation: Frozen water on the road makes it slippery, so "ice" fits; a tornado or a surge does not coat roads, and a heatwave dries them.
questions.meaning: water that has frozen and become hard
questions.example: Ice made the roads slippery.

questions.prompt: A powerful ___ hit the tropical island nation.
questions.explanation: A "cyclone" is a large storm with circling winds, the kind that hits tropical islands; a blizzard needs snow, and droughts and eruptions do not 'hit' like a storm.
questions.meaning: a large storm with circling winds
questions.example: A powerful cyclone hit the island.

questions.prompt: The ___ brought record-breaking temperatures.
questions.explanation: Record-breaking temperatures come from a long spell of very hot weather, a "heatwave"; a cyclone, snow or a wildfire does not itself bring record heat.
questions.meaning: a long period of very hot weather
questions.example: The heatwave broke temperature records.

questions.prompt: After the undersea earthquake, officials issued a ___ warning for the coast.
questions.explanation: An undersea earthquake can cause a "tsunami", a huge wave, so officials warn people on the coast.
questions.meaning: a huge wave caused by an earthquake
questions.example: Officials issued a tsunami warning.

questions.prompt: The storm ___ has caused significant coastal erosion.
questions.explanation: A storm "surge" is a sudden rise of sea water during a storm, and it wears away the coast.
questions.meaning: a sudden rise of sea water
questions.example: The surge damaged the coast.

units.title: Describing a Process
units.description: Sequencing and instructions — B1-level sequencing language for describing steps.

questions.prompt: ___ of all, you need to gather the ingredients.
questions.explanation: "first" completes the sentence "first of all, you need to gather the ingredients."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: before everything else
questions.example: First of all, gather the ingredients.

questions.prompt: After mixing the flour, the ___ step is to preheat the oven, and then you bake the cake.
questions.explanation: Preheating comes after mixing but before baking, so it is the "next" step, not the first or the last.
questions.meaning: coming after this one
questions.example: The next step is to preheat the oven.

questions.prompt: After that, you should ___ the flour and sugar.
questions.explanation: "mix" is correct because flour and sugar are combined into one mixture in baking. After "you should" we need a base verb that fits ingredients, which "mix" does.
questions.meaning: to put things together into one
questions.example: Mix the flour and sugar.

questions.prompt: Once the mixture is ready, you ___ it into the tin.
questions.explanation: The mixture is runny, so you "pour" it, letting it flow from the bowl into the tin.
questions.meaning: to make liquid flow out of a container
questions.example: Pour the mixture into the tin.

questions.prompt: ___ this, place the tin in the oven.
questions.explanation: "following" is correct because "Following this," means "After this," and links the next step to the one before. The other words do not work as a sequencing phrase.
questions.meaning: coming after something
questions.example: Following this, place the tin inside.

questions.prompt: While it bakes, you can ___ the kitchen.
questions.explanation: While the dish is in the oven you have free time, so you can "clean" the kitchen and tidy up the mess.
questions.meaning: to remove dirt from something
questions.example: You can clean the kitchen.

questions.prompt: After twenty minutes, ___ the cake to see if it's done.
questions.explanation: After twenty minutes you "check" the cake, which means you look at it to see whether it is cooked.
questions.meaning: to look to see if it is right
questions.example: Check the cake after twenty minutes.

questions.prompt: Then, you need to ___ it out of the oven to cool.
questions.explanation: To remove something from the oven you "take" it out, so "take it out of the oven" is the right phrase here.
questions.meaning: to remove from a place
questions.example: Take the tray out of the oven.

questions.prompt: Finally, you can ___ the cake with icing.
questions.explanation: "decorate" is correct because adding icing to make a cake look nice is decorating it, and "Finally" shows it is the last step.
questions.meaning: to add something to make it look nice
questions.example: Decorate the cake with icing.

questions.prompt: After everything else is done, the ___ stage involves cutting the pieces.
questions.explanation: "final" is correct because it means last, and "After everything else is done" shows cutting is the last stage. "First", "initial" and "early" all refer to the start.
questions.meaning: coming at the end
questions.example: The final stage is cutting the cake.

questions.prompt: Before you start, make sure you ___ your hands.
questions.explanation: "wash" is correct because we wash our hands with soap and water before preparing something. "Wash your hands" is the standard phrase for this.
questions.meaning: to clean something with water, often with soap
questions.example: Wash your hands first.

questions.prompt: To begin, the ___ step is to switch on the machine.
questions.explanation: "initial" is correct because it means first, and switching on a machine is the beginning of using it. "Final" means last, so it does not fit.
questions.meaning: first; at the beginning
questions.example: The initial step is to switch it on.

questions.prompt: Once it's ready, you should ___ off the power.
questions.explanation: "turn" is correct because "turn off" is the phrasal verb meaning to stop a machine or its power. The other words do not form a phrasal verb with "off" in this sense.
questions.meaning: to make a machine or light stop working
questions.example: Turn off the power.

questions.prompt: After the process is finished, ___ everything away.
questions.explanation: "put" is correct because "put away" is the phrasal verb for returning things to their proper place after you finish. The other options do not combine with "away" this way.
questions.meaning: to move something into a place
questions.example: Put the flour into the bowl.

questions.prompt: At the very end, the ___ thing you do is check the results.
questions.explanation: "last" is correct because "At the very end" shows this is the final step, and "the last thing you do" is the natural phrase. "Initial" means first and "following" means next.
questions.meaning: coming at the end
questions.example: The last thing is to check the results.

questions.prompt: To begin ___, gather all the necessary tools.
questions.explanation: "with" is correct because "to begin with" is a fixed phrase meaning 'first of all'. "At", "from" and "on" do not make this phrase.
questions.meaning: used in "to begin with", meaning first
questions.example: To begin with, gather the tools.

questions.prompt: Next, you ___ the pieces together so they lock into place.
questions.explanation: "fit" is correct because pieces are "fitted together" so they join properly. You mix liquids and tighten screws, not pieces that go together.
questions.meaning: to join things so they match
questions.example: Fit the pieces together carefully.

questions.prompt: Once the parts are assembled, you need to ___ the screws.
questions.explanation: "tighten" is correct because after the parts are assembled, you turn the screws until they are firm. You do not mix or pour screws, and "put" needs a place after it.
questions.meaning: to make something firmer
questions.example: Tighten the screws.

questions.prompt: After that, ___ the device before use.
questions.explanation: "test" is correct because you check that a device works before you use it. You do not pour, mix or rest a device.
questions.meaning: to try something to see if it works
questions.example: Test the device before use.

questions.prompt: The ___ step is often the most important.
questions.explanation: "closing" is correct because "the closing step" means the last step at the end of the process. "Clean", "fit" and "rest" do not describe a step's place in a sequence.
questions.meaning: coming at the end
questions.example: The closing paragraph sums up the whole process.

questions.prompt: Before finishing, you should ___ everything twice.
questions.explanation: "verify" is correct because before finishing you check that everything is right, and you check it twice. "Decorate", "pour" and "fit" do not mean checking.
questions.meaning: to make sure something is right
questions.example: Verify all the measurements before you continue.

questions.prompt: Once complete, you can ___ the finished product.
questions.explanation: "use" is correct because once a product is finished, the next thing you do is use it. You do not pour, rest or mix a finished product.
questions.meaning: to do something with a tool or thing
questions.example: Use a sharp knife to cut the bread.

questions.prompt: The process ___ with a simple inspection.
questions.explanation: "starts" is correct because a process "starts with" its first step, and the singular subject "the process" takes -s. "Checks", "fits" and "rests" do not mean 'begins'.
questions.meaning: begins
questions.example: The process starts with an inspection.

questions.prompt: After preparation, the next ___ is mixing.
questions.explanation: "step" is correct because "the next step" names the following stage of a process. "Fit", "clean" and "rest" do not mean a stage in a process.
questions.meaning: one part of a process
questions.example: The next step is mixing.

questions.prompt: Lastly, allow the mixture to ___ overnight.
questions.explanation: "rest" is correct because a mixture is left to stand untouched overnight, which is what "rest" means in cooking. "Use" and "take" do not suit "allow the mixture to ___ overnight".
questions.meaning: to stay still without being touched
questions.example: Let the mixture rest overnight.

units.title: Speaking: Saying What You Think
units.description: Say it out loud — Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I think the other option makes more sense.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I think the other option makes more sense." Use "makes more sense" to say politely that one choice is more logical than another.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Personally, I would handle it differently.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Personally, I would handle it differently." Starting with "Personally," shows this is just your own opinion, which makes disagreeing sound softer.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The main problem is the cost.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "The main problem is the cost." Use "The main problem is..." to name the most important reason against something.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It depends on how much time we have.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "It depends on how much time we have." Use "It depends on..." when your answer changes with a condition. Note the preposition is "on".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am not entirely convinced by that argument.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I am not entirely convinced by that argument." Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: On the whole, the changes have helped.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "On the whole, the changes have helped." Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would rather discuss this in person.
questions.explanation: "I would rather discuss this in person." uses "would rather" plus a base verb to say what you prefer, here meeting face to face instead of talking by email or phone.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That is a fair point, but I disagree.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "That is a fair point, but I disagree." Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:

questions.explanation: Target phrase: "The results were better than we hoped." Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We could try a completely different approach." Opinions, reasons and comparisons said out loud.

units.title: Say It Your Way: Opinions
units.description: Write the idea in English — Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Name cost as the biggest obstacle.
acceptableAnswers: The main problem is the cost.
The biggest problem is the cost.
Cost is the main issue.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The main problem is the cost." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that your answer will change with how much time you have.
acceptableAnswers: It depends how much time we have.
It depends on the time available.
That depends how much time there is.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It depends how much time we have." "It depends (on) + how much…" says that your answer changes with something, here the amount of time.

questions.prompt: Disagree politely with an argument.
acceptableAnswers: I am afraid I do not agree.
I'm not sure I agree with that.
I see it differently.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am afraid I do not agree." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that you would not do it the same way.
acceptableAnswers: I would handle it differently.
Personally, I'd do it another way.
I would approach it differently.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would handle it differently." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say results exceeded what you hoped for.
acceptableAnswers: The results were better than we hoped.
The results beat our expectations.
The results were better than expected.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The results were better than we hoped." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say there is no easy answer.
acceptableAnswers: There is no easy answer to that.
There's no simple answer.
That question has no easy answer.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "There is no easy answer to that." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Suggest trying a different approach.
acceptableAnswers: We could try a different approach.
Perhaps we should try another way.
Let's try a different approach.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We could try a different approach." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you have been thinking about it all week.
acceptableAnswers: I have been thinking about it all week.
I've been thinking about this all week.
It has been on my mind all week.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I have been thinking about it all week." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say it would make sense to wait.
acceptableAnswers: It would make sense to wait.
I think we should wait.
Waiting would make more sense.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It would make sense to wait." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you used to feel the same way.
acceptableAnswers: I used to feel the same way.
I felt the same way once.
I used to think that too.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I used to feel the same way." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Ask someone to explain what they mean.
acceptableAnswers: Could you explain what you mean?
What do you mean by that?
Can you say more about that?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Could you explain what you mean?" Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say the difference is not as big as it looks.
acceptableAnswers: The difference is smaller than it looks.
The gap is smaller than it seems.
The difference isn't as big as it looks.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The difference is smaller than it looks." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that we need to be realistic about the plan.
acceptableAnswers: We need to be realistic about this.
Let's be realistic here.
We should be realistic about it.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We need to be realistic about this." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you can see why someone thinks that.
acceptableAnswers: I can see why you think that.
I understand why you would say that.
I can see where you are coming from.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I can see why you think that." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that in your experience it rarely works.
acceptableAnswers: In my experience, that rarely works.
From what I have seen, it seldom works.
That has rarely worked in my experience.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "In my experience, that rarely works." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Suggest giving something a single try.
acceptableAnswers: It is worth trying at least once.
It's worth a try.
You should give it a try.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It is worth trying at least once." "Worth + -ing" says something is a good idea, and "at least once" matches a single try.

questions.prompt: Say that it is a good idea to make a decision quickly.
acceptableAnswers: The sooner we decide, the better.
It is better to decide soon.
The sooner a decision is made, the better.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The sooner we decide, the better." The pattern "the + comparative, the + comparative" links the two ideas: deciding earlier makes things better.

questions.prompt: Say you would like to hear their opinion.
acceptableAnswers: I would like to hear your opinion.
I'd like to know what you think.
I'd be interested to hear your view.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would like to hear your opinion." "Would like to" + verb is a polite way to say what you want.

questions.prompt: Say that would take far too long.
acceptableAnswers: That would take far too long.
That would take too much time.
It would take far too long.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That would take far too long." Opinions, reasons and comparisons, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you are fairly sure it can be managed.
acceptableAnswers: I am fairly sure we can manage it.
I'm reasonably confident we can do it.
I'm pretty sure we can manage it.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am fairly sure we can manage it." "Fairly sure" means quite but not completely certain, and "manage it" means succeed in doing it.

questions.prompt: Say that, on the whole, the changes have helped.
acceptableAnswers: On the whole, the changes have helped.
Overall, the changes helped.
By and large the changes have helped.
questions.explanation: "On the whole, the changes have helped." uses "on the whole" (or "overall" or "by and large") to give a general opinion while allowing for some exceptions.

questions.prompt: Say you would rather discuss it in person.
acceptableAnswers: I would rather discuss this in person.
I'd prefer to talk about it face to face.
I'd prefer to discuss it in person.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would rather discuss this in person." "Would rather" + verb (without "to") shows a preference.

questions.prompt: Concede a point while still disagreeing.
acceptableAnswers: That is a fair point, but I still disagree.
You have a point, though I do not agree.
I take your point, but I disagree.
questions.explanation: "That is a fair point, but I still disagree." first accepts the other person's point, then uses "but" to keep your own view.

questions.prompt: Choose between two options, preferring the second.
acceptableAnswers: The second option makes more sense.
I think the second one is better.
I'd go for the second option.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The second option makes more sense." "Makes more sense" compares the two options and says the second is more reasonable.

questions.prompt: Say you are not entirely convinced.
acceptableAnswers: I am not entirely convinced.
I'm not completely convinced.
I have my doubts about that.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am not entirely convinced." "Not entirely" means not completely, so it politely shows some doubt.

units.title: The Passive
units.description: Passive structures — Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.

questions.prompt: The report ___ written last week.
questions.explanation: "was" is correct because the passive needs a form of be that agrees with the singular "report", and "last week" makes it past. "Were" is plural, and "has" or "believed" do not form a past passive here.
questions.meaning: singular past of be, used in passives
questions.example: The report was written last week.

questions.prompt: The bridge is ___ repaired.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is "is being" + past participle, and the repair is in progress now, so "being" fills the gap before "repaired".
questions.meaning: shows that a passive action is in progress
questions.example: The bridge is being repaired.

questions.prompt: Nothing ___ been decided yet.
questions.explanation: "has" fits here. Rule to remember: Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.
questions.meaning: a helper verb for a passive perfect action
questions.example: Nothing has been decided yet.

questions.prompt: The letters ___ sent yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Letters" is plural and "yesterday" points to the past, so the passive needs "were" + the participle "sent".
questions.meaning: the plural past of be, for passives
questions.example: The letters were sent yesterday.

questions.prompt: He ___ given a warning.
questions.explanation: A warning is given to him in the past, so the past passive needs the singular helper "was" before "given".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for a past passive
questions.example: He was given a warning.

questions.prompt: The results will ___ announced soon.
questions.explanation: After the modal "will" you need the base form, so the future passive is "will be" + "announced", with "be" filling the gap.
questions.meaning: the plain verb form used after will
questions.example: The results will be announced soon.

questions.prompt: The room ___ cleaned every day.
questions.explanation: "Every day" signals a regular habit, so the present simple passive uses singular "is" with "The room" before "cleaned".
questions.meaning: present of be, used in present passives
questions.example: The room is cleaned every day.

questions.prompt: The car needs ___ .
questions.explanation: "repairing" fits here. Rule to remember: Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after needs
questions.example: The car needs repairing.

questions.prompt: She ___ said to be brilliant.
questions.explanation: In the reporting passive "is said to be", the form of be must agree with "She", so "is" is needed; "am" and "are" do not agree with "She". "Was" would also fit, so it is not offered.
questions.meaning: a form of be used to report opinions
questions.example: She is said to be brilliant.

questions.prompt: The house is ___ to have been built in 1820.
questions.explanation: The reporting passive "is thought to have been built" uses the participle "thought" after "is" to say what people believe about the house.
questions.meaning: believed by many people
questions.example: The house is thought to date from 1820.

questions.prompt: Mistakes ___ made.
questions.explanation: "Mistakes" is plural, so the passive needs the plural "were" before "made". "Was" and "is" are singular, and "can" would need "be".
questions.meaning: the plural past of be, used in passives
questions.example: Mistakes were made.

questions.prompt: The film ___ directed by Lean.
questions.explanation: "was" fits here. Rule to remember: Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.
questions.meaning: a past form of be, used in passives
questions.example: The film was directed by Lean.

questions.prompt: The data ___ being analyzed now.
questions.explanation: "Now" shows the action is in progress, so the present continuous passive needs "is being analyzed", with "is" agreeing with "The data".
questions.meaning: a present form of be, used in passives
questions.example: The data is being analyzed now.

questions.prompt: Tickets can ___ bought online.
questions.explanation: After the modal "be" is needed because the passive is modal + be + past participle: "can be bought". The other options cannot follow "can".
questions.meaning: the plain verb form used after can
questions.example: Tickets can be bought online.

questions.prompt: The law ___ have been changed.
questions.explanation: "must" + "have been changed" is a modal perfect passive meaning you are sure it happened. "ought" would need "to", so it does not fit.
questions.meaning: shows that you are sure it happened
questions.example: The law must have been changed.

questions.prompt: He got ___ in the accident.
