questions.explanation: "hurt" fits here. Rule to remember: Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.
questions.meaning: injured or in pain
questions.example: He got hurt in the accident.

questions.prompt: The matter is ___ investigated.
questions.explanation: The present continuous passive is is/are + "being" + past participle, so "is being investigated" means it is happening now.
questions.meaning: shows an action is happening now to something
questions.example: The matter is being investigated.

questions.prompt: The plan ___ approved next month.
questions.explanation: "next month" points to the future, so the future passive "will be" + approved is needed. "is" does not fit a plan not yet approved.
questions.meaning: shows a passive action in the future
questions.example: The plan will be approved next month.

questions.prompt: It is widely ___ that prices will rise.
questions.explanation: "It is widely believed that..." is a fixed passive reporting pattern, so the past participle "believed" follows "is widely".
questions.meaning: thought to be true by many people
questions.example: It is widely believed that prices will rise.

questions.prompt: The rules ___ to be followed.
questions.explanation: "have" + "to be followed" expresses obligation: the rules must be followed. The sentence needs "have to be" before the past participle.
questions.meaning: with "to", shows a rule or duty
questions.example: The rules have to be followed.

questions.prompt: The parcel should ___ been delivered.
questions.explanation: After "should" we use "have" + "been" + past participle for a past passive expectation: "should have been delivered".
questions.meaning: after should, shows an expected past event
questions.example: The parcel should have arrived.

questions.prompt: The offer was ___ down.
questions.explanation: "turned" fits here. Rule to remember: Passive = be + past participle; the doer becomes optional.
questions.meaning: to refuse an offer
questions.example: The offer was turned down.

questions.prompt: Our flight ___ canceled.
questions.explanation: "Our flight" is singular, so the passive needs "was" + canceled. "Were" is plural, and "has" or "been" alone cannot form the passive.
questions.meaning: a past form of be in a passive
questions.example: Our flight was canceled.

questions.prompt: The issue ___ dealt with promptly.
questions.explanation: "The issue" is singular and past, so the passive is "was" dealt with. "were" is plural, and "be" and "have" cannot stand alone here.
questions.meaning: a past form of be in a passive
questions.example: The issue was dealt with promptly.

questions.prompt: Nothing ___ be done about it.
questions.explanation: "can" + be done is a modal passive meaning it is not possible to do anything. "ought" would need "to".
questions.meaning: shows it is possible
questions.example: Nothing can be done about it.

units.title: Confusable Words
units.description: Choose precisely — These pairs are frequently mixed up by learners.

questions.prompt: Stress can ___ your sleep. (verb, to influence)
questions.explanation: The verb meaning to influence is "affect"; "effect" is usually a noun (a result), so we say "Stress can affect your sleep".
questions.meaning: to change or influence something
questions.example: Stress can affect your sleep.

questions.prompt: I ___ the piano every day.
questions.explanation: Here we need the verb "practice", which means to do something again and again to get better; "practical" is an adjective and "principle" is a rule.
questions.meaning: to do something again and again to improve
questions.example: I practice the piano every day.

questions.prompt: She refuses to lie on ___.
questions.explanation: "On principle" means because of a rule or belief, and a rule is a "principle"; "principal" means main or a head teacher.
questions.meaning: a basic rule that guides behavior
questions.example: I follow the principle of honesty.

questions.prompt: My shoes feel ___ today, so I need to tie them tighter.
questions.explanation: "loose" is an adjective meaning not tight, so it describes the shoes; "lose" is a verb meaning to stop having something.
questions.meaning: not fitting tightly
questions.example: My shoes feel loose today.

questions.prompt: The company changed ___ logo last year.
questions.explanation: "its" is the possessive (belonging to it), so it goes before "logo"; "it's" means "it is" or "it has".
questions.meaning: belonging to a thing or animal
questions.example: The dog wagged its tail.

questions.prompt: Can you give me some ___ about which course to take?
questions.explanation: After "some" we need the uncountable noun "advice"; "advise" is the verb and "advices" does not exist.
questions.meaning: a suggestion about what someone should do
questions.example: He gave me good advice.

questions.prompt: Driving a small car is more ___ than driving a big one because it uses less gas.
questions.explanation: "economical" means saving money, which fits a car that uses less gas; "economic" means connected with the economy.
questions.meaning: saving money or resources
questions.example: A small car is more economical.

questions.prompt: She loves reading ___ novels set in Victorian London.
questions.explanation: "historical" means about or set in the past, as in a novel set in Victorian times; "historic" means important in history.
questions.meaning: connected with past events
questions.example: She loves reading historical novels.

questions.prompt: Don't joke about her weight; she's very ___ about it.
questions.explanation: "sensitive" means easily hurt or upset, which is why you shouldn't joke; "sensible" means showing good judgment.
questions.meaning: easily hurt or upset
questions.example: She is sensitive about her age.

questions.prompt: The fridge made a ___ humming noise all night, without stopping once.
questions.explanation: "continuous" means going on without a break, matching "without stopping once"; "continual" means repeated again and again with pauses.
questions.meaning: going on without any break
questions.example: There was continuous noise all night.

questions.prompt: There were very ___ people at the meeting.
questions.explanation: "people" is a countable plural noun, so we use "few"; "less" and "little" go with uncountable nouns.
questions.meaning: a small number of; not many
questions.example: Few people came to the party.

questions.prompt: Which word do we use for a position in the middle of a group of three or more?
questions.explanation: "among" describes being inside a group of three or more seen as a whole; "between" is mainly used for two things.
questions.meaning: in the middle of three or more
questions.example: She stood among the crowd.

questions.prompt: I'm staying at home, but when you go to the office, please ___ this letter with you.
questions.explanation: The letter moves away from the speaker, who stays at home, so we use "take"; "bring" is for movement towards the speaker.
questions.meaning: to carry something away from here
questions.example: Take this to the office.

questions.prompt: Could you ___ me your pen for a minute?
questions.explanation: "lend" means you give something to someone for a short time, and it is followed by the person (lend me). You "borrow" something from someone, so "borrow me" is wrong.
questions.meaning: to give something for a short time
questions.example: Can you lend me a pen?

questions.prompt: If you know the answer, please ___ your hand.
questions.explanation: "raise" takes an object, and here the object is "your hand". "rise" has no object, as in "the sun rises".
questions.meaning: to lift something up
questions.example: Please raise your hand.

questions.prompt: Please ___ the baby gently on the bed.
questions.explanation: "lay" means to put something down, and it needs an object, here "the baby". "lie" has no object, as in "lie on the bed".
questions.meaning: to put something down flat
questions.example: Lay the book on the table.

questions.prompt: Can you ___ me to buy milk on the way home?
questions.explanation: "remind" means to make another person remember, and it is followed by the person and "to" (remind me to buy). "remember" is something you do yourself, so "remember me to buy" is wrong.
questions.meaning: to make someone remember something
questions.example: Please remind me to call him.

questions.prompt: Did she ___ you what time the meeting starts?
questions.explanation: "tell" is followed directly by the person you speak to (tell you). "say" needs "to" before the person, so "say you" is wrong.
questions.meaning: to give information to someone
questions.example: Tell me the truth.

questions.prompt: We went on a day ___ to the seaside.
questions.explanation: "trip" is a countable noun for one journey, so it fits "a day ___". "travel" is uncountable and means traveling in general, so "a day travel" is wrong.
questions.meaning: a short journey for a purpose
questions.example: We took a trip to the coast.

questions.prompt: She has too much ___ at the moment.
questions.explanation: "work" is uncountable, so it goes with "much". "job" is countable, so "much job" and "much jobs" are wrong.
questions.meaning: activity done to earn money
questions.example: I have a lot of work today.

questions.prompt: He is a ___ old man who rarely has visitors.
questions.explanation: "lonely" describes the sad feeling of having no company, and it can go before a noun (a lonely old man). "alone" just means without other people, and it cannot go before a noun.
questions.meaning: sad because you have no company
questions.example: He felt lonely in the big city.

questions.prompt: She studied ___ music at the conservatoire, mainly Bach and Mozart.
questions.explanation: "classical" names the traditional style of serious music, such as Bach and Mozart. "classic" means a typical or famous example of something, as in "a classic film".
questions.meaning: of the traditional style of serious music
questions.example: She plays classical music.

questions.prompt: The new medicine was very ___: the infection cleared up in two days.
questions.explanation: "effective" means it achieves the result you want, and here the infection cleared up. "efficient" means it works without wasting time or energy, which is not the point here.
questions.meaning: successful in giving the result you want
questions.example: This medicine is very effective.

questions.prompt: Please ___ that all the windows are closed before you leave.
questions.explanation: "ensure" means to make certain that something happens, so it fits "___ that all the windows are closed". "assure" and "reassure" need a person as the object (assure someone).
questions.meaning: to make certain that something happens
questions.example: Please ensure the door is locked.

questions.prompt: From his tone of voice, I ___ that he was upset.
questions.explanation: "infer" means the listener draws a conclusion from clues, here his tone of voice. "imply" is what the speaker does when suggesting something without saying it.
questions.meaning: to reach a conclusion from clues
questions.example: From his tone, I infer he is upset.

units.title: Linking Ideas
units.description: Discourse markers — Linkers signal contrast, cause, or addition — choose by logic.

questions.prompt: It was raining; ___ , we went out.
questions.explanation: Going out in the rain is the opposite of what you would expect, so you need a contrast linker: "nevertheless". "Therefore" shows a result, and "moreover" and "similarly" add or compare ideas.
questions.meaning: in spite of what was just said
questions.example: It rained; nevertheless, we went out.

questions.prompt: He was tired. ___ , he kept working.
questions.explanation: Working on despite being tired is a surprising contrast, and "Even so" can start a new sentence to show it, unlike "Despite", which needs a noun after it.
questions.meaning: used to add a surprising contrast
questions.example: He was tired. Even so, he kept working.

questions.prompt: ___ the cost, the project went ahead.
questions.explanation: "Despite" is followed directly by a noun phrase ("the cost") and means the project went ahead even though it was expensive.
questions.meaning: used to show something happened anyway
questions.example: Despite the cost, the project went ahead.

questions.prompt: She is talented; ___ , she lacks focus.
questions.explanation: The second clause is a contrast with being talented, so "however" fits after the semicolon, whereas "therefore" would show a result.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast
questions.example: She is talented; however, she lacks focus.

questions.prompt: ___ of the delay, we arrived on time.
questions.explanation: "In spite" fits here. Rule to remember: Linkers signal contrast, cause, or addition — choose by logic.
questions.meaning: despite
questions.example: In spite of the delay, we arrived on time.

questions.prompt: The plan failed ___ poor planning.
questions.explanation: Poor planning is the cause of the failure, and "due to" introduces a cause before a noun phrase.
questions.meaning: because of; caused by
questions.example: The flight was delayed due to bad weather.

questions.prompt: Most targets were met and costs fell. ___, the results were encouraging.
questions.explanation: The sentence gives a general conclusion about the results, so you need a summing-up word: "Overall".
questions.meaning: used to sum up the main idea
questions.example: Overall, the results were encouraging.

questions.prompt: He studied hard; ___ , he passed.
questions.explanation: Studying hard leads to passing, so you need a linker that shows a result: "therefore".
questions.meaning: used to show a result
questions.example: He studied hard; therefore, he passed.

questions.prompt: We have three things to discuss today. ___, let's review the numbers.
questions.explanation: The speaker announces three things to discuss, so the first point needs a sequencing word: "Firstly".
questions.meaning: used to begin a list of points
questions.example: Firstly, let's review the numbers.

questions.prompt: The data is old; ___ , it's still useful.
questions.explanation: Being old would suggest the data is useless, so the sentence needs a contrast linker: "nonetheless".
questions.meaning: in spite of that
questions.example: The data is old; nonetheless, it's useful.

questions.prompt: ___ addition, costs have risen.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase for adding a point is "In addition", so the missing word is "In".
questions.meaning: used in 'in addition' to add another point
questions.example: In addition, costs have risen.

questions.prompt: We must act ___ it's too late.
questions.explanation: "it's too late" is a point in time we must not reach, so the conjunction meaning 'earlier than' is needed: "before".
questions.meaning: earlier than a stated time
questions.example: We must act before it's too late.

questions.prompt: ___ as the report suggests, sales fell.
questions.explanation: "Just" combines with "as" to mean 'exactly in the way that', so "Just as the report suggests" fits; the other linkers cannot precede "as" like this.
questions.meaning: with "as", means exactly in the same way
questions.example: Just as the report suggests, sales fell.

questions.prompt: Sales fell, costs rose and key staff left. ___ , the strategy needs revision.
questions.explanation: "In short" introduces a brief conclusion before the comma, summing up that the strategy needs revision; "nevertheless" would signal contrast instead.
questions.meaning: used to give a brief conclusion
questions.example: In short, the strategy needs revision.

questions.prompt: She left early ___ she felt ill.
questions.explanation: Feeling ill is the reason she left early, so you need a conjunction that gives a reason: "because"; "although" would show a contrast instead.
questions.meaning: used to give a reason
questions.example: She left early because she felt ill.

questions.prompt: ___ contrast, exports grew.
questions.explanation: "In" completes the fixed phrase "In contrast", which introduces a difference from the previous point; the other options do not combine with 'contrast' here.
questions.meaning: used in 'in contrast' to show a difference
questions.example: In contrast, exports grew.

questions.prompt: He is, ___ , the best candidate (though some people may disagree).
questions.explanation: The clue says some people may disagree, so the claim needs hedging: "arguably"; "undoubtedly" would say nobody could disagree.
questions.meaning: probably, though some may disagree
questions.example: He is, arguably, the best candidate.

questions.prompt: The plan could save money. ___ hand, the risks are real.
questions.explanation: "On the other" completes the fixed phrase "On the other hand", which contrasts the risks with the money the plan could save.
questions.meaning: used to introduce an opposing point
questions.example: On the other hand, the risks are real.

questions.prompt: The trial failed; ___, funding stopped.
questions.explanation: Funding stopping is the result of the trial failing, so the cause-and-effect linker "consequently" fits; "Even so" would wrongly signal contrast.
questions.meaning: as a result
questions.example: The trial failed; consequently, funding stopped.

questions.prompt: ___ than complain, act.
questions.explanation: "Rather" pairs with "than" to mean 'instead of', so "Rather than complain, act" is correct; the other linkers cannot be followed by "than".
questions.meaning: used in 'rather than' to mean 'instead of'
questions.example: Rather than complain, try to fix the problem.

questions.prompt: ___ far, progress is slow.
questions.explanation: "So" forms the fixed phrase "So far", meaning 'up to now', which suits describing current slow progress.
questions.meaning: with "far", means up to now
questions.example: So far, progress is slow.

questions.prompt: We agreed, ___ with conditions.
questions.explanation: "albeit" means 'although' and is followed directly by a phrase, here "with conditions", conceding a limit on the agreement; the other options need a clause or a different structure.
questions.meaning: although; even though
questions.example: We agreed, albeit with conditions.

questions.prompt: ___ this in mind, we proceeded.
questions.explanation: "With" forms the phrase "With this in mind", meaning 'considering this', before the main clause.
questions.meaning: in "with this in mind": considering this
questions.example: With this in mind, we proceeded.

questions.prompt: The repairs start next month. ___, the elevator is still broken.
questions.explanation: "Meanwhile" means "in the time before something happens", so it links the period before the repairs start with the elevator still being broken.
questions.meaning: at the same time; in the meantime
questions.example: I'll cook dinner. Meanwhile, you can set the table.

questions.prompt: The claim is, ___, unproven.
questions.explanation: "however" can sit between commas in the middle of a sentence to add a contrast, as in "The claim is, however, unproven"; the other words cannot stand alone there.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast
questions.example: The claim is, however, unproven.

units.title: Reported Speech
units.description: Backshift and reporting verbs — Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.

questions.prompt: He said he ___ tired.
questions.explanation: After the past-tense reporting verb "said", the present "is" shifts back to "was". "He said he was tired" reports "I am tired".
questions.meaning: a past form of be in reported speech
questions.example: He said he was tired.

questions.prompt: She told me she ___ finished the report.
questions.explanation: "I have finished the report" shifts back to the past perfect after the past verb "told", so we need "had" before "finished the report".
questions.meaning: helper verb that forms the past perfect
questions.example: She told me she had finished.

questions.prompt: They said they ___ come later.
questions.explanation: Reporting "We will come later" after "said" shifts "will" back to "would", and "would" is followed by the bare infinitive "come".
questions.meaning: the reported form of will
questions.example: They said they would come later.

questions.prompt: He asked ___ I was free.
questions.explanation: A reported yes-or-no question is introduced with "if", so "Are you free?" becomes "He asked if I was free".
questions.meaning: used to report a yes-or-no question
questions.example: He asked if I was free.

questions.prompt: She asked me where I ___ . (Her question: "Where do you live?")
questions.explanation: The question "Where do you live?" shifts back to the past simple in reported speech, giving "lived". "Was" would answer a different question about being somewhere.
questions.meaning: the past tense of live
questions.example: She asked me where I lived.

questions.prompt: He admitted ___ the mistake.
questions.explanation: "Admit" is followed by an -ing form, so the sentence needs "making": "He admitted making the mistake".
questions.meaning: the -ing form of make, used after admit
questions.example: He admitted making the mistake.

questions.prompt: She refused ___ comment.
questions.explanation: "to" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after refuse
questions.example: She refused to comment.

questions.prompt: They denied ___ involved.
questions.explanation: "being" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after deny
questions.example: They denied being involved.

questions.prompt: He promised ___ help.
questions.explanation: "to" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after promise
questions.example: He promised to help.

questions.prompt: She suggested ___ a break.
questions.explanation: "taking" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after suggest
questions.example: She suggested taking a break.

questions.prompt: He warned us ___ to go.
questions.explanation: "not" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used to give a negative warning
questions.example: He warned us not to go.

questions.prompt: She explained that she ___ busy.
questions.explanation: The reporting verb "explained" is past, so "I am busy" shifts back to "was"; "were" doesn't agree with "she", and "being" and "has" can't come before "busy" here.
questions.meaning: a past form of be in reported speech
questions.example: She explained that she was busy.

questions.prompt: He insisted ___ paying.
questions.explanation: The verb "insist" takes the preposition "on" before an -ing form: "insisted on paying".
questions.meaning: a word that follows insist
questions.example: He insisted on paying.

questions.prompt: They announced that prices ___ rise.
questions.explanation: In reported speech the future "will rise" shifts back to "would" after the past verb "announced".
questions.meaning: the reported form of will
questions.example: They announced that prices would rise.

questions.prompt: She apologized ___ being late.
questions.explanation: We apologize "for" something, so "for" is followed by the -ing form "being late".
questions.meaning: a word that follows apologize
questions.example: She apologized for being late.

questions.prompt: He claimed he ___ seen nothing.
questions.explanation: "I saw nothing" is reported with the past perfect, so the helper verb "had" goes before "seen". "have" doesn't backshift after "claimed".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for reporting an earlier action
questions.example: He claimed he had seen nothing.

questions.prompt: She reminded me ___ call.
questions.explanation: "to" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after remind
questions.example: She reminded me to call.

questions.prompt: He complained ___ the noise.
questions.explanation: We complain "about" a problem, such as the noise, and complain to the person who can deal with it.
questions.meaning: a word that follows complain
questions.example: He complained about the noise.

questions.prompt: They agreed ___ postpone.
questions.explanation: "to" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after agree
questions.example: They agreed to postpone.

questions.prompt: She wondered ___ it was true.
questions.explanation: A reported yes/no question after "wondered" is introduced by "whether" (or if), not by "that", which reports statements.
questions.meaning: used to report a question with doubt
questions.example: She wondered whether it was true.

questions.prompt: He offered ___ drive us.
questions.explanation: "to" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after offer
questions.example: He offered to drive us.

questions.prompt: She accused him ___ lying.
questions.explanation: The verb "accuse" takes "of" before the charge: "accused him of lying".
questions.meaning: a word that follows accuse
questions.example: She accused him of lying.

questions.prompt: He recommended ___ the early train.
questions.explanation: "taking" fits here. Rule to remember: Tenses usually shift back one step when reporting.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after recommend
questions.example: He recommended taking the early train.

questions.prompt: She confirmed that she ___ attend.
questions.explanation: The direct words were "I will attend", and "will" shifts back to "would" after the past verb "confirmed".
questions.meaning: the reported form of will
questions.example: She confirmed that she would attend.

questions.prompt: He asked what time the meeting ___ .
questions.explanation: A reported question uses statement word order with no "did", so the past form "started" follows the subject "the meeting".
questions.meaning: began
questions.example: He asked what time the meeting started.

units.title: Strong Collocations
units.description: Natural word partners — Advanced fluency lives in collocation.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (rain that falls hard and fast): ___ rain
questions.explanation: In English, strong rain is "heavy" rain; we do not say strong rain or big rain.
questions.meaning: large in amount or very strong
questions.example: Heavy rain fell all night.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ evidence (convincing)"?
questions.explanation: Evidence that is so convincing it is hard to doubt is called "compelling" evidence; heavy, fierce and keen do not go with "evidence".
questions.meaning: so strong that it is hard to doubt
questions.example: The police found compelling evidence.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (large enough to matter): ___ difference
questions.explanation: A difference that is large enough to be important is a "significant" difference; widespread, heavy and thorough do not describe a difference.
questions.meaning: large enough to be important
questions.example: There is a significant difference between them.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ silence (complete)"?
questions.explanation: "utter" is the usual intensifier with "silence" and means total, complete silence; "heated", "firm" and "convincing" do not pair with it.
questions.meaning: complete; total
questions.example: They sat in utter silence.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (very serious): ___ mistake
questions.explanation: A very serious mistake with bad results is a "grave" mistake; fierce, keen and striking do not go with "mistake" in this sense.
questions.meaning: very serious and worrying
questions.example: He made a grave mistake.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ opportunity (rare)"?
questions.explanation: A "golden" opportunity is a fixed phrase for a rare, very good chance that you should not miss.
questions.meaning: very good and rare
questions.example: It was a golden opportunity.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (intense and angry): ___ debate
questions.explanation: A debate full of strong feeling and anger is a "heated" debate, as if the argument gets hot.
questions.meaning: full of strong feeling and anger
questions.example: They had a heated debate.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ progress (regular and continuing)"?
questions.explanation: We say "steady" progress for improvement that continues at a regular rate; 'high' or 'concerted' progress is not natural English.
questions.meaning: continuing at a regular rate
questions.example: She is making steady progress.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (very harsh and angry): ___ criticism
questions.explanation: We say "fierce" criticism for very harsh, angry disapproval; "golden", "convincing" and "complete" do not collocate with "criticism" in this sense.
questions.meaning: very strong and angry
questions.example: The plan met fierce criticism.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ demand (great)"?
questions.explanation: With demand we say "high" demand when a lot of people want something; thorough, convincing and heated do not go with "demand".
questions.meaning: great in amount or level
questions.example: There is high demand for tickets.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ impact (deep and powerful)"?
questions.explanation: A "profound" impact is a deep, powerful effect; we say a thorough check, a concerted effort and a heated debate, but these words do not describe an impact.
questions.meaning: having a deep and strong effect
questions.example: The news had a profound impact.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (fixed, cannot be changed): ___ deadline
questions.explanation: A "strict" deadline is one that is fixed and must be met exactly; "golden", "complete" and "convincing" do not pair with "deadline".
questions.meaning: that must be followed exactly
questions.example: We have a strict deadline.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ concern (increasing)"?
questions.explanation: We say "growing" concern when worry is increasing over time; "compelling", "concerted" and "fierce" do not collocate with "concern" this way.
questions.meaning: becoming bigger over time
questions.example: There is growing concern about prices.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (makes people believe it): ___ argument
questions.explanation: A "convincing" argument is one that makes people believe it; "keen", "striking" and "steady" do not collocate with "argument" in this sense.
questions.meaning: able to make you believe it
questions.example: She made a convincing argument.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ change (basic)"?
questions.explanation: A "fundamental" change affects the most basic part of something; 'sharp' change means sudden, not basic.
questions.meaning: affecting the most basic part
questions.example: We need a fundamental change.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (eager): take a ___ interest
questions.explanation: We say someone takes a "keen" interest in something when they are eager and enthusiastic about it.
questions.meaning: eager and strongly interested
questions.example: She takes a keen interest in art.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ traffic (crowded)"?
questions.explanation: English says "heavy" traffic when there are a lot of vehicles on the road, not 'sharp' or 'concerted' traffic.
questions.meaning: large in amount, as of traffic or rain
questions.example: Heavy traffic delayed us.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (detailed and complete): ___ knowledge
questions.explanation: A "thorough" knowledge of something is detailed and complete, with no gaps; "strict", "concerted" and "compelling" do not pair with "knowledge".
questions.meaning: complete and careful, with no gaps
questions.example: He has a thorough knowledge of law.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ apology (sincere)"?
questions.explanation: "heartfelt" means deeply and honestly felt, so "heartfelt apology" is the natural phrase for a sincere apology; the other words do not go with "apology".
questions.meaning: showing deep and honest feeling
questions.example: She offered a heartfelt apology.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (planned and done together): ___ effort
questions.explanation: "concerted" means planned and done together by several people, and "a concerted effort" is a fixed collocation.
questions.meaning: planned and done together by several people
questions.example: It needs a concerted effort.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (total): ___ failure
questions.explanation: We say a "complete" failure for something that failed totally; "heartfelt", "strict" and "fierce" do not collocate with "failure".
questions.meaning: total; in every way
questions.example: The plan was a complete failure.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ increase (sudden and large)"?
questions.explanation: A "sharp" increase is a sudden, large rise; "steady" means slow and regular, and "heavy" and "fundamental" do not pair with "increase" this way.
questions.meaning: sudden and large
questions.example: There was a sharp increase in prices.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (very noticeable): ___ resemblance
questions.explanation: "striking" means very noticeable, and "a striking resemblance" is the usual way to say two people or things look strongly alike.
questions.meaning: very noticeable, often in a surprising way
questions.example: There is a striking resemblance between them.

questions.prompt: Which word pairs with "___ decision (definite, not likely to change)"?
questions.explanation: A "firm" decision is definite and unlikely to change; "golden", "striking" and "growing" do not collocate with "decision".
questions.meaning: fixed and not likely to change
questions.example: He made a firm decision.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation (shared by many people): ___ support
questions.explanation: "widespread" support is support shared by many people in many places; "steady" support means constant over time, not broad.
questions.meaning: shared by many people over a large area
questions.example: The idea has widespread support.

units.title: Word Formation
units.description: Verb → noun — Suffix patterns are predictable once learned.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "analyze":
questions.explanation: The verb "analyze" becomes the noun "analysis" by changing -yse to -ysis, as in paralyse → paralysis.
questions.meaning: a careful study of something in parts
questions.example: The analysis took a week.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "decide": ___
questions.explanation: "Decide" drops -de and adds -sion to give "decision", like divide → division.
questions.meaning: a choice you make
questions.example: It was a hard decision.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "argue":
questions.explanation: Add -ment to "argue" and drop the final -e to get "argument" (not "arguement").
questions.meaning: a discussion where people disagree
questions.example: They had an argument about money.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "achieve": ___
questions.explanation: Add -ment to "achieve" to get "achievement"; here the final -e stays.
questions.meaning: something you did well with effort
questions.example: Passing the exam was a big achievement.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "succeed":
questions.explanation: "Succeed" becomes "success" by changing -ceed to -cess, so this noun has to be learned.
questions.meaning: doing well and getting what you wanted
questions.example: The show was a great success.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "fail": ___
questions.explanation: Add -ure to "fail" to get the noun "failure", like press → pressure.
questions.meaning: a lack of success
questions.example: The experiment ended in failure.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "maintain":
questions.explanation: "Maintain" becomes "maintenance": -ain changes to -en before -ance, so learn this spelling carefully.
questions.meaning: work to keep something in good condition
questions.example: The car needs regular maintenance.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "prove": ___
questions.explanation: "Prove" becomes "proof" by changing the final -ve to -f, like believe → belief.
questions.meaning: facts that show something is true
questions.example: Do you have proof of payment?

questions.prompt: Noun form of "choose":
questions.explanation: "Choose" becomes "choice"; both the vowel and the ending change, so this noun has to be learned.
questions.meaning: a range of things to pick from
questions.example: You have a choice of three meals.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "lose": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "lose" is "loss"; it does not follow a regular suffix rule, so learn the pair lose → loss.
questions.meaning: the state of no longer having something
questions.example: The loss of his job was a big shock.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "believe": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "believe" is "belief": the final -ve changes to -f, as in relieve → relief.
questions.meaning: something you accept as true
questions.example: It is my belief that he is honest.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "grow":
questions.explanation: Add -th to "grow" to make the noun "growth".
questions.meaning: the process of getting bigger
questions.example: The economy saw strong growth last year.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "know": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "know" is "knowledge": you add the unusual ending -ledge, so learn it as a set word.
questions.meaning: facts and skills you have learned
questions.example: He has a good knowledge of history.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "solve":
questions.explanation: The noun of "solve" is "solution": -lve becomes -lution, as in resolve → resolution.
questions.meaning: an answer to a problem
questions.example: We found a simple solution.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "apply": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "apply" is "application": the -y becomes -ic and you add -ation, as in multiply → multiplication.
questions.meaning: a formal request for a job or place
questions.example: I sent my application today.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "persuade":
questions.explanation: The noun of "persuade" is "persuasion": the -de ending changes to -sion, as in decide → decision.
questions.meaning: the act of making someone agree
questions.example: Persuasion is part of selling.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "expand": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "expand" is "expansion": the final -d changes to -sion, as in extend → extension.
questions.meaning: the process of getting bigger
questions.example: The company announced its expansion.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "respond":
questions.explanation: The noun of "respond" is "response": the final -d simply changes to -se, with no extra suffix.
questions.meaning: an answer or reaction
questions.example: We are waiting for a response.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "behave": ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "behave" is "behavior": drop the -e and add -ior.
questions.meaning: the way a person acts
questions.example: His behavior was rude.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "survive":
questions.explanation: The noun of "survive" is "survival": drop the -e and add -al, as in arrive → arrival.
questions.meaning: staying alive in difficult conditions
questions.example: The animals fought for survival.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "explain":
questions.explanation: The noun of "explain" is "explanation": add -ation, and the -ai- of the verb becomes -a-, so there is no i after the a.
questions.meaning: words or reasons that make something clear
questions.example: Her explanation was easy to follow.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "assume": ___
questions.explanation: The verb "assume" becomes the noun "assumption": the final -e goes and -ption is added, as in consume → consumption.
questions.meaning: something you accept as true without proof
questions.example: That is just an assumption.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "conclude":
questions.explanation: The verb "conclude" becomes the noun "conclusion": the ending -de changes to -sion, as in decide → decision.
questions.meaning: a final decision or opinion after thought
questions.example: We came to the same conclusion.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "refuse": ___
questions.explanation: The verb "refuse" becomes the noun "refusal": the final -e is dropped and -al is added, as in arrive → arrival.
questions.meaning: saying no to something
questions.example: The refusal surprised everyone.

questions.prompt: Noun form of "depart":
questions.explanation: The verb "depart" becomes the noun "departure" by adding -ure, as in fail → failure.
questions.meaning: the act of leaving a place
questions.example: Departure is at six.

units.title: Reporting & Hedging
units.description: Report what was said — Reported speech shifts tense back and changes time and place words.

questions.prompt: She said she ___ tired.
questions.explanation: The direct words were "I am tired", and after "said" the present "am" shifts back to "was".
questions.meaning: a past form of be in reported speech
questions.example: She said she was tired.

questions.prompt: He told ___ he would call.
questions.explanation: "Tell" must be followed directly by the person told, so "me" fits, whereas "say" would not take an object here.
questions.meaning: the word for the listener, after tell
questions.example: He told me he would call.

questions.prompt: They asked where I ___ from.
questions.explanation: The direct question was "Where do you come from?", and in reported speech the verb shifts back to the past, giving "came".
questions.meaning: the past of come
questions.example: They asked where I came from.

questions.prompt: She wondered ___ I had finished.
questions.explanation: "whether" completes the sentence "She wondered whether I had finished."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: used like 'if' to report a yes/no question
questions.example: She wondered whether I had finished.

questions.prompt: He admitted ___ the money.
questions.explanation: "Admit" is followed by the -ing form of the verb, so "taking" is right: "He admitted taking the money."
questions.meaning: said you did take something
questions.example: He admitted taking the money.

questions.prompt: She denied ___ anything wrong.
questions.explanation: "Deny" is followed by the -ing form, and "doing anything wrong" is the natural phrase, so "doing" is right.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after deny
questions.example: She denied doing anything wrong.

questions.prompt: He suggested ___ earlier.
questions.explanation: "leaving" completes the sentence "He suggested leaving earlier."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: the -ing form used after suggest
questions.example: He suggested leaving earlier.

questions.prompt: They insisted ___ paying the bill.
questions.explanation: The verb "insist" takes the preposition "on" before an -ing form, so we say "insisted on paying".
questions.meaning: a word that follows insist
questions.example: They insisted on paying the bill.

questions.prompt: She warned us ___ to touch it.
questions.explanation: A reported negative warning is formed with "not" before the infinitive, so "not to touch it" is right.
questions.meaning: told us to avoid something
questions.example: She warned us not to touch it.

questions.prompt: He apologized ___ being late.
questions.explanation: "Apologize" takes the preposition "for" before the thing you are sorry about, so we say "apologized for being late".
questions.meaning: a word that follows apologize
questions.example: He apologized for being late.

questions.prompt: She claimed ___ have seen him.
questions.explanation: "to" is correct because claim is followed by a to-infinitive, and here the perfect form "to have seen" refers to an earlier event.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after claim
questions.example: She claimed to have seen him.

questions.prompt: He refused ___ comment.
questions.explanation: Refuse takes a to-infinitive, so "to" goes before comment. It is not followed by an -ing form.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after refuse
questions.example: He refused to comment.

questions.prompt: They announced that the deal ___ off.
questions.explanation: After the past reporting verb "announced", the reported clause usually moves back to the past, so "was" fits: "the deal was off".
questions.meaning: a past form of be for a state
questions.example: They announced that the deal was off.

questions.prompt: She explained ___ the system worked.
questions.explanation: Explain takes a clause beginning with a wh-word to say the manner of something, so "how" introduces what she explained about the system.
questions.meaning: used to report the way something works
questions.example: She explained how the system worked.

questions.prompt: She complained ___ the delay.
questions.explanation: Complain is followed by "about" before the thing you are unhappy with. "Complain of" is mainly for illnesses.
questions.meaning: a word that follows complain
questions.example: She complained about the delay.

questions.prompt: She reminded me ___ lock the door.
questions.explanation: Remind someone is followed by a to-infinitive, so "to" comes before lock the door.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after remind
questions.example: She reminded me to lock the door.

questions.prompt: He accused her ___ lying.
questions.explanation: Accuse someone is followed by "of" and then an -ing form, as in accused her of lying.
questions.meaning: a word that follows accuse
questions.example: He accused her of lying.

questions.prompt: They agreed ___ meet on Friday.
questions.explanation: Agree takes a to-infinitive for a shared plan, so "to" goes before meet.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after agree
questions.example: They agreed to meet on Friday.

questions.prompt: She promised she ___ help.
questions.explanation: After the past verb promised, the original "I will help" shifts to "would" in reported speech.
questions.meaning: the reported form of will
questions.example: She promised she would help.

questions.prompt: He asked me ___ I needed anything.
questions.explanation: "if" introduces a reported yes/no question, as in asked me if I needed anything.
questions.meaning: used to report a yes-or-no question
questions.example: He asked me if I needed anything.

questions.prompt: She pointed ___ the flaw in the plan.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb point out means to draw attention to something, so "out" completes pointed out the flaw.
questions.meaning: to make someone notice a fact
questions.example: She pointed out the flaw in the plan.

questions.prompt: He implied that something ___ wrong.
questions.explanation: After the past verb implied, the reported clause shifts back to the past, so "was" fits something was wrong.
questions.meaning: a past form of be in reported speech
questions.example: He implied that something was wrong.

questions.prompt: They confirmed the flight ___ been delayed.
questions.explanation: The delay happened before they confirmed it, so reported speech backshifts to the past perfect: "had" been delayed.
questions.meaning: a helper verb for an earlier action
questions.example: They confirmed the flight had been delayed.

questions.prompt: She urged them ___ reconsider.
questions.explanation: The verb 'urge' is followed by an object and a to-infinitive, so "to" is needed before 'reconsider'.
questions.meaning: used before a verb after urge
questions.example: She urged them to reconsider.

questions.prompt: He maintained that he ___ innocent.
questions.explanation: After the past-tense 'maintained', the original 'I am innocent' shifts back to "was" innocent.
questions.meaning: a past form of be in reported speech
questions.example: He maintained that he was innocent.

units.title: Collocations
units.description: Words that go together — Natural English depends on the right partner word.

questions.prompt: Complete: "make a ___"
questions.explanation: English says "make a decision", so "decision" is the partner word here. We say "take a risk" and "do business", and "experience" does not follow "make a" in this sense.
questions.meaning: to choose after thinking
questions.example: You must make a decision today.

questions.prompt: Complete: "take a ___"
questions.explanation: We say "risk" after "take a": to take a risk means to do something that might go wrong. You make a mistake, keep a promise and meet a deadline.
questions.meaning: a chance of loss or danger
questions.example: It's worth taking a risk.

questions.prompt: Complete: "pay ___"
questions.explanation: pay → attention. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: careful listening or watching
questions.example: Please pay attention to the teacher.

questions.prompt: Complete: "draw a ___" ___
questions.explanation: draw a → conclusion. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: a final opinion reached after thought
questions.example: We drew a conclusion from the facts.

questions.prompt: Complete: "meet a ___"
questions.explanation: We "meet a deadline" when we finish work by the time it is due, so "deadline" is right. We keep a promise, not meet one.
questions.meaning: the time by which work must be done
questions.example: We met the deadline.

questions.prompt: Complete: "raise ___" ___
questions.explanation: raise → awareness. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: knowledge that something exists or matters
questions.example: The campaign raised awareness of the problem.

questions.prompt: Complete: "break the ___"
questions.explanation: "Break the news" is a fixed phrase meaning to tell someone important, often bad, information, so the answer is "news".
questions.meaning: information about recent events
questions.example: He had to break the news gently.

questions.prompt: Complete: "keep a ___"
questions.explanation: We "keep a promise" when we do what we said we would do, so "promise" is right. We make a decision, ask a question and face a challenge.
questions.meaning: a statement that you will do something
questions.example: She always keeps her promises.

questions.prompt: Complete: "run a ___"
questions.explanation: The verb "run" goes with "business": to run a business means to manage a company. We make a decision, make a mistake and take a photo.
questions.meaning: a company that sells goods or services
questions.example: He runs a small business.

questions.prompt: Complete: "hold a ___"
questions.explanation: We "hold a meeting" when we organize one and have it, so "meeting" is right. You face a challenge and take responsibility.
questions.meaning: an event where people come to talk
questions.example: The team holds a meeting each week.

questions.prompt: Complete: "reach an ___"
questions.explanation: We "reach an agreement" when people finally accept the same decision, so "agreement" is right. You make an effort and take an interest.
questions.meaning: a decision or arrangement that everyone involved accepts
questions.example: They reached an agreement last night.

questions.prompt: Complete: "set a ___"
questions.explanation: To "set a precedent" means to do something that becomes an example for the future, so "precedent" is right. We make a promise, a statement or a decision.
questions.meaning: an earlier event used as an example
questions.example: The ruling set a precedent.

questions.prompt: Complete: "bear in ___"
questions.explanation: "Bear in mind" is a fixed phrase meaning to remember something and think about it, so the answer is "mind".
questions.meaning: to remember to consider something
questions.example: Bear in mind that it's a long trip.

questions.prompt: Complete: "take ___"
questions.explanation: We "take responsibility" when we accept that something is our duty or our fault, so "responsibility" is right. We make a promise and gain experience.
questions.meaning: the duty to accept blame or care
questions.example: She takes responsibility for her work.

questions.prompt: Complete: "place an ___" ___
questions.explanation: place an → order. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: a request to buy goods
questions.example: We placed an order online.

questions.prompt: Complete: "gain ___"
questions.explanation: gain → experience. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: skill you gain by doing something
questions.example: He gained experience abroad.

questions.prompt: Complete: "cause ___" ___
questions.explanation: cause → damage. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: harm that spoils something
questions.example: The storm caused serious damage.

questions.prompt: Complete: "express ___"
questions.explanation: express → concern. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: a feeling of worry about something
questions.example: She expressed concern about safety.

questions.prompt: Complete: "launch a ___" ___
questions.explanation: launch a → campaign. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: a planned series of actions for a goal
questions.example: They launched a campaign to save the park.

questions.prompt: Complete: "strike a ___"
questions.explanation: "Strike a balance" is a fixed phrase meaning to find a fair mix between two things, so "balance" is the partner of "strike a".
questions.meaning: a fair mix of two things
questions.example: It's hard to strike a balance between work and rest.

questions.prompt: Complete: "face a ___"
questions.explanation: face a → challenge. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: a difficult task that tests you
questions.example: She faced a big challenge.

questions.prompt: Complete: "issue a ___" ___
questions.explanation: issue a → statement. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: an official announcement
questions.example: The company issued a statement.

questions.prompt: Complete: "conduct ___"
questions.explanation: conduct → research. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: careful study to find new facts
questions.example: Scientists conduct research on diseases.

questions.prompt: Complete: "achieve a ___" ___
questions.explanation: achieve a → goal. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: something you work to reach
questions.example: He achieved his goal.

questions.prompt: Complete: "lose ___"
questions.explanation: lose → patience. Natural English depends on the right partner word.
questions.meaning: the ability to wait calmly
questions.example: I lose patience in traffic.

units.title: Health & Medicine
units.description: Describing symptoms and care — Intermediate-plus vocabulary for talking about health.

questions.prompt: The doctor ___ a full recovery within weeks.
questions.explanation: The doctor is saying what will happen in the future, which is what "predicted" means; 'diagnosed' names an illness, not a recovery.
questions.meaning: said what would happen before it did
questions.example: The doctor predicted a full recovery.

questions.prompt: She's been ___ from a bad cold all week.
questions.explanation: We "suffer from" an illness, so "suffering" fits 'been ___ from a bad cold'. You relieve, treat or prevent an illness directly, with no 'from'.
questions.meaning: feeling pain or illness
questions.example: She has been suffering from a cold.

questions.prompt: He was ___ to hospital after the accident.
questions.explanation: A patient taken into hospital is "admitted" to it; the other words do not fit 'was ___ to hospital'.
questions.meaning: accepted into hospital as a patient
questions.example: He was admitted to hospital after the accident.

questions.prompt: The medicine should ___ the pain quickly.
questions.explanation: Medicine makes pain less, which is what "relieve" means; a person recovers or suffers, and doctors refer patients, so those verbs cannot take 'the pain' here.
questions.meaning: to make pain or worry less
questions.example: This medicine will relieve the pain.

questions.prompt: She's ___ to penicillin, so avoid it.
questions.explanation: The adjective that takes 'to' for a substance that makes you ill is "allergic", which is why she should avoid penicillin.
questions.meaning: made ill by something you eat or touch
questions.example: I'm allergic to nuts.

questions.prompt: The nurse took his ___ before the appointment.
questions.explanation: Nurses 'take' a patient's "temperature" with a thermometer; a doctor gives a diagnosis, and a patient has a check-up or takes medication.
questions.meaning: how hot or cold your body is
questions.example: The nurse took his temperature.

questions.prompt: He's on ___ to manage his blood pressure.
questions.explanation: 'On ___' with no article needs an uncountable noun for regular drugs, so "medication" fits; singular 'tablet' would need 'a'.
questions.meaning: medicine that a doctor gives you
questions.example: He takes medication for blood pressure.

questions.prompt: The wound needs to be ___ regularly.
questions.explanation: To 'dress' a wound means to cover it with a clean bandage, so after 'needs to be' we use the passive "dressed"; patients are admitted and diagnosed, and drugs are prescribed.
questions.meaning: covered with a clean bandage
questions.example: The wound was dressed twice a day.

questions.prompt: She was ___ with a mild infection.
questions.explanation: A patient is "diagnosed" with an illness when a doctor finds out what it is, so 'diagnosed with a mild infection' is the right pattern.
questions.meaning: found to have a particular illness
questions.example: She was diagnosed with a mild infection.

questions.prompt: Rest and fluids should help you ___.
questions.explanation: After 'help you' we need a base verb meaning to get well again, so "recover" fits; 'prevent' and 'refer' need an object, and rest would not help you 'suffer'.
questions.meaning: to get well again
questions.example: You should recover soon.

questions.prompt: The clinic offers a free ___ once a year.
questions.explanation: After "a free" we need a noun, and a routine medical examination once a year is a "check-up".
questions.meaning: a routine medical examination
questions.example: I have a check-up every year.

questions.prompt: He ___ his ankle playing soccer.
questions.explanation: Hurting an ankle with a sudden turning movement while playing soccer is described by "twisted"; the other verbs don't take 'his ankle' with this meaning.
questions.meaning: hurt a joint by turning it suddenly
questions.example: He twisted his ankle.

questions.prompt: The vaccine helps ___ the disease.
questions.explanation: "Helps" is followed by a base-form verb, and a vaccine's purpose is to stop a disease happening, so "prevent" is right.
questions.meaning: to stop something from happening
questions.example: The vaccine helps prevent the disease.

questions.prompt: She's been feeling ___ since yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Feeling" needs an adjective for a sick sensation, and "nauseous" means feeling that you may be sick. "Check-up" is a noun.
questions.meaning: feeling that you may be sick
questions.example: I felt nauseous all morning.

questions.prompt: The doctor ___ two weeks of rest.
questions.explanation: A doctor advising two weeks of rest "recommended" it; the other verbs don't fit a doctor suggesting treatment.
questions.meaning: advised as a good thing to do
questions.example: The doctor recommended two weeks of rest.

questions.prompt: His symptoms ___ after a few days.
questions.explanation: Symptoms that get better over a few days "improved"; the other words are not past-tense verbs that fit 'symptoms ___ after a few days'.
questions.meaning: got better
questions.example: His symptoms improved after a few days.

questions.prompt: The hospital ___ him overnight for observation.
questions.explanation: Hospitals "admitted" patients when they take them in, here overnight for observation. The other options are not past-tense verbs that fit.
questions.meaning: accepted into hospital as a patient
questions.example: The hospital admitted him overnight.

questions.prompt: She takes a daily ___ for her allergies: one small pill with water.
questions.explanation: The clue "one small pill with water" points to a "tablet"; a check-up, surgery or anaesthesia is not something you swallow every day.
questions.meaning: a small pill of medicine
questions.example: She takes a tablet every day.

questions.prompt: The surgeon ___ the operation successfully.
questions.explanation: A surgeon carries out an operation, and the verb for that is "performed"; you do not prevent, recover or admit an operation.
questions.meaning: carried out a task or action
questions.example: The surgeon performed the operation.

questions.prompt: He's ___ to a specialist for further tests.
questions.explanation: "He's ___ to a specialist" needs a past participle meaning sent on to another doctor, which is "referred".
questions.meaning: sent to another doctor or place
questions.example: He was referred to a specialist.

questions.prompt: The patient's condition remained ___, neither better nor worse.
questions.explanation: The clue "neither better nor worse" describes a condition that is not changing, so "stable" is right, not "improved".
questions.meaning: not changing; not getting worse
questions.example: The patient's condition stayed stable.

questions.prompt: She was given ___ before the procedure.
questions.explanation: "anaesthesia" completes the sentence "She was given anaesthesia before the procedure."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: drugs that stop you feeling pain
questions.example: She was given anaesthesia before the operation.

questions.prompt: The clinic is fully ___ for emergencies.
questions.explanation: "equipped" fits because "fully equipped for" means having all the tools and supplies needed, which is what a clinic needs for emergencies.
questions.meaning: having the tools and supplies needed
questions.example: The clinic is well equipped.

questions.prompt: His recovery has been slow but ___.
questions.explanation: "steady" fits because "slow but steady" describes progress that continues at an even pace; the other options describe illness, not recovery.
questions.meaning: continuing at an even, regular rate
questions.example: His recovery has been steady.

questions.prompt: The doctor advised him to ___ smoking.
questions.explanation: "quit" fits because "advised him to quit smoking" means to stop the habit; the other words cannot follow "to" and take "smoking" sensibly.
questions.meaning: to stop doing something
questions.example: He decided to quit smoking.

units.title: Technology & Media
units.description: Talking about devices and news — Everyday tech and media vocabulary at B2 level.

questions.prompt: My phone's ___ died, so I couldn't call.
questions.explanation: "battery" fits because a phone that "died" has run out of power, and the battery is what supplies it, so I couldn't call.
questions.meaning: a small device that gives power
questions.example: My phone's battery died.

questions.prompt: The app keeps ___ every time I open it.
questions.explanation: "crashing" fits because "keeps" must be followed by an -ing form, and an app that stops working suddenly is said to be crashing.
questions.meaning: suddenly stopping working
questions.example: The app keeps crashing.

questions.prompt: We need to ___ the software before using it.
questions.explanation: "update" fits because "need to" takes the base verb, and updating software brings it to the newest version before you use it.
questions.meaning: to change software to the newest version
questions.example: Please update the software.

questions.prompt: The article went ___ within hours.
questions.explanation: "viral" fits because "go viral" is the fixed phrase for content that spreads very fast online, here "within hours".
questions.meaning: spreading very fast online
questions.example: The video went viral.

questions.prompt: He ___ his password and got locked out.
questions.explanation: "forgot" fits because not remembering his password explains why he got locked out; the other past forms don't give that cause.
questions.meaning: could not remember
questions.example: He forgot his password.

questions.prompt: The company was ___ over a data breach.
questions.explanation: "criticized" fits because people publicly blame a company after a data breach; nobody praises, upgrades or debunks a company for that.
questions.meaning: blamed for doing something wrong
questions.example: The company was criticized over the breach.

questions.prompt: Streaming services have ___ how we watch TV.
questions.explanation: "changed" fits because "have changed how we watch TV" needs a past participle meaning made different, which is the effect of streaming.
questions.meaning: made something different
questions.example: Streaming has changed how we watch TV.

questions.prompt: She ___ the video before sharing it.
questions.explanation: "verified" fits because she checked that the video was genuine before passing it on; you cannot share a video you have deleted.
questions.meaning: checked that something is true
questions.example: She verified the video first.

questions.prompt: The signal ___ whenever it rains.
questions.explanation: "drops" fits because a signal that gets weaker or is lost when it rains is said to drop; the subject "signal" takes the -s form.
questions.meaning: gets weaker or lost
questions.example: The signal drops when it rains.

questions.prompt: This site collects your data without ___.
questions.explanation: "consent" means permission, and it is the only noun here that fits after 'without' to describe collecting data. The other options do not make sense in this sentence.
questions.meaning: permission to do something
questions.example: They collect data without consent.

questions.prompt: The report was ___ by several news outlets.
questions.explanation: "shared" fits the passive "was ___ by several news outlets" because outlets pass a report on to their audiences; the other words do not describe something outlets do to a report.
questions.meaning: passed on to other people
questions.example: Several outlets shared the report.

questions.prompt: He ___ his old laptop for a new one.
questions.explanation: "upgraded" means replaced with a better version, which matches swapping an old laptop 'for a new one'. The other words do not describe replacing a device.
questions.meaning: replaced with a better version
questions.example: He upgraded his old laptop.

questions.prompt: The false story was quickly ___ by fact-checkers.
questions.explanation: "debunked" means shown to be false, which fits a 'false story' dealt with by fact-checkers. 'Verified' would mean proved true, which contradicts 'false'.
questions.meaning: shown to be false
questions.example: Fact-checkers debunked the story.

questions.prompt: Most people now get news through social ___.
questions.explanation: "media" completes the fixed phrase 'social media', the websites and apps where people share news. The other words do not form a phrase with 'social'.
questions.meaning: ways of sharing news and information
questions.example: The story was all over the media last week.

questions.prompt: The website ___ if too many users log in.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a verb after 'The website', and "crashes" means suddenly stops working, which is what happens when too many users log in. The other options are nouns.
questions.meaning: suddenly stops working
questions.example: The website crashes if too many people log in.

questions.prompt: She backed up her files to the ___.
questions.explanation: Files are backed up online to "cloud" storage, so 'the cloud' is the natural phrase here. The other words are not places where files can be saved.
questions.meaning: online storage on distant computers
questions.example: She backed up her files to the cloud.

questions.prompt: The headline was clearly ___.
questions.explanation: "misleading" is an adjective meaning giving a false idea, and it describes a headline that does not honestly reflect the story. The other options do not describe a headline.
questions.meaning: giving a wrong or false idea
questions.example: The headline was clearly misleading.

questions.prompt: He swiped and ___ the news alert, so it vanished from his screen unread.
questions.explanation: To dismiss an alert is to swipe it away without opening it, so "dismissed" explains why it vanished from his screen unread.
questions.meaning: chose to ignore something
questions.example: He dismissed the alert.

questions.prompt: The device connects ___ to your phone.
questions.explanation: The gap needs an adverb to describe how the device 'connects', and "wirelessly" means without cables. The other options are not adverbs.
questions.meaning: without any cables
questions.example: The speaker connects wirelessly to your phone.

questions.prompt: Online ___ can spread faster than facts.
questions.explanation: "misinformation" means false information, which is what 'can spread faster than facts'. The other nouns do not describe things that compete with facts.
questions.meaning: false information that spreads
questions.example: Misinformation can spread faster than facts.

questions.prompt: The company issued a public ___.
questions.explanation: A company 'issued a public "apology"' is a fixed collocation meaning it said publicly that it was sorry. The other nouns do not go with 'issued a public'.
questions.meaning: a statement saying you are sorry
questions.example: The company issued a public apology.

questions.prompt: She disabled ___ to save her battery.
questions.explanation: "notifications" completes the sentence "She disabled notifications to save her battery."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: messages from an app on your phone
questions.example: I turned off notifications.

questions.prompt: The article relied on a source that was ___.
questions.explanation: A source you cannot trust is "unreliable", which describes a poor basis for a news article.
questions.meaning: that you cannot trust
questions.example: The article cited an unreliable source.

questions.prompt: His account was ___ after suspicious activity.
questions.explanation: "suspended" completes the sentence "His account was suspended after suspicious activity."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: stopped for a time
questions.example: His account was suspended.

questions.prompt: The platform introduced stricter privacy ___.
questions.explanation: "settings" completes the sentence "The platform introduced stricter privacy settings."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: choices that control how an app works
questions.example: Check your privacy settings.

units.title: Business & Negotiation
units.description: Deals and workplace talk — B2-level vocabulary for meetings and negotiations.

questions.prompt: We need to ___ a deal before the deadline.
questions.explanation: "close" completes the sentence "We need to close a deal before the deadline."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to finish an agreement successfully
questions.example: We want to close the deal.

questions.prompt: Both sides made a ___ to reach agreement.
questions.explanation: "compromise" completes the sentence "Both sides made a compromise to reach agreement."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: an agreement where each side gives something up
questions.example: Both sides reached a compromise.

questions.prompt: The company plans to ___ into new markets.
questions.explanation: "expand" completes the sentence "The company plans to expand into new markets."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to grow bigger
questions.example: The firm plans to expand abroad.

questions.prompt: We're hoping to ___ a long-term partnership.
questions.explanation: "build" completes the sentence "We're hoping to build a long-term partnership."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to create over time
questions.example: We want to build a partnership.

questions.prompt: The talks broke down over pricing ___.
questions.explanation: "disputes" completes the sentence "The talks broke down over pricing disputes."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: serious disagreements
questions.example: Pricing disputes ended the talks.

questions.prompt: She was promoted to ___ the new division.
questions.explanation: "head" completes the sentence "She was promoted to head the new division."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to lead a group or department
questions.example: She was promoted to head the division.

questions.prompt: The merger was finally ___ this week.
questions.explanation: "approved" completes the sentence "The merger was finally approved this week."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: officially accepted
questions.example: The merger was approved this week.

questions.prompt: We need to ___ the terms before signing.
questions.explanation: "finalize" completes the sentence "We need to finalize the terms before signing."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to agree the last details
questions.example: We need to finalize the terms.

questions.prompt: His proposal was ___ by the board.
questions.explanation: After "was" the sentence needs a past participle meaning the board refused the proposal, so "rejected" fits.
questions.meaning: refused to accept
questions.example: The board rejected his proposal.

questions.prompt: The company had to ___ several employees.
questions.explanation: The clue is "several employees": a company that has to do something to workers is ending their jobs, which is "lay off".
questions.meaning: to stop employing workers
questions.example: The company had to lay off staff.

questions.prompt: We're aiming to ___ costs by ten percent.
questions.explanation: "cut" completes the sentence "We're aiming to cut costs by ten percent."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to make smaller
questions.example: We aim to cut costs.

questions.prompt: The client asked the builder for a written ___ before the work started.
questions.explanation: A "quote" is the price a supplier puts in writing before doing a job, which is what the client wants before work starts.
questions.meaning: a price a seller says they will charge
questions.example: The client asked for a better quote.

questions.prompt: They reached a ___ after hours of talks, and both sides signed the contract.
questions.explanation: The signed contract shows a business agreement was made, which is a "deal"; a compromise would mean each side gave something up.
questions.meaning: an agreement in business
questions.example: They struck a deal.

questions.prompt: The firm plans to ___ with a rival company.
questions.explanation: Plans to join with a rival company so that the two become one is "merge", and it takes "with"; "expand" and "extend" do not.
questions.meaning: to join to form one company
questions.example: The firm plans to merge with a rival.

questions.prompt: We need more data before we can ___ which supplier to use.
questions.explanation: Only "decide" can be followed by "which supplier to use", meaning to choose after thinking; you cannot build or merge "which supplier".
questions.meaning: to choose after thinking
questions.example: We need more data to decide.

questions.prompt: The negotiation ___ down to price alone.
questions.explanation: The idiom "come down to" means to be decided by one main factor, and the past tense "came" matches the sentence.
questions.meaning: to be decided by one main thing
questions.example: It may come down to price.

questions.prompt: She's known for driving a hard ___.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase "drive a hard bargain" describes someone who negotiates tough terms, so "bargain" is the word.
questions.meaning: an agreement reached after both sides negotiate
questions.example: She drives a hard bargain.

questions.prompt: The board will ___ on the proposal tomorrow.
questions.explanation: After "will" you need a bare verb, and only "vote" is followed by "on" here. We "discuss", "approve" or "reject" a proposal with no "on".
questions.meaning: to formally choose by hand or ballot
questions.example: The board will vote tomorrow.

questions.prompt: We're under pressure to ___ a decision quickly.
questions.explanation: The collocation is "make a decision", and "under pressure to" needs a bare verb, so "make" fits.
questions.meaning: to choose after thinking
questions.example: We must make a decision quickly.

questions.prompt: The deal fell ___ at the last minute.
questions.explanation: "through" completes the sentence "The deal fell through at the last minute."; the other options do not make sense there.
questions.meaning: to fail to happen
questions.example: The deal could fall through.

questions.prompt: They agreed to ___ the contract for a year.
questions.explanation: We "extend" a contract when we make it last longer, which fits "for a year". We "expand" or "grow" a business, not the length of a contract.
questions.meaning: to make something last longer
questions.example: They agreed to extend the contract.

questions.prompt: The company issued new ___ to investors.
questions.explanation: Companies issue "shares" to investors, meaning parts of the company that people can own; the other words do not fit with "issued new".
questions.meaning: parts of a company that people can own
questions.example: The firm issued new shares.

questions.prompt: We need buy-in from all ___ involved.
questions.explanation: "stakeholders" are people with an interest in a business, and the plural fits "all ___ involved" when you need their buy-in.
questions.meaning: people with an interest in a business
questions.example: We need all stakeholders involved.

questions.prompt: The CEO announced a major ___ in strategy.
questions.explanation: A "shift" in strategy means a change of direction, and "major shift" is the natural collocation here.
questions.meaning: a change in direction
questions.example: The CEO announced a shift in strategy.

questions.prompt: Negotiations are still ___ ongoing.
questions.explanation: "very much" is used to stress that something is definitely happening, as in "still very much ongoing". "Very" alone cannot be used with "ongoing" here.
questions.meaning: to a great degree
questions.example: Negotiations are very much ongoing.

units.title: Crime & Law
units.description: Reporting incidents — B2-level vocabulary for news and crime reports.

questions.prompt: The suspect was ___ near the scene.
questions.explanation: After "was" you need a past participle, and "arrested" means taken by police, which fits a suspect found near the scene.
questions.meaning: taken by police for a suspected crime
questions.example: The suspect was arrested.

questions.prompt: Police are ___ the robbery as a priority case.
