questions.explanation: To "drain" fat is to let the liquid run out of the pan, which is what you do with excess fat. "reduce", "cool" and "roast" do not mean removing liquid.
questions.meaning: to let liquid flow away
questions.example: Drain the fat from the pan.

questions.prompt: Add the spices to ___ the dish more flavor.
questions.explanation: "give" completes the pattern 'give the dish more flavour', meaning to provide extra flavor. "chill", "fry" and "rest" cannot take 'more flavour' as their object.
questions.meaning: to add or produce a quality
questions.example: Spices give the dish more flavor.

questions.prompt: The chef used a whisk to ___ the eggs.
questions.explanation: To "beat" eggs is to mix them hard and quickly, which is what a whisk is for. "grill" and "roast" are cooking methods, and "thicken" does not describe mixing eggs.
questions.meaning: to mix quickly with a tool
questions.example: Beat the eggs with a whisk.

questions.prompt: You should ___ the cake before removing it from the tin.
questions.explanation: You "cool" a cake before taking it out of the tin so it holds its shape and does not break. "combine", "roll" and "coat" make no sense at this stage.
questions.meaning: to make or let something become less warm
questions.example: Cool the cake in the tin before turning it out.

questions.prompt: He likes to ___ the meat in breadcrumbs before frying.
questions.explanation: To "coat" the meat in breadcrumbs is to cover it with a layer of them before frying. "roast", "steam" and "beat" are not ways of covering food.
questions.meaning: to cover with a layer
questions.example: Coat the meat in breadcrumbs.

questions.prompt: You need to ___ the vegetables into small pieces.
questions.explanation: To "dice" vegetables is to cut them into small cubes, matching 'into small pieces'. "simmer", "preheat" and "rest" are not cutting verbs.
questions.meaning: to cut into small cubes
questions.example: Dice the vegetables.

questions.prompt: Let the meat ___ overnight in the fridge.
questions.explanation: To "chill" food is to keep it cold, which fits leaving meat in the fridge overnight. "enhance", "chop" and "drain" do not fit 'let the meat ___ overnight in the fridge'.
questions.meaning: to make cold; to keep in a fridge
questions.example: Chill the meat overnight.

questions.prompt: The sauce needs to ___ on the hob before you can serve it.
questions.explanation: A sauce left to cook on the hob will "thicken" as liquid evaporates, which is what it needs before serving. "grill" and "roast" are not used for sauces, and you do not chill something on the hob.
questions.meaning: to become thick
questions.example: The sauce will thicken as it cools.

units.title: Speaking: Longer Turns
units.description: Say it out loud — Multi-clause sentences to say in one breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: If I had known earlier, I would have said something.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "If I had known earlier, I would have said something." This third conditional talks about an unreal past; pause briefly at the comma and use the weak forms "I'd" and "would've" to keep it flowing.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The report suggests that demand is falling.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "The report suggests that demand is falling." Link "suggests" straight into the that-clause without a pause, and keep "that" weak and unstressed.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: What surprised me most was the reaction.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "What surprised me most was the reaction." In this What-cleft, keep the opening clause flowing, then put the main stress on "reaction".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Having read the whole thing, I changed my mind.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Having read the whole thing, I changed my mind." The opening "Having read" means "after I had read"; pause briefly after "thing" before the main clause.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It is not so much the price as the timing.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "It is not so much the price as the timing." Stress "price" and "timing" to bring out the contrast in the "not so much ... as" pattern.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We are under no obligation to accept it.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We are under no obligation to accept it." Say the formal fixed phrase "under no obligation" as one smooth unit, with the stress on "no".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The sooner this is resolved, the less it will cost.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "The sooner this is resolved, the less it will cost." In this "the sooner ..., the less ..." pattern, stress "sooner" and "less" and pause briefly at the comma.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would appreciate it if you could confirm.
questions.explanation: "I would appreciate it if you could confirm." is a polite, formal way to ask someone to do something. Link "appreciate it" smoothly and keep a courteous tone.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: There is a strong case for waiting.
questions.explanation: "There is a strong case for waiting." uses "a case for" + -ing to argue for an option. Stress "strong" and "waiting".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That rather depends on what we agree today.
questions.explanation: In "That rather depends on what we agree today.", "rather" softens the statement, a typical British hedge. Run "depends on what we agree" together in one breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am inclined to think it was a mistake.
questions.explanation: "I am inclined to think it was a mistake." uses "inclined to think" to give an opinion gently. Link it smoothly into "it was a mistake".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: By the time we arrived, everyone had left.
questions.explanation: In "By the time we arrived, everyone had left.", the past perfect "had left" shows the earlier event. Pause briefly at the comma, then keep going.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The decision was made without consulting us.
questions.explanation: "The decision was made without consulting us." combines the passive "was made" with "without" + -ing. Say it in one smooth breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I take your point, although I still have doubts.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I take your point, although I still have doubts." Multi-clause sentences to say in one breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We will need far more evidence than that.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We will need far more evidence than that." Put the stress on "far" to sound firmly unconvinced, and say the whole sentence in one breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It turned out to be much simpler than expected.
questions.explanation: "It turned out to be much simpler than expected." uses "turn out to be" for a result that surprised you. Link "turned out to be" and stress "much simpler".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The whole process took longer than planned.
questions.explanation: "The whole process took longer than planned." uses the short comparison "longer than planned". Stress "longer" and "planned".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am not sure that follows from what you said.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I am not sure that follows from what you said." Multi-clause sentences to say in one breath.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We should weigh the risks before committing.
questions.explanation: "We should weigh the risks before committing." uses "weigh the risks" (consider them carefully) and "before" + -ing. Stress "weigh" and "risks".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Given the circumstances, that seems reasonable.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Given the circumstances, that seems reasonable." "Given the circumstances" is an introductory phrase meaning "considering the situation", so pause briefly at the comma before the main clause.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It would be unwise to rush the decision.
questions.explanation: "It would be unwise to rush the decision." uses "It would be" + adjective + to-infinitive to give advice politely. Stress "unwise" and "rush".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The proposal has been revised several times.
questions.explanation: "The proposal has been revised several times." uses the present perfect passive "has been revised". Link "has been" lightly and stress "revised".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: What matters most is that it actually works.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "What matters most is that it actually works." The "What … is that …" pattern puts the emphasis on the final idea, so stress "actually works".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would be reluctant to change it now.
questions.explanation: "I would be reluctant to change it now." uses "would be reluctant to" to say no politely. Stress "reluctant" and "now".

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Had we acted sooner, this could have been avoided.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Had we acted sooner, this could have been avoided." "Had we acted" is a formal way of saying "If we had acted", so pause briefly at the comma before the result clause.

units.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns
units.description: Write the idea in English — Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns 1
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say that if you had known, you would have said something.
acceptableAnswers: If I had known, I would have said something.
Had I known, I would have spoken up.
I would have said something if I had known.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "If I had known, I would have said something." This is a third conditional: "if" + past perfect, then "would have" + past participle, for an imagined past.

questions.prompt: Say what surprised you most was the reaction.
acceptableAnswers: What surprised me most was the reaction.
The reaction was what surprised me most.
It was the reaction that surprised me most.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "What surprised me most was the reaction." Starting with "What … was" focuses attention on the reaction; "It was the reaction that …" does the same job.

questions.prompt: Say the report suggests demand is falling.
acceptableAnswers: The report suggests that demand is falling.
According to the report, demand is falling.
The report indicates falling demand.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The report suggests that demand is falling." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say it is not the price so much as the timing.
acceptableAnswers: It is not so much the price as the timing.
The issue is the timing rather than the price.
It's less about price than timing.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It is not so much the price as the timing." "Not so much X as Y" says that Y matters more than X.

questions.prompt: Say that your side is not obliged to accept the offer.
acceptableAnswers: We are under no obligation to accept it.
We do not have to accept it.
There is no obligation to accept.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We are under no obligation to accept it." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns 2
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say the sooner it is resolved the less it costs.
acceptableAnswers: The sooner this is resolved, the less it will cost.
Resolving it sooner will cost less.
The longer it takes, the more it costs.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The sooner this is resolved, the less it will cost." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Ask someone politely to confirm.
acceptableAnswers: I would appreciate it if you could confirm.
Could you please confirm?
Please confirm when you can.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would appreciate it if you could confirm." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say there is a strong case for waiting.
acceptableAnswers: There is a strong case for waiting.
A good argument can be made for waiting.
There are strong reasons to wait.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "There is a strong case for waiting." "A case for" + -ing means good arguments in favour of doing something.

questions.prompt: Say you are inclined to think it was a mistake.
acceptableAnswers: I am inclined to think it was a mistake.
I tend to think it was a mistake.
My feeling is that it was a mistake.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am inclined to think it was a mistake." "Inclined to think" gives a cautious opinion, softer than "I think".

questions.prompt: Say that by the time your group arrived, everyone had left.
acceptableAnswers: By the time we arrived, everyone had left.
Everyone had gone by the time we got there.
When we arrived, everyone had already left.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "By the time we arrived, everyone had left." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns 3
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Complain that a decision skipped your team.
acceptableAnswers: The decision was made without consulting us.
Nobody consulted us about the decision.
They decided without asking us.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The decision was made without consulting us." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Concede a point while keeping your doubts.
acceptableAnswers: I take your point, although I still have doubts.
I accept that, but I remain unconvinced.
Fair enough, though I still have reservations.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I take your point, although I still have doubts." "I take your point" concedes politely, and "although" introduces the doubt you keep.

questions.prompt: Reject a claim because there is far too little evidence for it.
acceptableAnswers: We will need far more evidence than that.
That is nowhere near enough evidence.
Much more evidence is needed.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We will need far more evidence than that." This turns the claim down by saying the evidence offered is not nearly enough to support it.

questions.prompt: Say it turned out simpler than expected.
acceptableAnswers: It turned out to be much simpler than expected.
It was far simpler than we thought.
In the end it was simpler than expected.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It turned out to be much simpler than expected." "Turn out to be" says how something proved to be in the end, and "simpler than expected" compares that result with what you thought.

questions.prompt: Say the process took longer than planned.
acceptableAnswers: The whole process took longer than planned.
It took longer than we had planned.
The process ran behind schedule.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The whole process took longer than planned." "Longer than planned" shortens "longer than we had planned", and "ran behind schedule" means the same thing.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns 4
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say you are not sure that follows.
acceptableAnswers: I am not sure that follows.
I don't think that follows.
That does not necessarily follow.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am not sure that follows." Here "follow" means to be a logical result, so this politely questions someone's reasoning.

questions.prompt: Say the risks should be weighed before committing.
acceptableAnswers: We should weigh the risks before committing.
Let's weigh the risks before we commit.
The risks need weighing before we commit.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We should weigh the risks before committing." Use "weigh" for comparing risks carefully, and "before" with "-ing" or a clause for the timing.

questions.prompt: Say that given the circumstances it seems reasonable.
acceptableAnswers: Given the circumstances, that seems reasonable.
In the circumstances, it seems fair enough.
That seems reasonable given the situation.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Given the circumstances, that seems reasonable." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say it would be unwise to rush.
acceptableAnswers: It would be unwise to rush the decision.
Rushing this would be a mistake.
We should not rush the decision.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "It would be unwise to rush the decision." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Note how often a proposal has changed.
acceptableAnswers: The proposal has been revised several times.
There have been several revisions to the proposal.
The proposal went through several revisions.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The proposal has been revised several times." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Longer Turns 5
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say what matters most is that it works.
acceptableAnswers: What matters most is that it actually works.
The important thing is that it works.
Above all, it has to work.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "What matters most is that it actually works." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you would be reluctant to change it now.
acceptableAnswers: I would be reluctant to change it now.
I'd rather not change it at this stage.
I am hesitant to change it now.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would be reluctant to change it now." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that acting sooner would have prevented it.
acceptableAnswers: Had we acted sooner, this could have been avoided.
If we had acted earlier, this would not have happened.
Acting sooner would have prevented this.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Had we acted sooner, this could have been avoided." Inverted "Had we acted" is a formal way to say "If we had acted" in a third conditional about a missed chance in the past.

questions.prompt: Say having read it all you changed your mind.
acceptableAnswers: Having read the whole thing, I changed my mind.
After reading all of it, I changed my mind.
Reading it in full changed my view.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Having read the whole thing, I changed my mind." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say that it rather depends on what is agreed today.
acceptableAnswers: That rather depends on what we agree today.
It depends what gets agreed today.
That hinges on today's decision.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That rather depends on what we agree today." Multi-clause ideas, written in your own words.

units.title: Idioms
units.description: Meaning match — Idioms are fixed: the words can't be swapped.

questions.prompt: "bite the bullet" means: ___
questions.explanation: To "bite the bullet" means to "accept something unpleasant" that you cannot avoid and just get on with it, as in 'I bit the bullet and paid the fine.'
questions.meaning: to accept something unpleasant and move on
questions.example: You will have to bite the bullet and pay.

questions.prompt: "hit the nail on the head" means:
questions.explanation: To "hit the nail on the head" means to "be exactly right", usually by describing a problem or its cause precisely.
questions.term: hit the nail on the head
questions.meaning: to be exactly right
questions.example: You've hit the nail on the head: that's exactly the problem.

questions.prompt: "under the weather" means: ___
questions.explanation: If you are "under the weather", you feel a bit ill, as in "I feel a bit under the weather today", so the answer is "slightly unwell".
questions.meaning: slightly unwell
questions.example: I feel a bit under the weather today.

questions.prompt: "a blessing in disguise" means:
questions.explanation: A blessing in disguise is something that seems bad at first but later turns out to be good for you, so it is "a hidden benefit".
questions.meaning: a bad thing that turns out good
questions.example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.

questions.prompt: "cut corners" means: ___
questions.explanation: If you cut corners, you skip steps to save time or money, so the result is poor: you "do something cheaply or badly".
questions.meaning: to do something cheaply or badly
questions.example: Builders who cut corners put people at risk.

questions.prompt: "on the fence" means:
questions.explanation: Someone sitting on the fence has not chosen either side yet, so "on the fence" means "undecided".
questions.meaning: undecided; not choosing a side
questions.example: On the issue of tax, she is on the fence.

questions.prompt: "the ball is in your court" means: ___
questions.explanation: In tennis, when the ball is in your court it is your turn to play, so the idiom means it is now your turn to act: "it's your decision".
questions.term: the ball is in your court
questions.meaning: it's your turn to decide
questions.example: We made the offer, so the ball is in your court.

questions.prompt: "let the cat out of the bag" means:
questions.explanation: To let the cat out of the bag is to tell people something that was meant to stay hidden, often by mistake, so it means "reveal a secret".
questions.term: let the cat out of the bag
questions.meaning: to reveal a secret by mistake
questions.example: He let the cat out of the bag about the party.

questions.prompt: "break the ice" means: ___
questions.explanation: To break the ice is to make people feel relaxed when they first meet, usually when someone is the first to "start a conversation".
questions.meaning: to ease the tension at a first meeting
questions.example: A joke helped to break the ice.

questions.prompt: "go the extra mile" means:
questions.explanation: If you go the extra mile, you do more than people expect of you, so you "make extra effort".
questions.meaning: to make an extra effort
questions.example: She will go the extra mile for clients.

questions.prompt: "throw in the towel" means:
questions.explanation: In boxing, a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight, so "throw in the towel" means to "give up".
questions.meaning: to give up
questions.example: After two years he threw in the towel.

questions.prompt: "a gray area" means: ___
questions.explanation: A gray area is neither clearly black nor clearly white, so it is a situation where the rules are not clear: "something unclear".
questions.meaning: a situation where rules are unclear
questions.example: The law here is a gray area.

questions.prompt: "call it a day" means:
questions.explanation: You say "let's call it a day" when you decide you have done enough for now, so it means "stop working".
questions.meaning: to stop working for the day
questions.example: It's late, so let's call it a day.

questions.prompt: "take it with a pinch of salt" means: ___
questions.explanation: If you take something with a pinch of salt, you don't fully believe it, so the idiom means to "be skeptical".
questions.term: take it with a pinch of salt
questions.meaning: to doubt that something is completely true
questions.example: If Tom says he's rich, take it with a pinch of salt.

questions.prompt: "back to square one" means:
questions.explanation: "start again" is right: going back to square one is like returning to the first square of a board game, so you have lost your progress and must begin again.
questions.meaning: to start again from the beginning
questions.example: The test failed, so we're back to square one.

questions.prompt: "in the long run" means: ___
questions.explanation: "eventually" is right: "in the long run" means over a long period of time, once things have had time to develop, so in the end.
questions.meaning: after a long time; in the end
questions.example: In the long run, saving pays off.

questions.prompt: "pull strings" means:
questions.explanation: "use influence" is right: to pull strings is to use your contacts or power behind the scenes, like a puppeteer pulling a puppet's strings.
questions.meaning: to use your influence to get something
questions.example: He had to pull strings to get the job.

questions.prompt: "the bottom line" means: ___
questions.explanation: "the essential point" is right: the bottom line is the final total on a set of accounts, so it means the most important fact once everything else is considered.
questions.meaning: the most important point
questions.example: The bottom line is that we need more money.

questions.prompt: "jump the gun" means:
questions.explanation: "act too soon" is right: to jump the gun comes from a runner starting before the starting gun fires, so it means doing something before the right time.
questions.meaning: to act too soon
questions.example: Don't jump the gun before the results arrive.

questions.prompt: "sit on one's hands" means: ___
questions.explanation: "do nothing" is right: if you sit on your hands, you fail to act when you could or should do something.
questions.meaning: to wait and do nothing
questions.example: It is wrong to sit on one's hands.

questions.prompt: "a steep learning curve" means: ___
questions.explanation: a steep learning curve → hard to learn quickly. Idioms are fixed — the words can't be swapped.
questions.meaning: something hard to learn at first
questions.example: The new software has a steep learning curve.

questions.prompt: "touch base" means:
questions.explanation: "make brief contact" is right: to touch base, from baseball, means to get in touch with someone briefly to check in or share an update.
questions.meaning: to make short contact with someone
questions.example: Let's touch base on Friday.

questions.prompt: "move the goalposts" means: ___
questions.explanation: "change the rules unfairly" is right: if someone moves the goalposts, they change the targets or conditions after you have started, so success becomes harder.
questions.meaning: to change the rules in an unfair way
questions.example: They keep moving the goalposts on us.

questions.prompt: "play devil's advocate" means:
questions.explanation: "argue the opposing view" is right: someone who plays devil's advocate takes the other side of an argument to test an idea, even if they do not believe it.
questions.meaning: to argue the other side for debate
questions.example: Let me play devil's advocate for a moment.

questions.prompt: "cost an arm and a leg" means: ___
questions.explanation: "be very expensive" is right: if something costs an arm and a leg, it costs so much that it feels like paying with parts of your body.
questions.term: cost an arm and a leg
questions.meaning: to be very expensive
questions.example: Repairing the roof will cost an arm and a leg.

units.title: Register
units.description: Informal → formal — Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "find out":
questions.explanation: "ascertain" is the formal verb for finding out the facts, as in "We must ascertain the cause of the fire"; "inform" means to tell someone, not to find out.
questions.meaning: to find the facts about something
questions.example: We must ascertain the cause of the fire.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "get": ___
questions.explanation: "obtain" is right: it is the formal word for "get" in the sense of acquiring something, as in "obtain a visa", whereas "request" only means asking for it.
questions.meaning: to get something by asking or effort
questions.example: You must obtain a visa first.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "help":
questions.explanation: "assist" is the formal way to say help, as in "Staff will assist passengers at the gate"; the other verbs mean delay, deal with or carry out.
questions.meaning: to help someone do something
questions.example: Staff will assist passengers at the gate.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "show": ___
questions.explanation: show → demonstrate. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to make something clear by showing it
questions.example: The results demonstrate a clear trend.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "start":
questions.explanation: start → commence. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to begin
questions.example: The course will commence in September.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "end": ___
questions.explanation: "terminate" is the formal verb for ending something such as a contract; "reduce" only makes something smaller, it does not end it.
questions.meaning: to bring something to an end
questions.example: The contract was terminated last week.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "need":
questions.explanation: "require" is the formal verb for need, common in rules and notices such as "All visitors are required to sign in"; the other verbs mean begin, set up or talk about.
questions.meaning: to officially say that someone must do something
questions.example: All visitors are required to sign in.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "tell": ___
questions.explanation: tell → inform. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to give someone facts
questions.example: Please inform us of any change.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "ask for":
questions.explanation: "request" is the formal verb for ask for, as in "I wish to request a refund"; the other options mean end, carry out or make bigger.
questions.meaning: to ask politely or formally for something
questions.example: I wish to request a refund.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "put off": ___
questions.explanation: put off → postpone. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to arrange for a later time
questions.example: The meeting was postponed until Friday.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "look at": ___
questions.explanation: look at → examine. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to look at something closely
questions.example: The doctor will examine the results.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "think about":
questions.explanation: think about → consider. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to think carefully about something
questions.example: Please consider our offer carefully.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "set up": ___
questions.explanation: In formal writing, "establish" replaces "set up" when you create something lasting, such as a company or a system ("They established the firm in 1990").
questions.meaning: to create something lasting
questions.example: They established the firm in 1990.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "go up":
questions.explanation: "increase" is the formal verb for "go up" when numbers or amounts rise ("Prices increased by 5%"), while "decline" means the opposite.
questions.meaning: to become greater in number or size
questions.example: Prices tend to increase in winter.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "go down": ___
questions.explanation: "decline" is the formal verb for "go down" when numbers or quality fall ("Sales declined last year").
questions.meaning: to become less or worse
questions.example: Sales continued to decline last year.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "leave out":
questions.explanation: leave out → omit. Academic and professional writing prefers Latinate verbs.
questions.meaning: to leave something out
questions.example: Please do not omit any details.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "deal with": ___
questions.explanation: "address" is the formal verb for "deal with" a problem or issue ("The committee must address these concerns"), while "examine" only means to look at something closely.
questions.meaning: to give attention to a problem
questions.example: The committee must address these concerns.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "point out":
questions.explanation: "indicate" is the formal verb for "point out" or show something ("The figures indicate a rise in costs").
questions.meaning: to show or point towards something
questions.example: The figures indicate a rise in costs.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "give up": ___
questions.explanation: "relinquish" is the formal verb for "give up" a right, power or claim, so it suits academic and professional writing.
questions.meaning: to give up a right or claim
questions.example: He chose to relinquish his title.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "talk about":
questions.explanation: "discuss" is the formal verb for "talk about" a subject in detail ("We will discuss the budget tomorrow").
questions.meaning: to talk about a subject in detail
questions.example: We will discuss the budget tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "make up":
questions.explanation: "constitute" is the formal verb for "make up" in the sense of forming the parts of a whole, as in "Women constitute half of the workforce."
questions.meaning: to form or be the parts of something
questions.example: Women constitute half of the workforce.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "cut down": ___
questions.explanation: "reduce" is the formal verb for "cut down" on an amount ("We aim to reduce waste by half").
questions.meaning: to make smaller in amount
questions.example: We aim to reduce waste by half.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "bring about":
questions.explanation: "induce" is a formal verb for "bring about", meaning to cause a state or change ("The drug can induce sleep").
questions.meaning: to cause something to happen
questions.example: The drug can induce sleep.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "carry out": ___
questions.explanation: "conduct" is the formal verb for "carry out" an activity such as research, a survey or an experiment.
questions.meaning: to organize and carry out an activity
questions.example: Researchers conduct tests in the lab.

questions.prompt: Formal equivalent of "back up":
questions.explanation: "corroborate" is the formal verb for "back up" a claim, meaning to support it with further evidence.
questions.meaning: to support a claim with more evidence
questions.example: New data corroborate the earlier findings.

units.title: Inversion & Emphasis
units.description: Advanced structures — Fronted negative and restrictive adverbials (Never, Rarely, Only then) trigger question word order.

questions.prompt: Never ___ I seen such chaos.
questions.explanation: After a fronted negative like "Never", the auxiliary comes before the subject, and 'seen' needs the present perfect, so "have" gives 'Never have I seen'. "did" and "was" do not fit 'seen'.
questions.meaning: helper verb put before the subject after never
questions.example: Never have I seen such chaos.

questions.prompt: Rarely ___ she complain.
questions.explanation: After the fronted negative "Rarely", the helper verb comes before the subject, and the third-person singular "she" needs "does" with the bare verb "complain".
questions.meaning: helper verb put before the subject after rarely
questions.example: Rarely does she complain.

questions.prompt: Not only ___ he late, but he was also rude.
questions.explanation: "Not only" at the start of the sentence forces inversion, so the verb "was" comes before the subject "he" in the first clause.
questions.meaning: past of be, put before the subject
questions.example: Not only was he late, but he was also rude.

questions.prompt: Hardly ___ we arrived when it rained.
questions.explanation: "Hardly ... when" links two past events, and after "Hardly" the past perfect is inverted: "had" comes before "we", giving "Hardly had we arrived".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for an earlier past action
questions.example: Hardly had we arrived when it rained.

questions.prompt: Under no circumstances ___ you leave the building before the alarm stops.
questions.explanation: After the fronted phrase "Under no circumstances", a modal comes before "you", and "should" gives a strong instruction about now, before the bare verb "leave"; "ought" would need 'to'.
questions.meaning: modal put before the subject in strong warnings
questions.example: Under no circumstances should you leave.

questions.prompt: Only then ___ I understand.
questions.explanation: "Only then" is a fronted limiting adverbial in a past-tense sentence, so it takes inversion with "did" before the subject "I" and the bare verb "understand".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for the past
questions.example: Only then did I understand.

questions.prompt: No sooner ___ he spoken than she left.
questions.explanation: "No sooner" is followed by the past perfect with inversion, so "had" goes before "he" and "than" introduces the second event: "No sooner had he spoken than she left".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for an earlier past action
questions.example: No sooner had he spoken than she left.

questions.prompt: Little ___ they know the truth.
questions.explanation: After the fronted negative "Little" (meaning 'not at all') in a past story, the helper "did" comes before the subject, followed by the bare verb "know".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for the past
questions.example: Little did they know the truth.

questions.prompt: So loud ___ the music that we left.
questions.explanation: When "So + adjective" opens the sentence for emphasis, the verb comes before the subject, so the past form "was" goes before "the music".
questions.meaning: an inverted pattern for strong effect
questions.example: So loud was the music that we left.

questions.prompt: Seldom ___ such talent appear.
questions.explanation: After "Seldom" the helper verb comes first, and the singular subject "such talent" needs "does", followed by the bare verb "appear".
questions.meaning: a helper verb placed first after seldom
questions.example: Seldom does such talent appear.

questions.prompt: Not until later ___ we hear the news.
questions.explanation: "Not until later" is a fronted negative time phrase about the past, so it takes inversion with "did" before "we" and the bare verb "hear".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for the past
questions.example: Not until later did we hear the news.

questions.prompt: Such ___ his anger that he shouted.
questions.explanation: When "Such" opens the sentence, the verb comes before the subject, so "was" goes before "his anger" in "Such was his anger that he shouted".
questions.meaning: a past form of be placed first
questions.example: Such was his anger that he shouted.

questions.prompt: In no way ___ this acceptable.
questions.explanation: "In no way" is a fronted negative, so the verb comes before the subject, and "is" links "this" directly to the adjective "acceptable".
questions.meaning: a form of be placed first
questions.example: In no way is this acceptable.

questions.prompt: Were ___ to leave, we'd struggle.
questions.explanation: "he" fits here. Rule to remember: Fronted negatives and adverbials trigger question word order.
questions.meaning: the man or boy already mentioned
questions.example: Were he to leave, we'd struggle.

questions.prompt: Had I ___ , I'd have helped.
questions.explanation: "Had I known" is the inverted third conditional ("If I had known"), so the past participle "known" is needed after the subject, matching "I'd have helped".
questions.meaning: been aware of something
questions.example: Had I known, I'd have helped.

questions.prompt: Should you ___ questions, ask.
questions.explanation: "Should you have questions" is an inverted conditional meaning "If you have questions"; after "should" and the subject comes the bare verb "have".
questions.meaning: to hold or experience something
questions.example: Should you have any questions, please ask.

questions.prompt: What I need ___ more time.
questions.explanation: This is a 'What...' cleft sentence, where "is" links the clause "What I need" to the thing needed, "more time".
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What I need is more time.

questions.prompt: It ___ she who solved it.
questions.explanation: In the cleft "It was she who...", "was" is past tense to match "solved", and the structure puts emphasis on "she".
questions.meaning: a sentence pattern that stresses a person
questions.example: It was she who solved it.

questions.prompt: Only by working together ___ we succeed.
questions.explanation: After the fronted "Only by working together", the modal comes before the subject, and "can" is followed by the bare verb "succeed"; "did" and "does" would need a different tense meaning.
questions.meaning: a modal verb of ability placed first
questions.example: Only by working together can we succeed.

questions.prompt: Nowhere ___ the report mention costs.
questions.explanation: "Nowhere" at the start forces inversion with do-support, and the singular subject "the report" takes "does", followed by the bare verb "mention".
questions.meaning: a helper verb placed first after nowhere
questions.example: Nowhere does the report mention costs.

questions.prompt: On no account ___ the door be opened.
questions.explanation: "must" fits here. Rule to remember: Fronted negatives and adverbials trigger question word order.
questions.meaning: a modal verb that forbids something
questions.example: On no account must the door be opened.

questions.prompt: Scarcely ___ she begun when he interrupted.
questions.explanation: "had" fits here. Rule to remember: Fronted negatives and adverbials trigger question word order.
questions.meaning: a helper verb for an earlier past action
questions.example: Scarcely had she begun when he interrupted.

questions.prompt: Never before ___ this happened.
questions.explanation: "has" forms the present perfect with "happened" for a statement about all time up to now, and after "Never before" it comes before the subject "this".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for a perfect action
questions.example: Never before has this happened.

questions.prompt: So rarely ___ it snow here.
questions.explanation: "So rarely" at the start triggers inversion with do-support, and the singular subject "it" takes "does", followed by the bare verb "snow".
questions.meaning: a helper verb placed first after so rarely
questions.example: So rarely does it snow here.

questions.prompt: Not once ___ he apologize.
questions.explanation: "Not once" is a fronted negative, so the auxiliary precedes the subject; "did" shows the past and is followed by the bare verb "apologize".
questions.meaning: a helper verb for the past
questions.example: Not once did he apologize.

units.title: Precision Connectors
units.description: Nuanced signposting — Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.

questions.prompt: The claim is plausible; ___, the evidence is thin.
questions.explanation: "that said" adds a contrast to the plausible claim: the evidence is thin despite that. "conversely" needs an opposing pair, and "accordingly" signals a result.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast to a claim
questions.example: The claim is plausible; that said, the evidence is thin.

questions.prompt: ___ , the two datasets differ in scope, so a direct comparison would be misleading.
questions.explanation: "Crucially" flags the key point that makes the comparison unsafe: the datasets differ in scope. "Conversely" and "Likewise" need an earlier statement to contrast with or compare to, and "Particularly" cannot start a sentence this way.
questions.meaning: used to stress a very important point
questions.example: Crucially, the two datasets differ in scope.

questions.prompt: Sales rose, ___ modestly.
questions.explanation: "albeit" means 'although' and introduces a limiting word after a clause: sales rose, though only modestly. The other options cannot link a clause to a single adverb this way.
questions.meaning: although; even though
questions.example: Sales rose, albeit modestly.

questions.prompt: ___, the policy achieved its aim, although some targets were missed.
questions.explanation: "Broadly speaking" gives an overall judgment that allows for exceptions, which matches "although some targets were missed". "Conversely" and "Hence" need an earlier statement to contrast with or follow from.
questions.meaning: in a general way
questions.example: Broadly speaking, the policy achieved its aim, although some targets were missed.

questions.prompt: The theory holds ___ certain conditions.
questions.explanation: "under" is the preposition used with conditions, so "holds under certain conditions" means it is true within those conditions. "Regardless" would need "of", and "unless" and "though" need a clause after them.
questions.meaning: within a set of conditions
questions.example: The theory holds under certain conditions.

questions.prompt: Most results matched earlier findings. ___, one sample contradicted them.
questions.explanation: "Notably" points out a single result that is worth attention, here the one sample that broke the pattern. "Similarly" signals agreement, and "Consequently" and "Accordingly" signal a result, so none of them fit.
questions.meaning: used to point out something worth noting
questions.example: Most results matched earlier findings. Notably, one sample contradicted them.

questions.prompt: The results are, ___ , inconclusive.
questions.explanation: "at best" means that even the most favourable reading of the results is only 'inconclusive'. "At least" would introduce a minimum positive point, which makes no sense with a negative word like 'inconclusive'.
questions.meaning: in the best possible case
questions.example: The results are, at best, inconclusive.

questions.prompt: ___ far as the data allows, we conclude X.
questions.explanation: "In so" completes the fixed phrase 'in so far as', meaning 'to the extent that'. The other options cannot be followed by 'far as'.
questions.meaning: to the degree that
questions.example: In so far as the data allows, we conclude X.

questions.prompt: ___ , the mechanism remains unclear.
questions.explanation: "As yet" means "up to now" and goes naturally with "remains unclear", suggesting this may change later. "In light of" needs a noun after it, and "For simplicity" does not fit a statement of fact.
questions.meaning: up to now; used when something may change
questions.example: As yet, the mechanism remains unclear.

questions.prompt: Prices rise when demand rises; ___, they fall when demand falls.
questions.explanation: "conversely" introduces the reverse of the first statement: rising demand raises prices, and falling demand lowers them. "hence" would wrongly make the second fact a result of the first.
questions.meaning: in the opposite way
questions.example: Some students prefer exams; conversely, others prefer coursework.

questions.prompt: ___ of the criticism, the model persists.
questions.explanation: "Regardless" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: in spite of something
questions.example: Regardless of criticism, the model persists.

questions.prompt: His argument is sound ___ its premises.
questions.explanation: "given" means 'taking into account', so the argument is sound when you consider its premises. "Under" is not used with premises, "albeit" cannot take a noun phrase here, and "regardless" would need 'of'.
questions.meaning: taking something into account
questions.example: His argument is sound given its premises.

questions.prompt: Many countries have reduced class sizes. ___, consider Finland.
questions.explanation: "By way of illustration" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: used to introduce an example
questions.example: By way of illustration, consider this case.

questions.prompt: The findings, ___ preliminary, are promising.
questions.explanation: "though" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: although; used before an adjective
questions.example: The findings, though preliminary, are promising.

questions.prompt: ___ , we assume linear growth.
questions.explanation: "For simplicity" explains that the assumption of linear growth is made to keep the model easy to handle. "In light of" needs a noun after it, and "As yet" refers to time, not to a reason for an assumption.
questions.meaning: to make things easier to explain
questions.example: For simplicity, we assume linear growth.

questions.prompt: The effect is small ___ statistically significant.
questions.explanation: "yet" links two adjectives in surprising contrast: the effect is small, but it is still significant. "hence" would wrongly suggest it is significant because it is small.
questions.meaning: but; used to add a surprising contrast
questions.example: The effect is small yet significant.

questions.prompt: The correlation is now established. ___, attention turns to causation.
questions.explanation: "Accordingly" shows that the next step follows from what came before: once the correlation is established, attention moves to causation. "Conversely" would signal a reversal, which is not what happens here.
questions.meaning: as a result; therefore
questions.example: The evidence was inconclusive; accordingly, the committee postponed its decision.

questions.prompt: The sample was small; ___, caution is advised.
questions.explanation: "hence" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: for this reason; as a result
questions.example: The sample was small; hence, caution is advised.

questions.prompt: ___ speaking, the trend is upward.
questions.explanation: "Generally" combines with the "speaking" already in the sentence to form the fixed phrase "Generally speaking". "Broadly speaking" would repeat "speaking", and "Arguably" and "At best" do not combine with it.
questions.meaning: in most cases; as a rule
questions.example: Generally speaking, the trend is upward.

questions.prompt: This is true ___ in urban settings.
questions.explanation: "particularly" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: especially; more than in other cases
questions.example: This is particularly true in cities.

questions.prompt: After years of mixed results, the hypothesis was ___ rejected.
questions.explanation: "Ultimately" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: in the end
questions.example: Ultimately, the hypothesis was rejected.

questions.prompt: The data ___ suggests a link, though some researchers would disagree.
questions.explanation: "arguably" signals a claim that can be defended but that others may dispute, which matches "though some researchers would disagree".
questions.meaning: it can be argued, though some disagree
questions.example: The data arguably suggests a link.

questions.prompt: ___ this evidence, revision is needed.
questions.explanation: "In light of" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: taking new facts into account
questions.example: In light of this evidence, revision is needed.

questions.prompt: The study is limited ___ its scope.
questions.explanation: "in terms of" fits here. Rule to remember: Each connector carries a distinct logical relationship.
questions.meaning: used to say which aspect you mean
questions.example: In terms of cost, the plan is realistic.

questions.prompt: Scientists have studied the question for decades. ___, no consensus has emerged.
questions.explanation: "To date" means "up to now", so it links decades of study to the fact that there is still no agreement.
questions.meaning: up to the present time
questions.example: To date, no consensus has emerged.

units.title: Academic Verbs
units.description: Precise reporting verbs — Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "state something as true without proof"? ___
questions.explanation: state something as true without proof → assert. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to state firmly that something is true
questions.example: Critics assert that the plan will fail.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "suggest indirectly"?
questions.explanation: "imply" means to suggest something indirectly, without stating it outright, which matches the definition given.
questions.meaning: to suggest something without saying it
questions.example: His silence seemed to imply guilt.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "provide evidence for"? ___
questions.explanation: provide evidence for → substantiate. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to prove a claim with evidence
questions.example: The data substantiate the claim.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "weaken an argument"?
questions.explanation: "undermine" means to weaken an argument or position, often gradually, so it matches "weaken an argument".
questions.meaning: to weaken something, often gradually or indirectly
questions.example: Doubt can undermine trust.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "say that something is caused by something else"? ___
questions.explanation: "attribute" means to say that something is caused by something else, and it is used with 'to', as in 'attribute the rise to pollution'.
questions.meaning: to say something is caused by
questions.example: Scientists attribute the rise to pollution.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "present as an example"?
questions.explanation: present as an example → illustrate. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to explain with an example
questions.example: Let me illustrate the point.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "question the validity of"? ___
questions.explanation: To "challenge" a claim is to question whether it is valid or true, as in "Some experts challenge the findings." "Qualify" only limits a claim, and "imply" suggests one.
questions.meaning: to question whether something is right
questions.example: Some experts challenge the findings.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "confirm a finding with further evidence"?
questions.explanation: "corroborate" means to back up an earlier finding with new evidence, as in "New data corroborate the earlier study".
questions.meaning: to support a finding with more evidence
questions.example: New data corroborate the earlier study.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "restate more clearly"? ___
questions.explanation: restate more clearly → clarify. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to make something easier to understand
questions.example: Please clarify what you mean.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "soften a claim"?
questions.explanation: To "qualify" a claim is to soften it by adding limits or conditions, for example "in most cases". "Substantiate" means the opposite: to support a claim with evidence.
questions.meaning: to limit or soften a claim
questions.example: You should qualify that statement.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "reach a conclusion from evidence"?
questions.explanation: "infer" means to work out a conclusion from evidence, whereas the speaker who suggests something "implies" it.
questions.meaning: to reach a conclusion from evidence
questions.example: We can infer a link from these facts.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "set out systematically"? ___
questions.explanation: set out systematically → delineate. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to describe or mark out in detail
questions.example: The report delineates the main duties.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "compare to establish difference"?
questions.explanation: compare to establish difference → differentiate. Reporting verbs encode your stance on a claim.
questions.meaning: to see or show how things differ
questions.example: It is hard to differentiate between the twins.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "put forward as a basis for argument"? ___
questions.explanation: "posit" means to put forward an idea as a starting point for an argument, as in "The author posits a new theory".
questions.meaning: to put forward as a basis for argument
questions.example: The author posits a new theory.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "put forward for consideration"?
questions.explanation: "propose" means to put an idea forward so that others can consider it, as in 'The authors propose a new model'; "assert" means to state something firmly.
questions.meaning: to put forward an idea to consider
questions.example: I propose a new schedule.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "examine in detail"? ___
questions.explanation: "scrutinise" means to examine something very carefully and in detail, as in 'Reviewers scrutinise the data'.
questions.meaning: to look at something very carefully
questions.example: Auditors scrutinise every account.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "reduce to essentials"?
questions.explanation: "distil" means to reduce something to its most important parts, as in 'distil a long report into three key points'.
questions.meaning: to reduce to the most important parts
questions.example: The essay distils years of research.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "show to be false"? ___
questions.explanation: "refute" means to prove that a claim is false, whereas "maintain" means to keep saying that a claim is true.
questions.meaning: to prove that a claim is false
questions.example: New evidence refutes the theory.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "give an approximate value"?
questions.explanation: "estimate" means to judge a rough value or amount; "infer" means to reach a conclusion from evidence, not to give a number.
questions.meaning: to judge a rough value or amount
questions.example: We estimate the cost at about ten thousand pounds.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "place in a category"? ___
questions.explanation: "classify" means to place things in categories or groups, as in 'Librarians classify books by subject'.
questions.meaning: to arrange things into groups
questions.example: Librarians classify books by subject.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "explain the reasons for"? ___
questions.explanation: "account for" means to explain the reasons for something, as in 'Poor sleep may account for the drop in scores'.
questions.meaning: to give the reasons for something
questions.example: Weather accounts for the delay.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "bring together findings"?
questions.explanation: "synthesise" means to bring findings from several sources together into one coherent whole.
questions.meaning: to combine information into one whole
questions.example: The review synthesises many studies.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "consider as a possibility"? ___
questions.explanation: Here "entertain" means to consider an idea as a possibility, as in 'She refused to entertain the thought of failure'.
questions.meaning: to think about an idea without accepting it
questions.example: The committee was willing to entertain the idea of a merger.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "keep insisting something is true despite objections"?
questions.explanation: "maintain" means to keep saying something is true even when others disagree, as in 'He maintained his innocence'.
questions.meaning: to keep saying something is true
questions.example: He maintained his innocence to the end.

questions.prompt: Which verb means "support with authority"? ___
questions.explanation: "endorse" means to publicly approve or back an idea or plan; "undermine" and "refute" oppose it.
questions.meaning: to publicly support an idea or person
questions.example: Several experts endorse the plan.

units.title: Hedging
units.description: Cautious academic language — Hedging protects claims from overstatement.

questions.prompt: The results ___ suggest a correlation.
questions.explanation: Plural "results" needs the plural verb "appear to"; "appears to", "seems to" and "tends" are singular forms.
questions.meaning: used to show something seems true
questions.example: The results appear to suggest a correlation.

questions.prompt: This ___ be attributed to sampling error.
questions.explanation: "may" is a modal verb that takes the base form 'be attributed' and expresses possibility, which is the hedge needed here. "Ought" would need 'to', and the other options cannot fill the gap.
questions.meaning: used to show something is possible
questions.example: This may be due to sampling error.

questions.prompt: The data ___ indicate causation. (negative hedge)
questions.explanation: The clue asks for a negative hedge: "do not necessarily" says the data may not show causation, without claiming the opposite is proven.
questions.meaning: used to say something is not always true
questions.example: The data do not necessarily indicate causation.

questions.prompt: It ___ that the effect is small.
questions.explanation: "seems" fits the fixed pattern 'It seems that...', with 'It' as a singular subject and a that-clause following. The other options do not form a grammatical sentence after 'It'.
questions.meaning: gives the impression that
questions.example: It seems that the effect is small.

questions.prompt: The trend is ___ consistent. (= in general, though not in every detail)
questions.explanation: The clue describes something true in general but not in every detail, which is exactly what "broadly" means in "broadly consistent".
questions.meaning: in a general way
questions.example: The trend is broadly consistent with earlier findings.

questions.prompt: Findings should be treated with ___ .
questions.explanation: "caution" fits here. Rule to remember: Hedging protects claims from overstatement.
questions.meaning: great care to avoid harm or mistakes
questions.example: Treat the findings with caution.

questions.prompt: There is ___ evidence of bias.
questions.explanation: "some" can go before an uncountable noun like "evidence" and means 'a limited amount', which softens the claim. "Many", "a few" and "several" are only used with plural countable nouns.
questions.meaning: an amount, but not a lot
questions.example: There is some evidence of bias.

questions.prompt: The link is ___ established, so more research is needed.
questions.explanation: The need for more research shows the link is not yet proven, so "not fully" is the hedge that fits; "widely established" would contradict it.
questions.meaning: not completely
questions.example: The link is not fully established.

questions.prompt: It is ___ that the model oversimplifies.
questions.explanation: 'It is possible that...' is the standard frame for suggesting something may be true without claiming it, so "possible" fits. "Tentative", "premature" and "approximate" do not normally take a 'that' clause after 'It is'.
questions.meaning: able to happen or be true
questions.example: It is possible that the model oversimplifies.

questions.prompt: The effect was ___ negligible. (= almost)
questions.explanation: The clue means "almost", and "virtually" means almost, so the effect was so small it could almost be ignored.
questions.meaning: almost; nearly
questions.example: The two results were virtually identical.

questions.prompt: These are ___ figures, not exact counts.
questions.explanation: The contrast with "not exact counts" shows the figures are rough, which is what "approximate" means.
questions.meaning: close to the real figure, but not exact
questions.example: These figures are only approximate.

questions.prompt: The theory is ___ contested. (= by many scholars)
questions.explanation: The clue says many scholars dispute the theory, and "widely" means by many people, so "widely contested" fits.
questions.meaning: by many people
questions.example: The theory is widely contested.

questions.prompt: One ___ argue the opposite.
questions.explanation: "could" is a modal, so it goes straight before the bare verb "argue" and makes a polite, hedged suggestion. "Ought" and "seems" would need "to", and "appear to" does not agree with the singular subject "One".
questions.meaning: used to say something is possibly true
questions.example: One could argue the opposite.

questions.prompt: The sample ___ not be representative.
questions.explanation: "might" fits here. Rule to remember: Hedging protects claims from overstatement.
questions.meaning: a modal verb for a weak possibility
questions.example: The sample might not be representative.

questions.prompt: Results were ___ inconclusive (= for the most part).
questions.explanation: "largely" means "for the most part", so it softens the claim that the results were inconclusive without saying they all were.
questions.meaning: for the most part
questions.example: Results were largely inconclusive.

questions.prompt: This ___ to support the hypothesis.
questions.explanation: "tends" agrees with the singular subject "This" and is followed by "to support", giving a cautious 'is inclined to' meaning; "could" cannot be followed by "to".
questions.meaning: is likely or inclined to do something
questions.example: This tends to support the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: The claim ___ further testing.
questions.explanation: The gap needs a verb taking "further testing" as its object, and "warrants" means 'justifies' or 'calls for', so the claim deserves more testing.
questions.meaning: makes something necessary or deserved
questions.example: The claim warrants further testing.

questions.prompt: There ___ to be a threshold effect.
questions.explanation: "appears" works in the hedging pattern "There appears to be..." and agrees with the singular "a threshold effect"; "might" would need "be" without "to".
questions.meaning: seems; looks as if something is true
questions.example: There appears to be a threshold effect.

questions.prompt: The evidence is ___ at best.
questions.explanation: "suggestive" means the evidence hints at something without proving it, which fits "at best" as a deliberately weak claim; the other words do not describe evidence this way.
questions.meaning: hinting at something, but not proving it
questions.example: The evidence is suggestive at best.

questions.prompt: Conclusions remain ___ (not final; open to change).
questions.explanation: "tentative" means not final and open to change, which matches the clue and hedges the conclusions.
questions.meaning: not final; open to change
questions.example: Conclusions remain tentative.

questions.prompt: The pattern is ___ apparent, so more data are needed.
questions.explanation: "only partly" limits how far the pattern can be seen, which hedges the claim that it is "apparent".
questions.meaning: not completely; only to some extent
questions.example: The pattern is only partly apparent.

questions.prompt: It would be ___ to generalise.
questions.explanation: "premature" means too early, so "It would be premature to generalise" cautiously warns against drawing broad conclusions yet.
questions.meaning: too early; before it is wise
questions.example: It would be premature to generalise.

questions.prompt: The difference is ___ significant.
questions.explanation: "marginally" fits here. Rule to remember: Hedging protects claims from overstatement.
questions.meaning: by a very small amount
questions.example: The difference is marginally significant.

questions.prompt: This is ___ the most important study in the field.
questions.explanation: "arguably" hedges a strong superlative claim ("the most important") by admitting that others may disagree.
questions.meaning: as could reasonably be claimed
questions.example: She is arguably the best player in the team.

questions.prompt: The mechanism is ___ understood.
questions.explanation: "poorly" is the natural adverb with "understood" to say that knowledge of the mechanism is limited; "virtually" and "marginally" do not collocate with it here.
questions.meaning: badly; not well enough
questions.example: The mechanism is poorly understood.

units.title: Legal & Formal Documents
units.description: Contract and policy language — Formal, legalistic register found in contracts, policies, and official notices.

questions.prompt: The tenant shall ___ the premises in good condition.
questions.explanation: After "shall" the sentence needs a base verb, and "maintain" fits the object "the premises" and the phrase 'in good condition'.
questions.meaning: to keep something in good condition
questions.example: The tenant shall maintain the premises.

questions.prompt: This agreement is ___ upon signature by both parties.
questions.explanation: "binding" means legally obliging the parties, and 'binding upon signature' is the standard contract phrase for when an agreement takes effect.
questions.meaning: legally required to be obeyed
questions.example: This agreement is binding on both parties.

questions.prompt: The clause shall be ___ null and void if breached.
questions.explanation: "deemed" completes 'shall be deemed null and void', the fixed legal phrase meaning 'treated as' void if the clause is breached.
questions.meaning: judged or considered to be
questions.example: Notice shall be deemed received two days after posting.

questions.prompt: Either party may ___ this contract with 30 days' notice.
questions.explanation: After "may" you need a base verb, and "terminate" fits 'this contract with 30 days' notice', meaning to end it officially.
questions.meaning: to end an agreement officially
questions.example: Either party may terminate this contract.

questions.prompt: The company reserves the ___ to amend these terms.
questions.explanation: "right" is the noun in the fixed phrase 'reserves the right to', meaning the company keeps the power to amend the terms.
questions.meaning: a legal claim or power to do something
questions.example: The company reserves the right to amend these terms.

questions.prompt: All disputes shall be ___ by arbitration.
questions.explanation: 'Shall be' needs a past participle, and "resolved" means settled, which fits disputes handled 'by arbitration'.
questions.meaning: settled; solved
questions.example: All disputes shall be resolved by arbitration.

questions.prompt: The parties hereby ___ to the following terms.
questions.explanation: "agree" is the base verb that follows 'the parties hereby' and takes 'to the following terms' to show formal acceptance.
questions.meaning: to accept something officially
questions.example: The parties hereby agree to these terms.

questions.prompt: This policy is ___ to change without prior notice.
questions.explanation: "subject" forms the fixed phrase 'is subject to change', meaning the policy may be altered.
questions.meaning: likely to be affected by; depending on
questions.example: This policy is subject to change.

questions.prompt: The signatory ___ that all information is accurate.
questions.explanation: The singular subject "The signatory" needs a third-person verb, and "warrants" means formally guarantees that the information is accurate.
questions.meaning: promises that a fact is true
questions.example: The signatory warrants that all details are accurate.

questions.prompt: Failure to comply may result in immediate ___.
questions.explanation: "termination" is the noun for the official ending of a contract, the usual consequence of failing to comply, and it follows 'immediate'.
questions.meaning: the act of ending something officially
questions.example: Failure to comply may result in termination.

questions.prompt: The agreement shall remain in ___ for two years.
questions.explanation: "effect" fits here. Rule to remember: Formal, legalistic register found in contracts, policies, and official notices.
questions.meaning: valid and in use
questions.example: The agreement shall remain in effect for two years.

questions.prompt: Nothing herein shall be ___ as legal advice.
questions.explanation: "construed" fits here. Rule to remember: Formal, legalistic register found in contracts, policies, and official notices.
questions.meaning: understood or interpreted in a certain way
questions.example: Nothing herein shall be construed as advice.

questions.prompt: The buyer shall ___ full payment within 14 days.
questions.explanation: "remit" means to send money, which is the verb needed with "full payment" in a contract. "maintain", "pass" and "terminate" do not describe paying money.
questions.meaning: to send money as payment
questions.example: The buyer shall remit full payment promptly.

questions.prompt: This clause is ___ from the rest of the contract.
questions.explanation: "severable" means a clause can be separated from the rest, so the contract stays valid if that clause is struck out. "This clause is ___ from the rest" needs an adjective of separation, which "legal", "right" and "binding" are not.
questions.meaning: able to be removed without affecting the rest
questions.example: Each provision of this agreement is severable.

questions.prompt: The undersigned hereby ___ receipt of the goods.
questions.explanation: "acknowledges" means formally admits that something was received, which fits "receipt of the goods". "resolves", "interprets" and "remits" do not take "receipt" as an object in this sense.
questions.meaning: admits that something is true or received
questions.example: The undersigned acknowledges receipt of the goods.

questions.prompt: The contract is governed by the ___ of this state.
questions.explanation: "laws" is the noun that completes the standard phrase "governed by the laws of this state", naming the rules that control the contract. "termination", "force" and "pass" do not make sense after "governed by the".
questions.meaning: the rules made by a government
questions.example: The contract is governed by the laws of this state.

questions.prompt: Any amendment must be made in ___.
questions.explanation: "writing" completes the fixed phrase "in writing", meaning on paper rather than spoken. The other options cannot follow "made in" here.
questions.meaning: written form, kept as an official record
questions.example: Any amendment must be made in writing.

questions.prompt: The company shall not be held ___ for delays.
questions.explanation: "liable" means legally responsible, and "held liable for" is the set phrase used when someone must answer for loss or delay. "severable" and "binding" do not collocate with "held ... for".
questions.meaning: legally responsible for something
questions.example: The company shall not be liable for delays.

questions.prompt: The parties agree to keep the terms ___.
questions.explanation: "confidential" means kept secret, which is what parties agree to do with the terms of a deal ("keep the terms confidential"). "liable" and "severable" do not describe how terms are kept.
questions.meaning: meant to be kept secret
questions.example: The parties shall keep the terms confidential.

questions.prompt: This document shall ___ all prior agreements.
questions.explanation: "supersede" fits here. Rule to remember: Formal, legalistic register found in contracts, policies, and official notices.
questions.meaning: to take the place of something older
questions.example: This document shall supersede all prior agreements.

questions.prompt: The recipient must ___ the terms before proceeding.
questions.explanation: After "must" the bare verb "accept" is needed, and "accept the terms" means agreeing to the conditions before going ahead. "warrants", "interpreted" and "resolved" have the wrong form after "must".
questions.meaning: to agree to terms or conditions
questions.example: The recipient must accept the terms.

questions.prompt: The obligation shall ___ to the successor entity.
questions.explanation: After "shall" you need the bare verb, so "pass" is right; an obligation "passes to" a successor when it is handed on to them, and "passes" or "passing" cannot follow "shall".
questions.meaning: to be handed on to someone else
questions.example: The obligation shall pass to the successor.

questions.prompt: Each party shall bear its own ___ costs.
questions.explanation: "legal" is the adjective that fits before "costs" to mean the fees of lawyers and court proceedings, a standard phrase in contracts. The other words cannot modify "costs" in this way.
questions.meaning: connected with the law
questions.example: Each party bears its own legal costs.

questions.prompt: The waiver shall not be ___ as a precedent.
questions.explanation: After "shall not be" you need a past participle, and "interpreted" fits the sense of how a waiver is understood: it must not be "interpreted as a precedent".
questions.meaning: explained or understood in a particular way
questions.example: The waiver shall not be interpreted as a precedent.

questions.prompt: The clause comes into ___ immediately upon execution.
questions.explanation: "come into force" is the fixed formal phrase meaning a clause becomes legally valid, so "force" is the noun needed after "comes into".
questions.meaning: legal validity; being officially in effect
questions.example: The clause comes into force upon execution.

units.title: Nuanced Character & Emotion
units.description: Precise personality vocabulary — C1-level adjectives for describing character and emotion.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "extremely careful with details"?
questions.explanation: extremely careful with details → meticulous. C1-level adjectives for describing character precisely.
questions.meaning: extremely careful about every detail
questions.example: A meticulous editor checked every line.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "boldly daring, sometimes reckless"? ___
questions.explanation: "audacious" describes someone who is boldly daring and willing to take risks, sometimes recklessly, which matches the definition.
questions.meaning: bold in a daring way, even reckless
questions.example: It was an audacious plan.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "refusing to change one's mind"?
questions.explanation: refusing to change one's mind → obstinate. C1-level adjectives for describing character precisely.
questions.meaning: stubborn; refusing to change your mind
questions.example: He remained obstinate despite the evidence.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "quick to notice small details"? ___
questions.explanation: "perceptive" means good at noticing and understanding things others miss, such as small details.
questions.meaning: quick to notice small details
questions.example: A perceptive teacher spotted the problem.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "excessively proud of oneself"?
questions.explanation: excessively proud of oneself → conceited. C1-level adjectives for describing character precisely.
questions.meaning: too proud of yourself
questions.example: The conceited actor ignored his fans.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "easily annoyed or irritated"? ___
questions.explanation: "irascible" describes someone who gets angry or annoyed very easily, which matches the definition; "obstinate" means stubborn and "fastidious" means fussy.
questions.meaning: easily made angry
questions.example: My irascible uncle shouted at the waiter.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "showing great attention to duty"?
