questions.explanation: A "conscientious" person takes their duties seriously and does their work carefully and thoroughly. "Reticent" instead means unwilling to talk.
questions.meaning: careful to do your duty well
questions.example: She is a conscientious worker.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "lacking confidence or self-esteem"? ___
questions.explanation: "insecure" describes someone who doubts themselves and lacks confidence. "naive" means too trusting, and "meticulous" and "frugal" are about care with detail and money.
questions.meaning: lacking confidence in yourself
questions.example: He felt insecure about his looks.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "careful and economical with money"?
questions.explanation: "frugal" describes someone who spends money carefully and avoids waste. It is usually a positive word, unlike stingy.
questions.meaning: careful not to waste money
questions.example: A frugal family saves every month.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "honest and direct in what one says"? ___
questions.explanation: "candid" describes someone who speaks frankly and truthfully, even when the truth is awkward. "capricious" means unpredictable and "conscientious" means careful and dutiful.
questions.meaning: honest and direct in what you say
questions.example: She gave a candid answer.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "avoiding unnecessary risk"? ___
questions.explanation: "prudent" describes someone who thinks ahead and avoids unnecessary risks. "fastidious" means fussy about detail and "irascible" means easily angered.
questions.meaning: careful to avoid danger or loss
questions.example: It's prudent to save for the future.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "having a sharp, cutting wit"?
questions.explanation: "acerbic" describes speech or humor that is sharp and bitingly critical, which is exactly a cutting wit. "audacious" means bold and "resourceful" means good at solving problems.
questions.meaning: sharp and bitter in a clever way
questions.example: Her acerbic wit stung him.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "easily influenced by others"? ___
questions.explanation: "impressionable" describes someone, often young, who is easily influenced by what others say or do. "insecure" is about lacking confidence, not about being swayed.
questions.meaning: easily affected by others
questions.example: Children are impressionable.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "showing no emotion on one's face"?
questions.explanation: "impassive" describes a face or manner that shows no feeling at all. "reticent" means unwilling to talk about your thoughts, which is not the same as a blank expression.
questions.meaning: showing no feeling on the face
questions.example: He stayed impassive during the verdict.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "tending to think the worst will happen"? ___
questions.explanation: "pessimistic" describes someone who expects things to go badly; it is the opposite of optimistic.
questions.meaning: expecting the worst result
questions.example: A pessimistic forecast scared investors.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "having strong, unshakeable opinions"?
questions.explanation: "dogmatic" describes someone who treats their opinions as undeniable truth and will not consider other views. "irascible" means easily angered and "obsequious" means too eager to please.
questions.meaning: holding opinions as unquestionable truth
questions.example: He is dogmatic about politics.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "quick to take offense"? ___
questions.explanation: "touchy" describes someone who is easily offended or upset by small things. "acerbic" describes sharp, critical speech aimed at others, not being easily hurt.
questions.meaning: easily hurt or offended
questions.example: She is touchy about her age.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "showing deep, genuine care"?
questions.explanation: "compassionate" describes someone who feels and shows real sympathy and care for people who are suffering.
questions.meaning: feeling kindness for others who suffer
questions.example: A compassionate nurse sat with her.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "lacking experience or worldliness"? ___
questions.explanation: "naive" describes someone with little experience of life who trusts people too easily. "conceited" means too proud of yourself and "imperturbable" means always calm.
questions.meaning: lacking experience of life
questions.example: It was naive to trust him.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "good at finding clever ways to solve problems"?
questions.explanation: "resourceful" describes someone who finds clever ways to deal with problems; "prudent" means careful to avoid risk, not inventive.
questions.meaning: good at finding ways to solve problems
questions.example: A resourceful cook made dinner from scraps.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "very concerned about detail and hard to please"?
questions.explanation: "fastidious" describes someone who pays great attention to detail and is hard to please; "irascible" means quick-tempered and "obsequious" means too eager to please.
questions.meaning: very careful about detail and hard to please
questions.example: He is fastidious about cleanliness.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "reluctant to reveal information"? ___
questions.explanation: "reticent" means unwilling to share your thoughts or information; "candid" is the opposite, meaning open and honest.
questions.meaning: unwilling to share your thoughts
questions.example: She was reticent about her past.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "having a calm, unshakeable temperament"?
questions.explanation: "imperturbable" describes someone who stays calm whatever happens; "meticulous" is about careful attention to detail, not temperament.
questions.meaning: never upset or worried by events
questions.example: The pilot stayed imperturbable in the storm.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "excessively eager to please"? ___
questions.explanation: "obsequious" means trying far too hard to please people, especially important ones; "acerbic" means sharp and sarcastic, the opposite of fawning.
questions.meaning: too eager to please or obey others
questions.example: The obsequious waiter bowed constantly.

questions.prompt: Which trait means "unpredictable and prone to sudden mood changes"?
questions.explanation: "capricious" describes someone whose moods and decisions change suddenly and without warning; "audacious" means bold and "frugal" means careful with money.
questions.meaning: changing mood or mind without warning
questions.example: Her capricious boss changed the plan every day.

units.title: Rhetoric & Persuasion
units.description: Argumentative language — C1-level vocabulary for constructing a persuasive argument.

questions.prompt: The speaker made a ___ case for reform.
questions.explanation: "compelling" is the natural collocation with "case", meaning so strong that it is hard to resist, which suits a speaker arguing for reform.
questions.meaning: very convincing
questions.example: She made a compelling case for reform.

questions.prompt: Her argument ___ on a single flawed assumption.
questions.explanation: "hinges" takes the preposition "on" and means depends entirely on one thing, which fits an argument resting on a single flawed assumption.
questions.meaning: depends completely on one thing
questions.example: The case hinges on a single assumption.

questions.prompt: The evidence ___ against his claim.
questions.explanation: "militates" is the verb that goes with "against" and means counts strongly against, so evidence that "militates against his claim" weakens it.
questions.meaning: counts against something or makes it less likely
questions.example: The evidence militates against his claim.

questions.prompt: This point ___ at the very heart of the debate.
questions.explanation: "strikes" forms the idiom "strikes at the heart of", meaning attacks or directly affects the most important part of something.
questions.meaning: attacks or affects something at its core
questions.example: This argument strikes at the heart of the problem.

questions.prompt: The policy has been ___ criticized by experts.
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the participle "criticized", and "widely" gives the natural collocation "widely criticized", meaning criticized by many people.
questions.meaning: by many people in many places
questions.example: The policy was widely criticized.

questions.prompt: His speech was designed to ___ public opinion.
questions.explanation: After "to" you need the base verb, and "sway" means to influence, so a speech designed to "sway public opinion" aims to change what people think.
questions.meaning: to change what people think
questions.example: He tried to sway public opinion.

questions.prompt: The argument ___ down to a matter of values.
questions.explanation: "boils" completes the phrasal verb "boils down to", meaning is essentially a matter of, and agrees with the singular subject "The argument".
questions.meaning: to be simply a matter of
questions.example: It boils down to values.

questions.prompt: She ___ her point with a striking example.
questions.explanation: "illustrated" means showed or explained by giving an example, which matches "with a striking example".
questions.meaning: explained with an example
questions.example: She illustrated her point well.

questions.prompt: The rhetoric was ___ but ultimately hollow.
questions.explanation: An adjective is needed after "was", and "persuasive" describes rhetoric that sounds convincing, which sets up the contrast with "ultimately hollow".
questions.meaning: able to make people believe something
questions.example: The speech was persuasive but hollow.

questions.prompt: His claim does not ___ up to scrutiny.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is "stand" up to scrutiny, meaning to survive close examination; the other options cannot follow "does not ___ up to".
questions.meaning: to be strong enough to bear a test
questions.example: His claim does not stand up to scrutiny.

questions.prompt: The debate ___ on questions of fairness.
questions.explanation: "turns" on means 'depends on', and a debate that turns on fairness hinges on that question; the other verbs do not take "on" in this sense.
questions.meaning: to depend on
questions.example: The debate turns on fairness.

questions.prompt: She skilfully ___ the opposing argument.
questions.explanation: "dismantled" is a past-tense verb meaning she took the argument apart skilfully; the other bank words are present-tense forms or do not take an argument as object.
questions.meaning: took apart piece by piece
questions.example: She dismantled the opposing argument.

questions.prompt: The speech was carefully ___ to appeal to emotion.
questions.explanation: A speech designed to appeal to emotion is "crafted", meaning made with skill and care; "dismantled" and "unpicked" mean taking apart, which does not fit.
questions.meaning: made with skill and care
questions.example: The speech was carefully crafted.

questions.prompt: His conclusion ___ naturally from the evidence.
questions.explanation: A conclusion "follows" from evidence, meaning it is a logical result of it; the sentence needs a present-tense verb taking "from".
questions.meaning: comes as a logical result
questions.example: His conclusion follows from the evidence.

questions.prompt: The argument gained ___ as more facts emerged.
questions.explanation: "traction" collocates with "gained" to mean an idea attracting growing support, which fits facts emerging; "doubt" would not suit a gain in support.
questions.meaning: growing support or progress
questions.example: The argument gained traction.

questions.prompt: She ___ the audience with a powerful anecdote.
questions.explanation: To win over an audience is to persuade them to support you, so the past form "won over" fits a powerful anecdote; "gave up", "turned down" and "ran into" do not make sense here.
questions.meaning: persuaded someone to support you
questions.example: She won over the audience.

questions.prompt: The claim is ___ by a wealth of research.
questions.explanation: "substantiated" means supported by evidence, which is what a wealth of research does for a claim; "persuaded", "convinced" and "swayed" describe people, not claims.
questions.meaning: shown to be true by evidence
questions.example: The claim is substantiated by research.

questions.prompt: His tone ___ conviction rather than certainty.
questions.explanation: A tone can convey a feeling, meaning it communicates it to listeners, so the past form "conveyed" fits; "unpicked", "won over" and "dismantled" cannot take "conviction" as their object.
questions.meaning: made an idea or feeling known
questions.example: His tone conveyed conviction.

questions.prompt: The counterargument ___ to address the core issue.
questions.explanation: "fails" is right because "fail to + verb" means not manage to do something, and a counterargument that does not deal with the core issue has failed; "succeeds" would need "in addressing", and "avoids" and "misses" cannot be followed by "to address".
questions.meaning: does not do what is needed
questions.example: The counterargument fails to address the issue.

questions.prompt: She ___ her opponent's logic point by point.
questions.explanation: To unpick an argument point by point is to take it apart step by step, like undoing stitches, so the past form "unpicked" fits; the other verbs do not describe analyzing an opponent's logic.
questions.meaning: took apart step by step
questions.example: She unpicked her opponent's logic.

questions.prompt: The rhetoric ___ more heat than light.
questions.explanation: The idiom is "generate more heat than light", meaning to cause anger rather than useful understanding, so the past form "generated" completes it; the other words do not form this fixed phrase.
questions.meaning: caused or produced
questions.example: The debate generated more heat than light.

questions.prompt: His appeal was ___ rather than rational.
questions.explanation: "emotional" is right because the sentence contrasts the appeal with "rational", so it needs a word meaning based on feeling rather than reason.
questions.meaning: based on feeling, not reason
questions.example: His appeal was emotional.

questions.prompt: The argument ___ scrutiny remarkably well.
questions.explanation: "withstands" is right because an argument that survives close examination 'withstands scrutiny'; the other words do not take 'scrutiny' as an object.
questions.meaning: survives a test or attack
questions.example: The argument withstands scrutiny.

questions.prompt: She ___ the audience's skepticism head-on.
questions.explanation: "addressed" is right because "head-on" signals tackling the skepticism directly, and you address a doubt; you win over or sway people, not their skepticism, and you cannot ignore something head-on.
questions.meaning: dealt with directly
questions.example: She addressed the audience's skepticism.

questions.prompt: The speech left little room for ___.
questions.explanation: "doubt" is right because "little room for doubt" is the set phrase for something so convincing that nobody can question it; the other nouns do not form this phrase.
questions.meaning: a feeling of not being sure
questions.example: The speech left little room for doubt.

units.title: Scientific & Technical Prose
units.description: Precision in research writing — C1-level vocabulary for describing scientific findings.

questions.prompt: The experiment was ___ under controlled conditions.
questions.explanation: "conducted" is right because experiments are 'conducted' (carried out) under set conditions; 'analysed' would describe the data, not running the experiment.
questions.meaning: carried out an activity
questions.example: The experiment was conducted in controlled conditions.

questions.prompt: The results were ___ across multiple trials, so the finding was confirmed.
questions.explanation: "consistent" is right because results that stay the same across multiple trials confirm a finding; "divergent" or "preliminary" results would not confirm it.
questions.meaning: always giving the same result
questions.example: The results were consistent across trials.

questions.prompt: The hypothesis was ___ by the data.
questions.explanation: "supported" is right because data can back up a hypothesis ('by the data'), whereas a hypothesis is not observed, developed or published by data.
questions.meaning: gave evidence in favour of
questions.example: The data supported the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Looking closely at the data, researchers ___ a significant correlation.
questions.explanation: "observed" is right because "looking closely at the data" describes noticing something, and researchers observe a correlation that they find in their data.
questions.meaning: noticed by watching carefully
questions.example: Researchers observed a significant correlation.

questions.prompt: The findings ___ from earlier studies.
questions.explanation: "diverge" is right because it takes 'from' and means the findings differ from earlier studies; it is also the plural present form that agrees with 'findings'.
questions.meaning: differ or move apart
questions.example: The findings diverge from earlier studies.

questions.prompt: The sample size was ___ to ensure reliability.
questions.explanation: "sufficient" is right because a sample size can be big enough 'to ensure reliability'; the other options do not describe size or adequacy.
questions.meaning: enough for what is needed
questions.example: The sample size was sufficient.

questions.prompt: The variables were ___ controlled, with every measurement checked twice.
questions.explanation: Checking every measurement twice shows extreme care, so "meticulously" (with great attention to detail) fits; "largely" would mean the control was only partial.
questions.meaning: with extreme care
questions.example: The variables were meticulously controlled.

questions.prompt: The study's ___ limits its generalisability.
questions.explanation: "scope" is right because a study's range (its sample or coverage) is what limits how widely its results apply; 'rigour' would strengthen a study, and 'conclusions' and 'addresses' are plural, so they do not agree with 'limits'.
questions.meaning: the range of what is covered
questions.example: The study's scope limits its use.

questions.prompt: The data was ___ using standard statistical methods.
questions.explanation: "analyzed" is right because the data is examined 'using standard statistical methods'; it is a past participle that fits after 'was'. The other words do not make sense in this passive sentence.
questions.meaning: examined closely to find results
questions.example: The data was analyzed statistically.

questions.prompt: The results were ___ reproducible.
questions.explanation: "largely" is right because an adverb is needed before the adjective 'reproducible', and it means 'for the most part'. 'Published' and 'validity' are not adverbs, and 'meticulously' does not describe how reproducible results are.
questions.meaning: for the most part
questions.example: The results were largely reproducible.

questions.prompt: The team ___ a novel methodology.
questions.explanation: "developed" is right because a team creates a new methodology, and the past simple verb takes it as an object. 'Carry' is the wrong form, and 'deemed' or 'observed' do not mean creating a method.
questions.meaning: created over time
questions.example: The team developed a new method.

questions.prompt: The findings ___ implications for future research.
questions.explanation: "carry" is right because 'carry implications' is the set collocation, and the plural subject 'findings' takes the base form. The other words cannot take 'implications' as their object.
questions.meaning: to involve something as a consequence
questions.example: The findings carry implications for future work.

questions.prompt: The experiment was ___ due to funding cuts.
questions.explanation: "discontinued" is right because 'due to funding cuts' tells us the experiment was stopped. 'Supported' and 'published' do not follow from a loss of funding, and 'addresses' is the wrong form.
questions.meaning: stopped; no longer continued
questions.example: The experiment was discontinued.

questions.prompt: The paper was ___ in a peer-reviewed journal.
questions.explanation: "published" is right because papers appear in a journal when they are published. 'Presented' is used for talks at conferences, and 'carry' is the wrong form.
questions.meaning: printed or put out for the public
questions.example: The paper was published in a journal.

questions.prompt: The results ___ the initial hypothesis.
questions.explanation: "confirm" is right because results can show that a hypothesis is true, and the plural subject 'results' takes the base form. The other options do not make sense with 'the initial hypothesis'.
questions.meaning: to show that something is true
questions.example: The results confirm the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: The methodology has since been ___ by other researchers for use in their own studies.
questions.explanation: "for use in their own studies" means other researchers took the method and used it themselves, which is exactly what "adopted" means.
questions.meaning: taken and used by others
questions.example: The method was adopted by other researchers.

questions.prompt: The study's ___ have been widely debated.
questions.explanation: "conclusions" is right because the plural 'have been debated' needs a plural noun, and a study's conclusions are naturally open to debate. 'Scope' and 'validity' are singular, and 'presented' is a verb.
questions.meaning: final judgements based on evidence
questions.example: The study's conclusions are debated.

questions.prompt: The data set was ___ for anomalies.
questions.explanation: "screened" is right because checking data 'for anomalies' is called screening it. 'Confirm' and 'diverge' are the wrong form, and 'detailed' does not mean checking for problems.
questions.meaning: checked for problems
questions.example: The data was screened for anomalies.

questions.prompt: The researchers ___ several confounding variables.
questions.explanation: "controlled for" is right because researchers 'control for' confounding variables, meaning they remove their effect from the analysis. The other verbs do not take this meaning with variables.
questions.meaning: took steps to remove the effect of
questions.example: They controlled for confounding variables.

questions.prompt: The findings were ___ with caution.
questions.explanation: "presented" is right because 'presented with caution' means the findings were shown to others in a careful, qualified way. 'Adopted' and 'replicated' do not go naturally with 'with caution' here, and 'addresses' is the wrong form.
questions.meaning: shown to others
questions.example: The findings were presented with caution.

questions.prompt: The experiment's ___, meaning whether it truly measures what it claims, remains a subject of debate.
questions.explanation: The blank needs a singular noun after "The experiment's" to match "remains", and "validity" (whether the results are sound) is what scientists debate here.
questions.meaning: the quality of being sound and true
questions.example: The experiment's validity is debated.

questions.prompt: The results were ___ statistically significant.
questions.explanation: "deemed" means judged or considered, and "were deemed statistically significant" is the standard way to report a judgment about results. "Observed", "developed" and "screened" do not take an adjective complement in this way.
questions.meaning: judged or considered
questions.example: The results were deemed significant.

questions.prompt: The team ___ their methodology step by step in the appendix.
questions.explanation: To "detail" something means to explain it fully, so "detailed" fits a method that is set out step by step in an appendix.
questions.meaning: explained in full
questions.example: The team detailed their methods.

questions.prompt: The study ___ a gap in the existing literature.
questions.explanation: The study deals with a gap in the literature, and the verb that collocates with "a gap" in that sense is "addresses". "Analyzed" and "adopted" do not combine with a gap, and "controlled for" applies to variables.
questions.meaning: deals with a problem or issue
questions.example: The study addresses a gap in the literature.

questions.prompt: The conclusions are ___ by the limited sample.
questions.explanation: "constrained" means limited, and a small sample limits how far the conclusions can go; the other words do not describe what a sample does to conclusions.
questions.meaning: limited or held back
questions.example: The conclusions are constrained by the sample.

units.title: Diplomatic Language
units.description: Softening and hedging in formal talk — C1-level diplomatic phrasing for sensitive conversations.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Language 1
lessons.subtitle: Softening and hedging in formal talk

questions.prompt: With all due ___, I have to disagree with that assessment.
questions.explanation: "respect" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level diplomatic phrasing for sensitive conversations.
questions.meaning: polite regard for someone's feelings
questions.example: With all due respect, I disagree.

questions.prompt: Given the new risks, it might be ___ to reconsider the timing of this decision.
questions.explanation: "prudent" means wise and careful, which is the diplomatic way to suggest rethinking a decision because of new risks.
questions.meaning: wise and careful
questions.example: It might be prudent to wait.

questions.prompt: We would ___ appreciate a more detailed explanation.
questions.explanation: "Appreciate" collocates with "greatly" (meaning very much), while "strongly appreciate" and "kindly appreciate" are not idiomatic.
questions.meaning: very much
questions.example: We would greatly appreciate more detail.

questions.prompt: Perhaps we could ___ this matter from a different angle.
questions.explanation: "approach" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level diplomatic phrasing for sensitive conversations.
questions.meaning: to tackle a problem in a particular way
questions.example: Let us approach this from another angle.

questions.prompt: It's not entirely ___ that the plan will succeed.
questions.explanation: "It's not entirely clear that..." is a diplomatic way to express doubt, because "clear" is the adjective that goes with "It's... that" to talk about certainty.
questions.meaning: certain or obvious
questions.example: It's not entirely clear that it will work.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Language 2
lessons.subtitle: Softening and hedging in formal talk

questions.prompt: There are, ___, a few concerns we should address first.
questions.explanation: The commas around the blank mark a contrast inserted mid-sentence, which "however" provides. "While" starts a clause, and "sincerely" and "clear" do not link ideas.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast
questions.example: There are, however, a few concerns.

questions.prompt: We understand your ___, but the budget remains fixed.
questions.explanation: Your "position" is your view or stance in a negotiation, so "We understand your position, but..." politely acknowledges it before disagreeing.
questions.meaning: someone's opinion or stance on an issue
questions.example: We understand your position, but the budget is fixed.

questions.prompt: It would be ___ to say the negotiations went smoothly; in fact, there were several heated disagreements.
questions.explanation: The second clause shows the talks went badly, so "generous" is a polite understatement: calling them smooth judges them too kindly. "Advisable" would recommend saying something untrue, and "grateful" and "clear" cannot describe saying something.
questions.meaning: judging something more kindly than it deserves
questions.example: It would be generous to say it went well.

questions.prompt: Let's not ___ this issue any further today.
questions.explanation: "belabour" means to spend too long on a point, so "Let's not belabour this issue" is a polite way to move on. "Refrain" would need "from", "maintain" does not fit the meaning, and "considering" is not a base verb after "not".
questions.meaning: to talk about something for too long
questions.example: Let's not belabour the issue today.

questions.prompt: We ___ acknowledge the difficulties this has caused.
questions.explanation: "Acknowledge" collocates with "fully" (meaning completely), giving a strong, formal admission of the problem.
questions.meaning: completely
questions.example: We fully acknowledge the difficulties.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Language 3
lessons.subtitle: Softening and hedging in formal talk

questions.prompt: It might be worth ___ a compromise instead.
questions.explanation: "worth" is followed by the -ing form of a verb, and "considering" is the only -ing form in the bank. "Treat" and "understand" are base forms, and "clear" is an adjective.
questions.meaning: thinking about something carefully
questions.example: It's worth considering a compromise.

questions.prompt: We remain open to ___ should circumstances change.
questions.explanation: "discussion" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level diplomatic phrasing for sensitive conversations.
questions.meaning: talk about a subject
questions.example: We remain open to discussion.

questions.prompt: While we ___ your concerns, the decision stands.
questions.explanation: "understand" fits the pattern "While we understand X, the decision stands", which politely concedes the other side's feelings before refusing. "Express" would mean we voice your concerns ourselves, which does not make sense here.
questions.meaning: know why someone feels something
questions.example: While we understand your concerns, the decision stands.

questions.prompt: It would be ___ to comment further at this stage, as the investigation is still ongoing.
questions.explanation: "premature" means too early, and an ongoing investigation makes it too early to comment.
questions.meaning: too early
questions.example: It would be premature to comment.

questions.prompt: We'd like to ___ our gratitude for your patience.
questions.explanation: "express" is the verb that collocates with "gratitude" when you put thanks into words. "Refrain" needs "from", "belabour" means to dwell on a point, and "treat" does not fit.
questions.meaning: to show a feeling in words
questions.example: We would like to express our gratitude.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Language 4
lessons.subtitle: Softening and hedging in formal talk

questions.prompt: There is, ___, room for further discussion.
questions.explanation: "admittedly" is a sentence adverb that concedes a point, so "There is, admittedly, room for further discussion" sounds like a cautious concession. "Fully", "greatly" and "sincerely" do not work as commenting adverbs in this position.
questions.meaning: used to concede a point against your argument
questions.example: There is, admittedly, room for discussion.

questions.prompt: We should ___ from making any hasty judgements.
questions.explanation: "refrain" is followed by "from" and means to hold yourself back, as in "refrain from making hasty judgements". The other words do not take "from" in this way.
questions.meaning: to hold yourself back from doing something
questions.example: We should refrain from hasty judgements.

questions.prompt: It may be ___ to revisit this proposal next quarter.
questions.explanation: "advisable" means wise or recommended, so "It may be advisable to revisit this proposal" is a tactful suggestion about timing. "Generous", "clear" and "reluctant" do not fit a suggestion about what to do next quarter.
questions.meaning: wise to do
questions.example: It may be advisable to revisit this.

questions.prompt: We ___ hope this matter can be resolved amicably.
questions.explanation: "sincerely" collocates with "hope" to show genuine good will, as in "We sincerely hope this can be resolved". "Admittedly", "fully" and "greatly" do not combine naturally with "hope".
questions.meaning: in an honest, true way
questions.example: We sincerely hope this can be resolved.

questions.prompt: Let us ___ the matter with the care it deserves.
questions.explanation: "treat" is right because we treat a matter with care, meaning we handle it in a certain way. "Attend" would need "to", "refrain" needs "from", and you do not "clear up" a matter with care.
questions.meaning: to deal with something in a certain way
questions.example: Let us treat the matter carefully.

lessons.title: Diplomatic Language 5
lessons.subtitle: Softening and hedging in formal talk

questions.prompt: It would be ___ to overstate the challenges ahead.
questions.explanation: "easy" completes the set phrase 'It would be easy to overstate...', which warns politely that exaggeration is a tempting mistake. 'Prudent' and 'premature' do not fit this frame.
questions.meaning: not hard to do
questions.example: It would be easy to overstate the challenges.

questions.prompt: We trust this explanation will ___ any confusion.
questions.explanation: "clear up" is the phrasal verb that means to remove confusion or a misunderstanding. The other words cannot take 'any confusion' as an object after 'will'.
questions.meaning: to resolve a misunderstanding or confusion
questions.example: This should clear up any confusion.

questions.prompt: Some concerns, ___ valid, fall outside our remit.
questions.explanation: "while" can introduce a short concession before an adjective, meaning 'although they are valid'. 'Despite' needs a noun or -ing form, and 'because' and 'whereas' cannot be shortened like this.
questions.meaning: although; often used without a verb
questions.example: Some concerns, while valid, are outside our remit.

questions.prompt: We ___ that further consultation is required.
questions.explanation: "maintain" followed by 'that' means to firmly state a position, which suits a formal statement about what is required. 'Discuss', 'belabour' and 'treat' cannot take a 'that' clause.
questions.meaning: to claim that something is true
questions.example: We maintain that more consultation is needed.

questions.prompt: It is with some ___ that we must decline the offer.
questions.explanation: "reluctance" fits 'It is with some ___ that we must decline', the polite formula for saying we refuse unwillingly. 'Delight', 'respect' and 'discussion' do not express unwillingness.
questions.meaning: an unwillingness to do something
questions.example: It is with some reluctance that we decline.

units.title: Idiomatic Expressions II
units.description: Advanced idioms — Match idioms that go beyond the basics to their meanings.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to jump on the bandwagon" means… ___
bank: to get to the point quickly
questions.explanation: A bandwagon is a trend that everyone hurries to join, so "to join something popular" is the meaning, often said slightly critically.
questions.meaning: to join a trend because others have
questions.example: Many firms want to jump on the bandwagon.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to read between the lines" means…
questions.explanation: When you read between the lines, you notice what someone means but does not say directly, so the idiom means "to understand hidden meaning".
questions.meaning: to understand a hidden meaning
questions.example: You have to read between the lines.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to bite the bullet" means… ___
bank: to have both good and bad effects
questions.explanation: To bite the bullet is to face something unpleasant that you cannot avoid, such as apologizing, so it means "to accept something difficult".
questions.meaning: to make yourself do something difficult or unpleasant
questions.example: He had to bite the bullet and apologize.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to burn bridges" means…
choices: to seem bad but turn out good
questions.explanation: If you burn bridges, you damage a relationship so badly that you cannot go back, so the idiom means "to end a relationship badly".
questions.meaning: to end a relationship badly
questions.example: Try not to burn bridges when you quit.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to see eye to eye" means… ___
bank: to use influence to get something
questions.explanation: People who see eye to eye share the same opinion, so the idiom means "to agree completely". It is often used in the negative, as in "We rarely see eye to eye."
questions.meaning: to agree completely
questions.example: We rarely see eye to eye on politics.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to go the extra mile" means…
choices: to have both good and bad effects
questions.explanation: To go the extra mile is to do more than is expected of you, so the idiom means "to make extra effort".
questions.meaning: to make an extra effort
questions.example: She is willing to go the extra mile for you.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to cut to the chase" means… ___
bank: to get to the point quickly
questions.answer: to get to the point quickly
questions.explanation: To cut to the chase is to skip the unimportant details and talk about the main issue, so the idiom means "to get to the point quickly".
questions.meaning: to get to the point quickly
questions.example: Let's cut to the chase.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to hit the nail on the head" means…
choices: to be caught doing something wrong
questions.explanation: A carpenter who hits a nail exactly on its head has struck it perfectly, so the idiom means "to be exactly right" about something.
questions.term: to hit the nail on the head
questions.meaning: to be exactly right
questions.example: You managed to hit the nail on the head there.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be on the same page" means… ___
questions.explanation: People on the same page are reading the same text, so the idiom means "to have the same understanding" of a plan or situation.
questions.term: to be on the same page
questions.meaning: to have the same understanding
questions.example: We need to be on the same page.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to throw in the towel" means…
questions.explanation: In boxing, a trainer throws a towel into the ring to admit defeat, so the idiom means "to give up".
questions.meaning: to give up
questions.example: He decided to throw in the towel after a year.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to keep someone at arm's length" means…
questions.explanation: Holding someone a whole arm away stops them getting near you, so the idiom means "to avoid becoming close".
questions.term: to keep someone at arm's length
questions.meaning: to avoid becoming close
questions.example: It's unkind to keep someone at arm's length for no reason.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to have a change of heart" means… ___
questions.explanation: Your "heart" here stands for your feelings about a decision, so the idiom means "to change one's opinion".
questions.term: to have a change of heart
questions.meaning: to change your opinion
questions.example: It's not too late to have a change of heart.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be caught red-handed" means…
choices: to be caught doing something wrong
questions.explanation: The image is of someone found with blood still on their hands, so the idiom means "to be caught doing something wrong" in the act.
questions.meaning: to be caught doing something wrong
questions.example: The burglar didn't expect to be caught red-handed.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to take something with a pinch of salt" means… ___
questions.explanation: A pinch of salt makes something easier to swallow, so the idiom means "to not fully believe it", that is, to treat it with some doubt.
questions.term: to take something with a grain of salt
questions.meaning: to not fully believe something
questions.example: Try to take something with a grain of salt.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to beat around the bush" means…
choices: to get to the point quickly
to have both good and bad effects
questions.explanation: Beating the bushes around something instead of going straight to it means "to avoid speaking directly" about the main point.
questions.meaning: to avoid speaking directly
questions.example: There's no need to beat around the bush with me.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be a blessing in disguise" means… ___
bank: to seem bad but turn out good
questions.answer: to seem bad but turn out good
questions.explanation: A blessing "in disguise" looks like bad luck at first, so the idiom means "to seem bad but turn out good".
questions.term: to be a blessing in disguise
questions.meaning: something that seems bad but proves good
questions.example: Losing that job turned out to be a blessing in disguise.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to let the cat out of the bag" means…
choices: to seem bad but turn out good
questions.explanation: "to reveal a secret" is right because letting the cat out of the bag means telling something that was meant to stay hidden, often by accident.
questions.term: to let the cat out of the bag
questions.meaning: to reveal a secret
questions.example: Try not to let the cat out of the bag.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to go back to the drawing board" means… ___
bank: to use influence to get something
questions.explanation: "to start planning again" is right because you go back to the drawing board when a plan has failed and you must begin again from the start.
questions.term: to go back to the drawing board
questions.meaning: to start planning again
questions.example: We had to go back to the drawing board.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to raise the bar" means…
questions.explanation: "to increase the standard expected" is right because the image is a high-jump bar being raised, so everyone has to do better to clear it.
questions.meaning: to increase the standard expected
questions.example: She aims to raise the bar for everyone.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be under the weather" means… ___
questions.explanation: to be under the weather → to feel slightly unwell. Advanced idioms beyond the basics.
questions.meaning: to feel slightly unwell
questions.example: I seem to be under the weather today.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to pull strings" means… ___
bank: to use influence to get something
questions.answer: to use influence to get something
questions.explanation: "to use influence to get something" is right because pulling strings means using your contacts or power, like a puppeteer moving a puppet, to get what you want.
questions.meaning: to use influence to get something
questions.example: He pulled strings to get the job.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be a double-edged sword" means…
choices: to have both good and bad effects
to be caught doing something wrong
questions.explanation: A sword with two sharp edges can cut its user as well as the enemy, so the idiom means "to have both good and bad effects".
questions.meaning: to have both good and bad effects
questions.example: Fame can prove to be a double-edged sword.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to keep one's fingers crossed" means… ___
questions.explanation: "to hope for good luck" is right because people cross their fingers, or say they are keeping them crossed, when they hope something will go well.
questions.meaning: to hope for good luck
questions.example: It helps to keep one's fingers crossed.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to be at a crossroads" means…
questions.explanation: At a crossroads you must choose which road to take, so the idiom means "to face an important decision".
questions.meaning: to face an important decision
questions.example: The firm appears to be at a crossroads.

questions.prompt: The idiom "to weather the storm" means… ___
bank: to be caught doing something wrong
questions.explanation: To weather something is to come through it without being destroyed, so the idiom means "to survive a difficult period".
questions.meaning: to survive a difficult period
questions.example: The company managed to weather the storm.

units.title: Complex Passive & Causative
units.description: Advanced passive structures — C1-level passive and causative constructions.

questions.prompt: The report is believed to have been ___ to the press deliberately.
questions.explanation: "leaked" means secretly given out, and 'to the press' shows who received the report. 'Printed', 'signed' and 'manipulated' do not combine with 'to the press'.
questions.meaning: secretly made known
questions.example: The report was leaked deliberately.

questions.prompt: It is thought that the decision will be ___ soon, so the old rule will apply again.
questions.explanation: "reversed" means a decision is changed to the opposite, and 'the old rule brought back' shows it will be undone completely. 'Revised' only means changed a little, and 'renewed' or 'stolen' do not suit a decision.
questions.meaning: changed to the opposite
questions.example: The decision will be reversed soon.

questions.prompt: The building is said to have been ___ by a famous architect in the 1920s.
questions.explanation: "designed" fits because the clue says the building was not built until the 1950s, so only the planning happened in the 1920s. 'Completed' contradicts the clue, and 'confirmed' and 'reviewed' do not describe what happens to a building.
questions.meaning: planned and drawn up
questions.example: The building was designed in the 1920s.

questions.prompt: She had her car ___ while she was on vacation.
questions.explanation: "stolen" completes the structure 'had her car + past participle', describing something bad that happened to her car. 'Translated', 'leaked' and 'surprised' make no sense with a car.
questions.meaning: taken by a thief
questions.example: She had her car stolen.

questions.prompt: He got his proposal ___ by the board.
questions.explanation: "approved" fits 'got his proposal ___ by the board', since a board formally approves proposals. 'Repaired' and 'designed' do not suit a proposal.
questions.meaning: accepted officially
questions.example: He got his proposal approved.

questions.prompt: The bridge, which has been under construction for three years, is due to be ___ next year.
questions.explanation: "completed" fits because 'after three years of building work' shows the bridge will be finished next year. A new bridge is not renewed or revised, and it must already have been designed before building began.
questions.meaning: finished
questions.example: The bridge is due to be completed next year.

questions.prompt: It is rumored that the company is planning ___, so hundreds of staff could lose their jobs.
questions.explanation: After 'is planning' with no object we need a noun, and the plural noun "layoffs" means job cuts. 'Lay off', 'laying off' and 'laid off' are verb forms that would need an object such as 'staff'.
questions.meaning: job cuts when a company dismisses staff
questions.example: The company is planning layoffs.

questions.prompt: The contract is expected to be ___ by Friday.
questions.explanation: A contract is expected to be "signed" by a deadline, so the past participle completes the passive 'to be ___'. Fled, stolen and manipulated do not fit a contract here.
questions.meaning: put your name on a document
questions.example: The contract will be signed by Friday.

questions.prompt: She had the documents ___ into French before the meeting.
questions.explanation: "Into French" points to a change of language, so "translated" is right; "had + object + past participle" means someone else did it for her.
questions.meaning: changed into another language
questions.example: She had the documents translated.

questions.prompt: The changes are said to have ___ efficiency, and output has risen sharply.
questions.explanation: 'are said to have + past participle' reports a past result, and the clue 'output has risen sharply' shows the effect was positive, so "improved" fits. Reviewed, reversed and confirmed do not match a rise in output.
questions.meaning: made better
questions.example: Changes are said to have improved efficiency.

questions.prompt: He had his passport ___ at the embassy.
questions.explanation: The causative 'had + object + past participle' needs a participle for something done to a passport, and an embassy "renewed" it. Fled, compromised and manipulated do not suit this routine service.
questions.meaning: made valid for another period
questions.example: He had his passport renewed.

questions.prompt: It is widely believed that the treaty will be formally ___ by parliament next month.
questions.explanation: A treaty is officially approved by a vote, so it is "ratified"; "will be + past participle" gives the future passive.
questions.meaning: formally approved
questions.example: The treaty will be ratified.

questions.prompt: The results are yet to be independently ___ by a second lab.
questions.explanation: Results are checked and shown to be true, so they are "confirmed"; "are yet to be + past participle" means this has not happened yet.
questions.meaning: shown to be true
questions.example: The results are yet to be confirmed.

questions.prompt: She got her essay ___ before submitting it.
questions.explanation: Before you submit an essay, you have it checked for mistakes, so it is "proofread"; "got + object + past participle" means someone else did it.
questions.meaning: checked for mistakes
questions.example: She got her essay proofread.

questions.prompt: The suspect is alleged to have ___ the country.
questions.explanation: 'Is alleged to have' needs a past participle, and 'to have "fled" the country' is the set phrase for a suspect escaping abroad. 'Stolen', 'surprised' and 'renewed' do not describe a suspect's escape.
questions.meaning: ran away quickly
questions.example: The suspect is alleged to have fled.

questions.prompt: The proposal is being carefully ___ by the committee.
questions.explanation: A committee looks at a proposal and thinks about it, and the passive 'is being carefully ___' collocates with "considered". Repaired, compromised and manipulated do not describe how a committee handles a proposal.
questions.meaning: thought about carefully
questions.example: The proposal is being considered.

questions.prompt: It is understood that negotiations are still ___, with no deal yet.
questions.explanation: 'Still … with no deal yet' shows the talks have not finished, so "ongoing" is the word that fits after 'are'. 'Concluded', 'finalised' and 'settled' would all contradict 'no deal yet'.
questions.meaning: continuing now
questions.example: Negotiations are ongoing.

questions.prompt: He had the storm-damaged roof ___.
questions.explanation: The causative 'had + object + past participle' means he arranged for someone to do it, and a storm-damaged roof needs to be "repaired". Serviced, fled and approved do not fit damage.
questions.meaning: fixed after damage
questions.example: He had the roof repaired.

questions.prompt: The findings are reported to have ___ researchers.
questions.explanation: "surprised" fits because findings can cause researchers to feel shock, and the pattern 'are reported to have + past participle' needs a verb that takes 'researchers' as its object. 'Signed', 'fled' and 'serviced' make no sense with researchers as the object.
questions.meaning: caused someone to feel surprise at something unexpected
questions.example: The findings surprised researchers.

questions.prompt: She had her application ___ by a lawyer to check it for errors.
questions.explanation: The causative 'had her application ___' needs a past participle, and a lawyer checking for errors means "reviewed". 'Renewed' would mean extending it, which is not what the clue describes.
questions.meaning: checked by an expert
questions.example: She had her application reviewed.

questions.prompt: The policy is expected to be ___ next year to reflect the new regulations.
questions.explanation: A policy is changed to make it better, so it is "revised"; "is expected to be + past participle" reports a future passive.
questions.meaning: changed to make better
questions.example: The policy will be revised next year.

questions.prompt: It is claimed that the figures were ___.
questions.explanation: "manipulated" fits because 'it is claimed that the figures were...' suggests dishonest tampering with numbers. 'Serviced', 'fled' and 'signed' do not make sense with figures.
questions.meaning: changed in a dishonest way
questions.example: The figures were manipulated.

questions.prompt: He had the engine ___ before the long trip.
questions.explanation: 'Have + object + past participle' describes arranging for someone else to do a job, and an engine checked before a long trip is "serviced". 'Reversed', 'surprised' and 'translated' do not suit an engine.
questions.meaning: checked and maintained by a mechanic
questions.example: He had the engine serviced.

questions.prompt: The event is scheduled to take ___ in June.
questions.explanation: An event that happens is said to take "place", so 'scheduled to take place in June' means it will happen then. 'Take part', 'take care' and 'take turns' describe what people do, not an event happening.
questions.meaning: to happen
questions.example: The event will take place in June.

questions.prompt: The data is believed to have been ___.
questions.explanation: Data that has been made unsafe by a breach is "compromised"; "is believed to have been + past participle" reports a past passive event.
questions.meaning: made less safe or secret
questions.example: The data was compromised.

units.title: Formal Emails & Correspondence
units.description: Professional written English — C1-level phrases for formal written communication.

questions.prompt: I am writing to ___ your attention to a recent issue.
questions.explanation: The fixed formal phrase is 'draw your attention to', meaning 'make you notice', so the answer is "draw". 'Look', 'address' and 'hesitate' do not form this collocation with 'attention'.
questions.meaning: to make someone notice or think about
questions.example: I wish to draw your attention to a problem.

questions.prompt: Please do not ___ to contact me if you need further information.
questions.explanation: The set formal phrase is 'do not hesitate to contact me', meaning 'feel free to contact me', so the answer is "hesitate". 'Treat', 'reach' and 'regret' do not fit before 'to contact'.
questions.meaning: to pause because you are unsure
questions.example: Please do not hesitate to contact me.

questions.prompt: I would be ___ if you could confirm receipt of this email.
questions.explanation: The polite formula 'I would be grateful if you could...' is the standard way to make a formal request, so the answer is "grateful". 'Sincere' describes honesty, and 'prompt' and 'to' do not fit the structure.
questions.meaning: thankful
questions.example: I would be grateful for a reply.

questions.prompt: With reference ___ our earlier conversation, I am attaching the report.
questions.explanation: The fixed formal phrase is 'with reference "to"', meaning 'about'. 'Reference' is never followed by 'of', 'on' or 'about' in this phrase.
questions.meaning: about; concerning
questions.example: With reference to our call, please find the report attached.

questions.prompt: I ___ forward to hearing from you soon.
questions.explanation: The closing phrase 'I look forward to hearing from you' uses the verb "look" with 'forward to' to show pleasant anticipation. 'Address', 'reach' and 'regret' do not form this phrase.
questions.meaning: to wait for something with pleasure
questions.example: I look forward to hearing from you.

questions.prompt: Please find ___ the requested documents.
questions.explanation: "attached" is correct because "Please find attached" is the fixed formal phrase for pointing to a file sent with an email. The other options do not combine with "find" in this way.
questions.meaning: joined to an email as a file
questions.example: Please find attached the documents.

questions.prompt: I am writing ___ behalf of the marketing department.
questions.explanation: "on" is correct because the fixed phrase is "on behalf of", meaning as the representative of a person or group. "For behalf", "to behalf" and "by behalf" do not exist.
questions.meaning: part of the phrase "on behalf of"
questions.example: I am writing on behalf of the team.

questions.prompt: Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to ___ out.
questions.explanation: "reach" is correct because "reach out" is the phrasal verb meaning to contact someone. "Draw out", "address out" and "let out" do not mean this.
questions.meaning: to make contact with someone
questions.example: Please feel free to reach out.

questions.prompt: I apologize ___ any inconvenience this may have caused.
questions.explanation: "for" is correct because the verb "apologize" takes "for" before the thing you are sorry about. "Apologize to" would need a person, such as "to you".
questions.meaning: introduces what you are sorry about
questions.example: I apologize for any inconvenience.

questions.prompt: We would like to ___ you for your continued support.
questions.explanation: "thank" is correct because "thank you for" is the standard way to express gratitude for something. The other verbs do not take "you for your support".
questions.meaning: to say you are grateful
questions.example: We would like to thank you for your support.

questions.prompt: I am ___ to inform you that your application has been successful.
questions.explanation: "pleased" is correct because "I am pleased to inform you" is the formal phrase for sharing good news, such as a successful application. "Sorry" and "afraid" introduce bad news, and "regretful" is not used in this phrase.
questions.meaning: happy to do something
questions.example: I am pleased to inform you of the result.

questions.prompt: Following ___ discussion, I have revised the proposal.
questions.explanation: "our" is correct because "following" is followed directly by a noun phrase, and "our discussion" refers to the talk both writer and reader had. "Following" does not take "to", "on" or "of" here.
questions.meaning: belonging to us
questions.example: Following our discussion, I revised the plan.

questions.prompt: Please let me know if this ___ with your schedule.
questions.explanation: "fits" is correct because the subject "this" is singular, so the present-tense verb needs the -s ending. "Fits with your schedule" means it is suitable for your plans.
questions.meaning: is suitable for
questions.example: Please tell me if this fits your schedule.

questions.prompt: I trust this email finds you ___.
questions.explanation: "well" is correct because "I trust this email finds you well" is a fixed formal greeting wishing the reader good health. The other words do not complete it.
questions.meaning: in good health
questions.example: I trust this email finds you well.

questions.prompt: We ___ to inform you that the position has been filled.
questions.explanation: "regret" is correct because "We regret to inform you" is the formal way to give disappointing news, such as a filled position. "Apologize" and "thank" are not followed by "to inform", and "sorry" would need "are" before it.
questions.meaning: to feel sorry about something
questions.example: We regret to inform you that the post has been filled.

questions.prompt: Kindly ___ me know your availability for next week.
questions.explanation: "let" is correct because "let me know" is the fixed pattern for asking someone to tell you something, and "kindly" makes it polite. "Make", "have" and "get" do not form this phrase.
questions.meaning: to tell me
questions.example: Kindly let me know your availability.

questions.prompt: I am writing to ___ up on my previous email.
questions.explanation: "follow" is correct because "follow up on" means to take further action on an earlier matter, here a previous email. "Draw up" means to prepare a document, and "take up" and "address" do not have this meaning.
questions.meaning: to ask again about an earlier matter
questions.example: I am writing to follow up on my email.

questions.prompt: Please ___ this matter as a priority.
questions.explanation: "treat" is correct because "treat something as a priority" is the set phrase for dealing with a matter urgently. "Deal" would need "with", and "look" and "think" do not take an object followed by "as".
questions.meaning: to handle in a certain way
questions.example: Please treat this matter as a priority.

questions.prompt: I would appreciate it if you could ___ this at your earliest convenience.
questions.explanation: "address" is right because 'address a matter' means to deal with it, the formal verb used with 'at your earliest convenience'. 'Draw', 'reach' and 'regret' do not take 'this' as a thing to be dealt with.
questions.meaning: to deal with a problem
questions.example: Please address this at your earliest convenience.

questions.prompt: We are ___ forward to a successful collaboration.
questions.explanation: "looking" is correct because after "We are" the continuous form needs the -ing verb, giving the fixed phrase "be looking forward to". "Look", "looked" and "to look" cannot follow "are" here.
questions.meaning: to wait for something with pleasure
questions.example: We are looking forward to working together.

questions.prompt: Please accept our ___ apologies for the delay.
questions.explanation: "sincere" is right because 'sincere apologies' is the standard collocation for a heartfelt formal apology. 'Grateful' describes a person's feeling and does not describe apologies.
questions.meaning: honest and heartfelt
questions.example: Please accept our sincere apologies.

questions.prompt: I am ___ that you found the presentation useful.
questions.explanation: "glad" is right because 'glad that' expresses pleasure at news that has already happened. 'Eager' looks forward to something in the future, and 'prompt' and 'sincere' do not describe a feeling about news.
questions.meaning: pleased
questions.example: I am glad you found it useful.

questions.prompt: Should circumstances ___, please inform us immediately.
questions.explanation: "change" is right because 'Should circumstances change' is an inverted conditional meaning 'If circumstances change', which needs a bare verb after the subject. The other words are not verbs.
questions.meaning: to become different
questions.example: Should circumstances change, please let us know.

questions.prompt: We remain at your ___ should you require further assistance.
questions.explanation: "disposal" is right because 'at your disposal' is the fixed formal phrase for 'available to help you'. 'At your convenience', 'at your request' and 'at your discretion' are real phrases but mean something else.
questions.meaning: the power to use something as you wish
questions.example: We remain at your disposal.

questions.prompt: I look forward to your ___ response.
questions.explanation: "prompt" is right because 'a prompt response' means a quick reply, the usual formal wish after 'I look forward to your'. 'Grateful' and 'sincere' do not describe the speed of a reply.
questions.meaning: done quickly
questions.example: I look forward to your prompt reply.

units.title: Nominalisation
units.description: Turning verbs into abstract nouns — C1-level nominalisation, common in academic and formal writing.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to decide" is…
questions.explanation: to decide → decision. C1-level nominalisation, common in academic and formal writing.
questions.meaning: a choice made after thought
questions.example: The committee reached a decision.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to argue" is… ___
questions.explanation: to argue → argument. C1-level nominalisation, common in academic and formal writing.
questions.meaning: a reason put forward against or for something
questions.example: Her main argument was that the plan cost too much.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to analyze" is…
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in "-yse" form their noun with "-ysis", so "to analyze" becomes "analysis".
questions.meaning: a careful study of something in parts
questions.example: The analysis took weeks.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to conclude" is… ___
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in "-clude" drop "-de" and add "-sion", so "to conclude" becomes "conclusion".
questions.meaning: a final decision reached after thought
questions.example: We reached a clear conclusion.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to assume" is…
questions.explanation: "Assume" drops its final "e" and takes "-ption", giving the noun "assumption", just as consume becomes consumption.
questions.meaning: something you accept as true without proof
questions.example: It was a false assumption.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to describe" is… ___
questions.explanation: to describe → description. C1-level nominalisation, common in academic and formal writing.
questions.meaning: words that say what something is like
questions.example: Give a full description of the thief.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to explain" is…
questions.explanation: The noun from "explain" is "explanation": the stem changes to "explan-" and loses the "i", so "explaination" is a common misspelling.
questions.meaning: words that make something clear
questions.example: Her explanation was easy to follow.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to suggest" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Suggest" takes the suffix -ion to form the noun "suggestion", as in "make a suggestion".
questions.meaning: an idea you offer to others
questions.example: He made a helpful suggestion.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to develop" is…
questions.explanation: "To develop" forms its noun with the suffix "-ment", giving "development".
questions.meaning: growth or a new step forward
questions.example: There was a major development in the case.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to require" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Require" takes the suffix -ment to form the noun "requirement", meaning something that is needed.
questions.meaning: something that is needed
questions.example: Fitness is a requirement for the job.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to fail" is… ___
questions.explanation: The verb "to fail" becomes the noun "failure" by adding -ure, a form common in formal and academic writing.
questions.meaning: a lack of success
questions.example: The plan ended in failure.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to succeed" is…
questions.explanation: The noun from "succeed" (to achieve a goal) is the irregular form "success", with no -ment or -ance suffix.
questions.meaning: something that does well or achieves its aim
questions.example: The film was a huge success.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to propose" is… ___
questions.explanation: "To propose" drops the final "e" and adds "-al", giving "proposal" for a plan put forward.
questions.meaning: a plan offered for others to consider
questions.example: Our proposal was accepted.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to reduce" is…
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in "-duce" change to "-duction", so "to reduce" becomes "reduction".
questions.meaning: a fall in amount or size
questions.example: There was a big reduction in cost.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to improve" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Improve" takes the suffix -ment to form the noun "improvement", as in "an improvement in sales".
questions.meaning: a change that makes something better
questions.example: We saw an improvement in sales.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to discover" is…
questions.explanation: "To discover" simply adds "-y" to form its noun, giving "discovery".
questions.meaning: finding something new, or the thing found
questions.example: The discovery changed medicine.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to expand" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Expand" drops -d and takes -sion, giving "expansion", like extend → extension; there is no -ment or -ation form.
questions.meaning: growth in size or range
questions.example: The firm planned its expansion abroad.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to achieve" is…
questions.explanation: "Achieve" forms its noun with -ment, giving "achievement", like improve → improvement.
questions.meaning: something done well with effort
questions.example: Graduating was a great achievement.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to establish" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Establish" takes the suffix -ment to form the noun "establishment", as in "the establishment of a new school".
questions.meaning: the act of founding something
questions.example: The establishment of the school took years.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to interpret" is…
questions.explanation: "Interpret" adds -ation, not just -ion, giving "interpretation", like present → presentation.
questions.meaning: an explanation of what something means
questions.example: Each critic offered a different interpretation.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to justify" is…
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in -ify change to -ification, so "justify" becomes "justification", like clarify → clarification.
questions.meaning: a good reason for an action
questions.example: She could offer no justification.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to maintain" is… ___
questions.explanation: The noun of "maintain" is "maintenance": the -ai- of the verb changes to -e- and it takes -ance, so "maintainance" is a common misspelling.
questions.meaning: work to keep something in good condition
questions.example: The road needs regular maintenance.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to produce" is…
questions.explanation: "Produce" drops the final -e and adds -tion to form the noun "production".
questions.meaning: the process of making goods
questions.example: Production rose last year.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to recognize" is… ___
questions.explanation: "Recognize" drops -ise and takes -ition, giving "recognition", like compete → competition.
questions.meaning: praise or respect for what someone has done
questions.example: She won recognition for her work.

questions.prompt: The noun form of "to resolve" is…
questions.explanation: "Resolve" changes -ve to -u- and adds -tion, giving "resolution", like solve → solution.
questions.meaning: a solution to a problem
questions.example: We found a resolution to the dispute.

units.title: Cleft Sentences
units.description: Emphasis through structure — C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.

questions.prompt: ___ was John who broke the vase, not me.
questions.explanation: "it" is right because a cleft sentence for emphasis opens with dummy 'it' plus 'was', as in 'It was John who...'. The other words cannot start the sentence this way.
questions.meaning: a word that puts focus on one part
questions.example: It was John who broke the vase.

questions.prompt: What I really need ___ a good night's sleep.
questions.explanation: "is" is right because in a wh-cleft the clause 'What I really need' is a singular subject, so it takes 'is' to link it to 'a good night's sleep'. 'Am' does not agree with that subject.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What I really need is sleep.

questions.prompt: It was the manager ___ made the final decision.
questions.explanation: "who" is right because in 'It was the manager ___ made the final decision' the blank is the subject of 'made' and refers to a person. 'Whom' is only for objects, so it cannot replace the subject here.
questions.meaning: links a person to a clause
questions.example: It was the manager who decided.

questions.prompt: What surprised me most ___ his honesty.
questions.explanation: "was" is right because the cleft 'What surprised me most' is in the past, so it links to 'his honesty' with 'was'. 'That' and 'who' cannot serve as the main verb.
questions.meaning: a past form of be linking two parts
questions.example: What surprised me most was his honesty.

questions.prompt: It was ___ in 1990 that the company was founded, but in 1992.
questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence, "not" can sit after "It was" to deny the stated time and put the focus on it. 'It was not in 1990 that the company was founded' means the founding happened at some other time.
questions.meaning: a word that makes a sentence negative
questions.example: It was not in 1990 that the company was founded.

questions.prompt: What we need to do ___ act quickly.
questions.explanation: "is" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What we need to do is act quickly.

questions.prompt: It was because of the delay ___ we missed the flight.
questions.explanation: In an 'It was ... that' cleft, the focused phrase 'because of the delay' is always followed by "that", never 'which', 'what' or 'why', before the rest of the sentence 'we missed the flight'.
questions.meaning: introduces the rest after the focused part
questions.example: It was because of the delay that we missed it.

questions.prompt: What annoys me most ___ people who are always late.
questions.explanation: The clause 'What annoys me most' is a singular subject in the present tense ('annoys'), so it is linked to 'people who are always late' with "is".
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What annoys me most is lateness.

questions.prompt: It ___ the weather that ruined our plans.
questions.explanation: The event 'ruined our plans' is in the past and 'It' is singular, so the cleft opens with "was".
questions.meaning: a past form of be for focus
questions.example: It was the weather that ruined our plans.

questions.prompt: What she wants ___ a bit of peace and quiet.
questions.explanation: "is" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What she wants is peace and quiet.

questions.prompt: It was only ___ that I realized my mistake.
questions.explanation: 'It was only ___ that I realised' needs a time word as the focus, and "later" fits the sense 'only after some time did I realise'.
questions.meaning: at a time after something
questions.example: It was only later that I realized.

questions.prompt: What matters most to me ___ my family's happiness.
questions.explanation: In a "What ..." cleft the verb be links the opening clause to the focus, and with the present 'matters' it is "is", before 'my family's happiness'.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What matters most is my family.

questions.prompt: It was the teacher ___ noticed the problem first.
questions.explanation: The focus, "the teacher", is a person and the subject of "noticed", so we use "who"; "which" and "what" are not used for people, and "whom" cannot be a subject.
questions.meaning: links a person to a clause
questions.example: It was the teacher who noticed it.

questions.prompt: What I admire about her ___ her determination.
questions.explanation: "is" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What I admire about her is her determination.

questions.prompt: It was ___ during the meeting that he resigned, but the day after.
questions.explanation: The clue 'but the day after' shows the meeting was the wrong time, so the cleft must deny it with "not": 'It was not during the meeting that he resigned'.
questions.meaning: a word that makes a sentence negative
questions.example: It was not during the meeting that he resigned.

questions.prompt: What we found strange ___ his sudden silence.
questions.explanation: 'What we found strange' is a singular subject and 'found' is past, so the linking verb before 'his sudden silence' is "was".
questions.meaning: a sentence pattern that stresses one thing
questions.example: What we found strange was his silence.

questions.prompt: It was the noise ___ woke everyone up.
questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence the focused thing ("the noise") is followed by a relative clause, and for a non-person we use "that"; "who" is only for people.
questions.meaning: links a thing to a clause
questions.example: It was the noise that woke everyone.

questions.prompt: What she really meant ___ something quite different.
questions.explanation: "was" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a past form of be linking two parts
questions.example: What she really meant was something different.

questions.prompt: It was not until later ___ we understood the plan.
questions.explanation: The pattern 'It was not until + time + that + clause' needs "that" to introduce the clause after 'later'.
questions.meaning: links a time to a clause
questions.example: It was not until later that we understood.

questions.prompt: What impressed the judges most ___ his confidence.
questions.explanation: 'What impressed the judges most' is a wh-clause subject, and a past event is linked to the focus with "was".
questions.meaning: a past form of be linking two parts
questions.example: What impressed the judges most was his confidence.

questions.prompt: It ___ the traffic, not the weather, that delayed us.
questions.explanation: "was" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a past form of be for focus
questions.example: It was the traffic that delayed us.

questions.prompt: What I regret most ___ not speaking up sooner.
questions.explanation: The wh-clause 'What I regret most' counts as a singular subject, so it takes "is"; 'are' and 'am' do not agree with it, and the bare form 'be' cannot be the main verb.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What I regret most is not speaking up.

questions.prompt: It was her ___ who suggested the idea first.
questions.explanation: "colleague" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cleft sentence structures for emphasis.
questions.meaning: a person you work with
questions.example: It was her colleague who suggested it.

questions.prompt: What worries me ___ the lack of preparation.
questions.explanation: 'What worries me' is a singular wh-clause subject, so it takes "is"; 'are' needs a plural subject, 'am' needs 'I', and 'being' is not a finite verb.
questions.meaning: a form of be that links two parts
questions.example: What worries me is the lack of preparation.

questions.prompt: It ___ the noise that kept me awake last night.
questions.explanation: The sentence needs a verb that agrees with 'It', and "was" does; 'am' goes only with 'I', and 'that' and 'not' leave the sentence without a verb.
questions.meaning: a past form of be linking two parts
questions.example: It was the noise that kept me awake last night.

units.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have
units.description: Fixed verb-noun pairs — C1-level fixed collocations with common light verbs.

lessons.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have 1
lessons.subtitle: Fixed verb-noun pairs

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"…
questions.explanation: "a decision" goes with make (make a decision), while we say take action, have a shower and do homework.
questions.meaning: a choice reached after thinking
questions.example: I must make a decision today.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"… ___
