questions.explanation: With make we use "an effort" (make an effort = try hard); we do someone a favour, have a shower and have a conversation.
questions.meaning: hard work to do something
questions.example: She made an effort to smile.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"…
questions.explanation: We say "a mistake" after "make"; research and damage go with "do", and a risk goes with "take".
questions.meaning: something you did that was wrong
questions.example: Anyone can make a mistake.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"… ___
questions.explanation: We say make "progress" for moving forward towards a goal; we take a risk, have a shower and have or take a look.
questions.meaning: forward movement towards a goal
questions.example: You are making progress.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"…
questions.explanation: We say make "a difference" when something changes a situation; we take or have a look, take a risk and take or have a nap.
questions.meaning: a change for the better
questions.example: Your help made a difference.

lessons.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have 2
lessons.subtitle: Fixed verb-noun pairs

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"… ___
questions.explanation: We say do "homework" for schoolwork done at home; we take action, make a difference and take advantage.
questions.meaning: schoolwork done at home
questions.example: Do your homework before dinner.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"…
questions.explanation: We say do "business" for buying and selling; we take notice, make a decision and make a mistake.
questions.meaning: buying and selling goods
questions.example: We do business with many countries.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"… ___
questions.explanation: We say do "damage" when something causes harm; we take a break, make a mistake and make arrangements.
questions.meaning: harm that spoils something
questions.example: The storm did damage to the roof.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"…
questions.explanation: We say do "research" for careful study to find facts; we take a break, make a decision and make progress.
questions.meaning: a careful study to find facts
questions.example: They do research on diseases.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"… ___
questions.explanation: We say do someone "a favour" for a kind act; we make a decision, take a look and make an effort.
questions.meaning: a kind act you do for someone
questions.example: Could you do me a favour?

lessons.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have 3
lessons.subtitle: Fixed verb-noun pairs

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"… ___
questions.explanation: We say take "responsibility" when we accept a duty or the blame; we do harm, make a mistake and make progress.
questions.meaning: to accept that something is your duty
questions.example: Take responsibility for your actions.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"…
questions.explanation: With "take" the fixed phrase is "a risk" (take a risk), meaning do something that might go wrong. We make a mistake, do harm and have an argument.
questions.meaning: a chance of loss or danger
questions.example: It's worth taking a risk.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"… ___
questions.explanation: take → advantage. C1-level fixed collocations with common light verbs.
questions.meaning: to use a chance well
questions.example: Take advantage of the offer.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"…
questions.explanation: With "take" the fixed phrase is "notice" (take notice), meaning pay attention. We do a favour, make a mistake and have an impact.
questions.meaning: attention paid to something
questions.example: Take no notice of him.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"… ___
questions.explanation: With "take" the fixed phrase is "a break" (take a break), meaning have a short rest. We do harm, make a mistake and have an argument.
questions.meaning: a short rest
questions.example: Let's take a break.

lessons.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have 4
lessons.subtitle: Fixed verb-noun pairs

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"…
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "an argument" (have an argument), meaning quarrel. We make a difference, take a risk and make a mistake.
questions.meaning: a quarrel with someone
questions.example: They had an argument last night.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"… ___
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "a conversation" (have a conversation), meaning talk with someone. We make an effort, make a mistake and make progress.
questions.meaning: a talk with someone
questions.example: We had a long conversation.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"…
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "an impact" (have an impact on something), meaning have an effect. We take action, make a mistake and do harm.
questions.meaning: an effect on something
questions.example: The law will have an impact.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"… ___
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "a look" (have a look), meaning look at something quickly. We make an effort, take a risk and make a decision.
questions.meaning: a short act of looking at something
questions.example: Have a look at this.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"…
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "a chance" (have a chance), meaning have an opportunity. We make a decision, do damage and make an effort.
questions.meaning: an opportunity to do something
questions.example: You have a chance to win.

lessons.title: Collocations with Make, Do, Take & Have 5
lessons.subtitle: Fixed verb-noun pairs

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"…
questions.explanation: With "make" the fixed phrase is "an impression" (make an impression), meaning make people notice and remember you. We have a conversation, do homework and do business.
questions.meaning: a first feeling about a person
questions.example: She hoped to make an impression.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "do"… ___
questions.explanation: With "do" the fixed phrase is "harm" (do harm), meaning cause damage. We make a decision, have a chance and take advantage.
questions.meaning: damage or pain
questions.example: Smoking can do serious harm to your health.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "take"…
questions.explanation: With "take" the fixed phrase is "action" (take action), meaning do something to deal with a problem. We make an effort, do homework and do research.
questions.meaning: steps taken to deal with something
questions.example: We must take action now.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "have"… ___
questions.explanation: With "have" the fixed phrase is "doubts" (have doubts), meaning feel unsure. We take action, make a mistake and do harm.
questions.meaning: feelings of not being sure
questions.example: I have doubts about the plan.

questions.prompt: Complete the collocation with "make"…
questions.explanation: We say make "arrangements" when we plan something in advance. The other options go with different verbs: do research, do homework, take a look.
questions.meaning: plans made in advance
questions.example: She made arrangements for the trip.

units.title: Euphemisms & Indirect Language
units.description: Softening sensitive topics: polite, indirect ways to say difficult things, such as "passed away" for "died".

questions.prompt: The phrase "to pass away" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "To pass away" is a gentle, polite way of saying "to die", used to soften news of a death.
questions.meaning: to die
questions.example: Sadly, he is about to pass away.

questions.prompt: The phrase "to let someone go" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: Employers say "to let someone go" to avoid the blunt word, so it means "to fire someone".
questions.meaning: to fire someone
questions.example: The firm had to let someone go.

questions.prompt: The phrase "between jobs" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "Between jobs" suggests a short pause before the next job instead of saying someone has no work, so it means "unemployed".
questions.meaning: unemployed
questions.example: She is between jobs at the moment.

questions.prompt: The phrase "economical with the truth" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: "Economical with the truth" suggests someone gives out as little truth as possible, a soft way of calling them "dishonest".
questions.meaning: not telling the whole truth
questions.example: The minister was economical with the truth.

questions.prompt: The phrase "pre-owned" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: Sellers say "pre-owned" because it sounds better than "second-hand", which means someone else owned it before.
questions.meaning: second-hand
questions.example: We bought a pre-owned car.

questions.prompt: The phrase "downsize" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: Companies say "downsize" to soften the news of job cuts, so it means "reduce staff numbers".
questions.meaning: to reduce staff numbers
questions.example: The firm plans to downsize.

questions.prompt: The phrase "in a delicate condition" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "In a delicate condition" is an old-fashioned, discreet way to say a woman is "pregnant".
questions.meaning: pregnant, in old-fashioned polite language
questions.example: She was in a delicate condition.

questions.prompt: The phrase "senior moment" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: senior moment → forgetfulness. C1-level euphemisms for sensitive or blunt topics.
questions.meaning: a short lapse of memory, often joked about
questions.example: Sorry, I had a senior moment and forgot your name.

questions.prompt: The phrase "differently abled" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "Differently abled" was coined to soften "disabled", but many disabled people now find it dated or patronising.
questions.meaning: a euphemism for disabled, often seen as patronising
questions.example: He is differently abled.

questions.prompt: The phrase "economically disadvantaged" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: "Economically disadvantaged" describes a lack of money in formal terms to avoid the blunt word "poor".
questions.meaning: poor
questions.example: The fund helps economically disadvantaged families.

questions.prompt: The phrase "correctional facility" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: A "correctional facility" is where people are held to 'correct' their behavior after a crime, so it is an official, softer name for "prison".
questions.meaning: prison
questions.example: He was sent to a correctional facility.

questions.prompt: The phrase "collateral damage" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "Collateral damage" is a military euphemism for people or property hurt by accident during an attack, so it means "unintended harm".
questions.meaning: harm accidentally caused to civilians or bystanders
questions.example: Officials called the civilian deaths collateral damage.

questions.prompt: The phrase "letting you go" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: A manager says "letting you go" to soften the news that your job is ending, so it means "firing you".
questions.meaning: firing you
questions.example: I'm sorry, we are letting you go.

questions.prompt: The phrase "put to sleep" (about a pet) is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: When people say a pet was "put to sleep", they mean it was killed painlessly, so it softens "euthanised".
questions.meaning: killed painlessly; euthanised
questions.example: The old dog was put to sleep.

questions.prompt: The phrase "vertically challenged" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: "Vertically challenged" is a jokey, mock-polite way of saying "short"; it plays on politically correct phrases such as "visually impaired".
questions.meaning: short
questions.example: He is vertically challenged.

questions.prompt: The phrase "a bit under the weather" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "A bit under the weather" is a gentle, informal way to say you are "slightly ill", for example with a cold, without giving details.
questions.meaning: slightly ill
questions.example: I'm a bit under the weather.

questions.prompt: The phrase "of a certain age" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: "Of a certain age" avoids stating someone's age directly and politely means "older", usually middle-aged or beyond.
questions.meaning: older
questions.example: A woman of a certain age waved.

questions.prompt: The phrase "enhanced interrogation" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "Enhanced interrogation" is an official-sounding term that critics say hides the harsh physical methods it describes, which are "torture".
questions.meaning: a euphemism for torture
questions.example: Officials called it enhanced interrogation; critics called it torture.

questions.prompt: The phrase "negative growth" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: "Negative growth" is business jargon that avoids saying a company or economy is shrinking, so it is a polite way of saying "decline".
questions.meaning: decline
questions.example: The firm reported negative growth.

questions.prompt: The phrase "downsized position" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: downsized position → job cut. C1-level euphemisms for sensitive or blunt topics.
questions.meaning: job cut
questions.example: His downsized position was removed.

questions.prompt: The phrase "substance abuse" is a polite way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: "Substance abuse" is the clinical, softer term used instead of naming the problem directly, so it means "drug addiction".
questions.meaning: harmful use of drugs or alcohol
questions.example: He is being treated for substance abuse.

questions.prompt: The phrase "in between opportunities" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: Saying someone is "in between opportunities" makes unemployment sound temporary and positive, so it means "currently without a job".
questions.meaning: currently without a job
questions.example: She is in between opportunities.

questions.prompt: The phrase "not the sharpest tool in the shed" is a humorous, indirect way of saying… ___
questions.explanation: A "sharp" mind is a quick one, so saying someone is not the sharpest tool is an indirect way of calling them "not very intelligent".
questions.term: not the sharpest tool in the shed
questions.meaning: not very intelligent
questions.example: He's not the sharpest tool in the shed.

questions.prompt: The phrase "letting nature take its course" is a polite way of saying…
questions.explanation: Doctors and families say they are "letting nature take its course" when they decide not to treat an illness any further, so it means "not intervening medically".
questions.meaning: choosing not to treat an illness
questions.example: The family agreed on letting nature take its course.

questions.prompt: Calling someone "economical" is a polite way of saying they are… ___
questions.explanation: "Economical" puts a positive spin on not liking to spend money, so it is a polite way of calling someone "cheap or stingy".
questions.meaning: careful with money; can politely mean stingy
questions.example: He's rather economical with money; he never buys a round.

units.title: Contrast & Concession
units.description: Advanced linking of opposing ideas — C1-level connectors for contrast and concession.

questions.prompt: ___ the heavy rain, the match went ahead as planned.
questions.explanation: "despite" is a preposition meaning 'in spite of' and takes a noun phrase ('the heavy rain'); the other options are linking adverbs that can't open the sentence this way.
questions.meaning: in spite of
questions.example: Despite the rain, the match went ahead.

questions.prompt: The plan succeeded, ___ several early setbacks.
questions.explanation: "notwithstanding" is a formal preposition meaning 'in spite of', so it can come directly before the noun phrase "several early setbacks"; "nevertheless" and "however" are adverbs that need a clause, and "on the contrary" does not express concession.
questions.meaning: in spite of; used in formal writing
questions.example: It worked, notwithstanding several setbacks.

questions.prompt: ___ he was exhausted, he kept working.
questions.explanation: "although" is a conjunction that introduces a full clause ('he was exhausted') expressing concession; 'despite' needs a noun and 'yet'/'however' cannot start a subordinate clause.
questions.meaning: even though
questions.example: Although he was tired, he kept working.

questions.prompt: The project failed ___ the team's best efforts.
questions.explanation: "in spite of" introduces a contrast and is followed by a noun phrase ("the team's best efforts"), so it links the failure to the effort. "in any case" and "on the other hand" cannot take a noun phrase here, and "in case of" has the wrong meaning.
questions.meaning: despite
questions.example: The project failed in spite of our efforts.

questions.prompt: He accepted the offer, ___ his initial doubts.
questions.explanation: "regardless of" is followed by a noun phrase ("his initial doubts") and means 'without being affected by'. "still" and "nevertheless" are adverbs that cannot introduce a noun phrase, and "regardless" on its own cannot take "his initial doubts" without "of".
questions.meaning: without being affected by
questions.example: He accepted the offer regardless of his doubts.

questions.prompt: The company thrived, ___ competitors struggled badly.
questions.explanation: "whereas" joins two clauses that contrast with each other (the company thrived, competitors struggled). "in spite of" needs a noun phrase, and "on the contrary" and "in any case" do not link the clauses like this.
questions.meaning: used to compare two contrasting facts
questions.example: The firm thrived whereas rivals struggled.

questions.prompt: He stayed calm ___ his colleagues panicked.
questions.explanation: "while" joins two clauses and shows two things happening at the same time in contrast (he stayed calm, they panicked). "nevertheless" and "even so" are adverbs that cannot join clauses without punctuation, and "despite" cannot be followed by a full clause.
questions.meaning: whereas; used to contrast two facts
questions.example: Some people love city life, while others prefer the countryside.

questions.prompt: The results were disappointing; ___, the team kept trying.
questions.explanation: "however" is a linking adverb used after a semicolon and followed by a comma, introducing the contrast (disappointing results, yet they kept trying). "while" and "although" are conjunctions that do not follow a semicolon like this, and "despite" needs a noun phrase.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast
questions.example: The results were poor; however, the team kept trying.

questions.prompt: The setbacks were serious; ___, morale remained high.
questions.explanation: "nevertheless" is a linking adverb that works after a semicolon and before a comma, showing morale stayed high in spite of the setbacks; "despite" needs a noun phrase, and "although" and "even though" are conjunctions that cannot sit between a semicolon and a comma like this.
questions.meaning: in spite of that
questions.example: The setbacks were serious; nevertheless, morale stayed high.

questions.prompt: The plan had flaws; it worked out well ___.
questions.explanation: "nonetheless" is an adverb that can end a clause and means 'in spite of that': the plan had flaws but worked. 'In spite of' needs a noun after it, and 'although' and 'whereas' must introduce a clause.
questions.meaning: in spite of what was said
questions.example: The plan had flaws; it worked nonetheless.

questions.prompt: Sales were falling, ___ the company kept hiring.
questions.explanation: "yet" is a conjunction, so it can join two full clauses after a comma and add a surprising contrast: hiring while sales fall. "Even so" and "however" would need a semicolon or a new sentence, and "despite" needs a noun.
questions.meaning: but; used to add a surprising contrast
questions.example: Sales fell, yet the company kept hiring.

questions.prompt: The risks were high; he took the job ___.
questions.explanation: "even so" means 'in spite of that' and can stand alone at the end of the clause: the risks were high, but he took the job anyway. "Despite" needs a noun, and "although" and "yet" must introduce a clause.
questions.meaning: in spite of that
questions.example: It was risky; he took the job even so.

questions.prompt: It was a difficult year; ___, profits rose.
questions.explanation: "that said" comes at the start of a clause and adds a contrast to what was just said: the year was hard, but profits still rose. "Contrary to", "regardless of" and "despite" all need a noun after them.
questions.meaning: used to add a contrast to a claim
questions.example: It was hard; that said, profits rose.

questions.prompt: He is, ___ talented, still very inexperienced.
questions.explanation: "albeit" means 'although' and can be followed by just an adjective, so "albeit talented" means 'although talented'. 'Despite' needs a noun or -ing form, and 'nevertheless' and 'all the same' cannot introduce a shortened concession like this.
questions.meaning: although; adds a limiting word or phrase
questions.example: The trip was a success, albeit a short one.

questions.prompt: ___ the results are disappointing, we should continue.
questions.explanation: "granted that" introduces a full clause that admits a point (the results are disappointing) before the main clause. "be that as it may" and "nevertheless" stand alone rather than introducing a clause, and "in spite of" needs a noun phrase.
questions.meaning: admitting that something may be true
questions.example: Granted that it's disappointing, we should continue.

questions.prompt: The evidence is weak; ___, it may still be true.
questions.explanation: "be that as it may" accepts the point just made (the evidence is weak) and then disagrees with it, and it works at the start of a clause. "Despite" and "contrary to" need a noun, and "granted that" needs a clause.
questions.meaning: used to accept a point but still disagree
questions.example: Be that as it may, we should go on.

questions.prompt: He was tired; he finished the race ___.
questions.explanation: "all the same" means 'in spite of that' and sits naturally at the end of the clause: he was tired but finished anyway. "Despite" needs a noun, and "still" does not work at the end here.
questions.meaning: in spite of that
questions.example: He was tired; he finished the race all the same.

questions.prompt: The rules are strict; ___, exceptions are sometimes made.
questions.explanation: "on the other hand" introduces a contrasting point: the rules are strict, but exceptions are sometimes made.
questions.meaning: used to give an opposing point
questions.example: The apartment is quite small; on the other hand, it's very cheap.

questions.prompt: Critics say it failed, but it didn't; ___, it was a huge success.
questions.explanation: "on the contrary" rejects a statement and says the opposite is true: it didn't fail, it was in fact a huge success. "In any case" does not reverse a claim, "whereas" joins two clauses, and "in spite of" needs a noun.
questions.meaning: used to say the opposite is true
questions.example: Business isn't slowing down. On the contrary, sales are up 20%.

questions.prompt: He apologized; ___, the damage had already been done.
questions.explanation: "for all that" means 'in spite of that': he apologized, but the apology could not undo the damage. "In spite of" needs a noun, and "in addition" and "as a result" do not express contrast.
questions.meaning: in spite of that
questions.example: For all that, the damage was done.

questions.prompt: The odds were against them; they pressed on ___.
questions.explanation: "still" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level connectors for contrast and concession.
questions.meaning: even so; used to add a contrast
questions.example: It was pouring with rain. Still, they pressed on.

questions.prompt: The forecast was poor; ___, they went ahead with the trip.
questions.explanation: "in any case" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level connectors for contrast and concession.
questions.meaning: anyway; whatever the situation
questions.example: It might rain, but we're going in any case.

questions.prompt: ___ appearances, the company was struggling.
questions.explanation: "contrary to" + noun means 'against what seems true', so "contrary to appearances" says the company looked fine but was really struggling. "Owing to" and "in view of" give a cause, and "nevertheless" cannot take a noun.
questions.meaning: opposite to what is believed or expected
questions.example: Contrary to appearances, the firm was struggling.

questions.prompt: ___ popular belief, the theory has been disproven.
questions.explanation: "contrary to what most think" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level connectors for contrast and concession.
questions.meaning: against what most people think
questions.example: Contrary to what most think, bats are not actually blind.

questions.prompt: Experts warned against it; they proceeded with the plan ___.
questions.explanation: The experts warned against the plan, but they went ahead anyway. "regardless" at the end of the clause means 'without paying attention to the warning', which fits this contrast.
questions.meaning: despite problems or what others say
questions.example: They were told it was risky, but they went ahead regardless.

units.title: Academic Cohesion
units.description: Linking ideas across a text — C1-level cohesive devices for academic writing.

questions.prompt: ___ mentioned earlier, the results support the hypothesis.
questions.explanation: "as" begins the fixed phrase "As mentioned earlier", which points back to something already said; "like mentioned earlier" is an informal error and is not acceptable in academic writing.
questions.meaning: in the way that
questions.example: As mentioned earlier, the results support it.

questions.prompt: Having discussed cost, the ___ point to consider is the sample size.
questions.explanation: Cost has already been discussed, so the sample size is the point that comes after it: "next" points forward, while the other words point back.
questions.meaning: coming straight after this one
questions.example: The next point to consider is the sample size.

questions.prompt: Having established this, we can now ___ to the next issue (move our attention).
questions.explanation: "turn" is correct because "turn to" is the set phrase for moving on to a new topic; "address" takes a direct object ("address the next issue"), so it cannot be followed by "to".
questions.meaning: to move your attention to something new
questions.example: We can now turn to the next issue.

questions.prompt: This ___ raises further questions about the methodology.
questions.explanation: "finding" is correct because "This" needs a singular noun, and "raises" agrees with it; "findings" would need "These", and "found" and "finds" are verb forms.
questions.meaning: a result that people discover
questions.example: This finding raises further questions.

questions.prompt: Building ___ this idea, the next chapter examines causation.
questions.explanation: "on" is correct because "build on" is the phrasal verb meaning to develop something already stated, so "Building on this idea" links to the next chapter.
questions.meaning: a word used to add to an idea
questions.example: Building on this idea, the next chapter examines causes.

questions.prompt: The ___ section will explore alternative explanations.
questions.explanation: "following" is correct because "the following section" is the standard way to point to the part that comes straight after.
questions.meaning: coming straight after
questions.example: The following section explores alternatives.

questions.prompt: In ___ of the above, further research is needed.
questions.explanation: "light" is correct because "in light of" is a fixed phrase meaning 'considering', which explains why further research is needed.
questions.meaning: taking something into account
questions.example: In light of the above, more research is needed.

questions.prompt: To ___ up, the study has several key limitations.
questions.explanation: "sum" is correct because "to sum up" is the fixed phrase used to introduce a concluding summary.
questions.meaning: to give the main points at the end
questions.example: To sum up, the study has limits.

questions.prompt: This leads us ___ to the question of validity.
questions.explanation: "onward" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cohesive devices for academic writing.
questions.meaning: forward in a text or process
questions.example: From this point onward, the discussion focuses on validity.

questions.prompt: The study mentioned ___ supports this conclusion.
questions.explanation: "Mentioned above" means 'written earlier in this text', so "above" refers back to a study the reader has already seen.
questions.meaning: written earlier in the text
questions.example: The study mentioned above supports this conclusion.

questions.prompt: Broadly ___, the findings align with prior research.
questions.explanation: "speaking" is correct because "broadly speaking" is a fixed phrase meaning 'in general', which fits a general comparison with prior research.
questions.meaning: in a general way
questions.example: Broadly speaking, the findings match prior research.

questions.prompt: This ___ ties in with the earlier discussion of ethics.
questions.explanation: "point" is correct because "This" needs a singular noun that "ties in" agrees with; "points" would need "These", and "pointing" and "pointed" are verb forms.
questions.meaning: an idea or argument in a discussion
questions.example: This point ties in with the earlier discussion.

questions.prompt: The argument outlined above rests upon ___ core assumptions.
questions.explanation: "three" fits here. Rule to remember: C1-level cohesive devices for academic writing.
questions.meaning: the number 3
questions.example: The argument rests upon three core assumptions.

questions.prompt: Taking this ___ account, the results seem reliable.
questions.explanation: "into" is correct because the idiom is "take something into account", meaning to consider it; the other prepositions do not form this phrase.
questions.meaning: links a fact to a result
questions.example: Taking this into account, the results seem reliable.

questions.prompt: The following ___ of the report, headed 'Discussion', builds on the previous analysis.
questions.explanation: "section" is the part of a report that has a heading such as 'Discussion', and "The following section" is a standard academic signpost to the next part of the text.
questions.meaning: a part of a longer text
questions.example: The following section builds on the analysis.

questions.prompt: This brings us ___ to the central argument (we return to it).
questions.explanation: "back" completes the phrase "brings us back to", which is used to return to an earlier point such as the central argument; the clue (we return to it) rules out the other particles.
questions.meaning: to return a discussion to an earlier point
questions.example: This brings us back to the central argument.

questions.prompt: The data ___ referred to can be found in the appendix.
questions.explanation: "previously" is correct because an adverb is needed to describe the verb "referred to"; "previous", "prior" and "preceding" are adjectives, so they cannot modify a verb here.
questions.meaning: earlier, for example earlier in a text
questions.example: The data previously referred to is in the appendix.

questions.prompt: It is ___ noting the limitations of this approach.
questions.explanation: "worth" is followed by an -ing form in the fixed phrase "It is worth noting", used to draw attention to a point; "worthy" would need "of".
questions.meaning: deserving to be done, mentioned or considered
questions.example: It is worth noting the limits of this approach.

questions.prompt: This ___ leads into a discussion of policy implications.
questions.explanation: "naturally" is an adverb meaning 'in a logical way', so "naturally leads into" shows that one topic follows easily from another.
questions.meaning: as you would expect; as a logical result
questions.example: This naturally leads into policy implications.

questions.prompt: The ___ analysis (= carried out later) reveals a clear pattern.
questions.explanation: "subsequent" means coming later in time, so "The subsequent analysis" refers to the analysis done afterwards; "consequential" means important, and "consecutive" and "successive" describe things in a series.
questions.meaning: coming later
questions.example: The subsequent analysis reveals a clear pattern.

questions.prompt: As ___ in Table 2, the results vary by region.
questions.explanation: "shown" completes the fixed phrase "As shown in Table 2", used to point readers to evidence in a table.
questions.meaning: displayed or demonstrated, as in a table
questions.example: As shown in Table 2, results vary.

questions.prompt: This ___ us to the final point of the discussion.
questions.explanation: "brings" is the verb needed after "This" and before "us to", forming "This brings us to the final point" to introduce the next topic.
questions.meaning: leads us to a point
questions.example: This brings us to the final point.

questions.prompt: The closing chapter will ___ these concerns in detail.
questions.explanation: "address" takes a direct object, so "address these concerns" works; "attend" needs "to", and "deal" and "cope" need "with" before "these concerns".
questions.meaning: to deal with a problem
questions.example: The closing chapter will address these concerns.

questions.prompt: Consistent ___ prior research, the findings confirm the theory.
questions.explanation: "with" is the preposition that follows "consistent", as in "consistent with prior research", meaning in agreement with it.
questions.meaning: together or in agreement
questions.example: Consistent with prior research, the findings confirm it.

questions.prompt: In ___ words, the results were not as expected.
questions.explanation: "other" completes the fixed phrase "In other words", used to restate something in a different way.
questions.meaning: said in a different way
questions.example: Sales fell sharply. In other words, the plan failed.

units.title: Speaking: Register and Nuance
units.description: Say it out loud — Idiomatic and formal phrasing said aloud.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am afraid that rather misses the point.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "I am afraid that rather misses the point." This is a polite but firm way to say a comment is not relevant, and "I am afraid" softens the criticism.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Let me argue the other side for a moment.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Let me argue the other side for a moment." Use it in a discussion to put forward the opposing view, often to test an idea rather than because you believe it.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That is easier said than done.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "That is easier said than done." This everyday idiom means something sounds simple but is hard to do in practice.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We are splitting hairs over the wording.
questions.explanation: In "We are splitting hairs over the wording.", "split hairs" means to argue about tiny, unimportant differences, so the speaker is saying the disagreement over the wording does not really matter.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The argument does not really hold water.
questions.explanation: In "The argument does not really hold water.", "hold water" means to be logical and convincing, so the speaker is politely saying the argument is weak.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would hesitate to draw that conclusion.
questions.explanation: "I would hesitate to draw that conclusion." is a cautious, formal way to disagree: "would hesitate" softens your view that the evidence does not support the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: This has been on the back burner for months.
questions.explanation: In "This has been on the back burner for months.", "on the back burner" means postponed and given low priority; it is an informal to neutral idiom.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious.
questions.explanation: In "In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious.", "in hindsight" means looking back after something has happened, when it is easy to see what was missed.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We are talking at cross purposes here.
questions.explanation: In "We are talking at cross purposes here.", "at cross purposes" means two people misunderstand each other because each is talking about something different.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That would set an unfortunate precedent.
questions.explanation: In "That would set an unfortunate precedent.", "set a precedent" means to create an example that others will follow in future, and "unfortunate" is a formal, polite way of saying it would be a bad one.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I am inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt.
questions.explanation: In "I am inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt.", "give someone the benefit of the doubt" means to trust them when you are not sure, and "I am inclined to" makes the opinion sound measured.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The proposal is ambitious, to put it mildly.
questions.explanation: In "The proposal is ambitious, to put it mildly.", "to put it mildly" signals deliberate understatement: the speaker really means the proposal is probably unrealistic.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We should not throw the baby out with the bathwater.
questions.explanation: "We should not throw the baby out with the bathwater." means we should not reject something valuable just because part of it is bad; it is a common, neutral idiom.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That is a distinction without a difference.
questions.explanation: "That is a distinction without a difference." is a formal, slightly critical way to say that two things are described differently but are the same in practice.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would go so far as to call it reckless.
questions.explanation: In "I would go so far as to call it reckless.", "go so far as to" introduces a stronger claim than the listener might expect, which makes it a firm but formal way to give an opinion.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The findings are suggestive rather than conclusive.
questions.explanation: In "The findings are suggestive rather than conclusive.", "suggestive" means the results point towards something without proving it. "Rather than conclusive" is a careful academic way to limit a claim.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It is a question of priorities, not resources.
questions.explanation: In "It is a question of priorities, not resources.", the structure "a question of X, not Y" is a formal way to say the real issue is X and not Y.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We have painted ourselves into a corner.
questions.explanation: "We have painted ourselves into a corner." is an idiom meaning our own choices have left us with no good way out. It is neutral in tone and common in meetings.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: That interpretation strikes me as a stretch.
questions.explanation: In "That interpretation strikes me as a stretch.", "strikes me as" softens the opinion. "A stretch" means a reading that goes further than the evidence allows.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: Let us not lose sight of the original aim.
questions.explanation: In "Let us not lose sight of the original aim.", "lose sight of" means forget about something important. "Let us not..." is a formal, inclusive way to give a gentle reminder.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: The tone of the letter was unmistakable.
questions.explanation: In "The tone of the letter was unmistakable.", "unmistakable" means impossible to misread, so the writer's attitude was completely clear. It is a precise, fairly formal adjective.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: I would put it slightly more carefully than that.
questions.explanation: "I would put it slightly more carefully than that." is a diplomatic way to disagree. You offer more cautious wording without saying directly that the other person is wrong.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: This is where the argument starts to unravel.
questions.explanation: In "This is where the argument starts to unravel.", "unravel" means to come apart like loose thread. "This is where..." points to the exact moment the reasoning begins to fail.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: We are effectively back where we started.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "We are effectively back where we started." Here "effectively" means "in practice", and "back where we started" means no progress has been made.

questions.prompt: Say this aloud:
questions.answer: It bears repeating that nothing was agreed.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "It bears repeating that nothing was agreed." "It bears repeating" is a formal way to say something is worth saying again for emphasis.

units.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance
units.description: Write the idea in English — Idiomatic and formal phrasing, written in your own words.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance 1
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say politely that an argument misses the point.
acceptableAnswers: I am afraid that rather misses the point.
With respect, that misses the point.
That rather misses the point, I think.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I am afraid that rather misses the point." "I am afraid" and "rather" soften the criticism, which keeps it polite.

questions.prompt: Offer to argue the opposing side for a moment.
acceptableAnswers: Let me argue the other side for a moment.
Allow me to take the opposing view.
Let me put the opposite case.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Let me argue the other side for a moment." "Let me" offers politely, and "for a moment" shows this is not your real view.

questions.prompt: Dismiss a suggestion as impractical, idiomatically.
acceptableAnswers: That is easier said than done.
Easier said than done.
Saying it is easier than doing it.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That is easier said than done." Idiomatic and formal phrasing, written in your own words.

questions.prompt: Say you are arguing over trivial wording.
acceptableAnswers: We are splitting hairs over the wording.
This is a quibble about wording.
We are arguing over details of wording.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "We are splitting hairs over the wording." "Splitting hairs" means arguing about tiny, unimportant differences.

questions.prompt: Say an argument does not stand up.
acceptableAnswers: The argument does not hold water.
That argument does not stand up.
The argument falls apart under scrutiny.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The argument does not hold water." An argument that does not "hold water" has a weakness that makes it fail.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance 2
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say you would hesitate to draw that conclusion.
acceptableAnswers: I would hesitate to draw that conclusion.
I'd be cautious about concluding that.
I am reluctant to conclude that.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would hesitate to draw that conclusion." "Would hesitate" disagrees tentatively, which is typical of careful academic speech.

questions.prompt: Say something has been postponed for months.
acceptableAnswers: This has been on the back burner for months.
It has been postponed for months.
This has been set aside for months.
questions.explanation: "This has been on the back burner for months." uses an idiom for something that has been put aside as a low priority, so nothing has happened with it for months. A plain version such as "It has been postponed for months." is also accepted.

questions.prompt: Say that in hindsight the warnings were obvious.
acceptableAnswers: In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious.
Looking back, the signs were clear.
With hindsight the warnings were plain.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "In hindsight, the warning signs were obvious." "In hindsight" means judging now, after the event, what was not clear at the time.

questions.prompt: Say two people are misunderstanding each other.
acceptableAnswers: We are talking at cross purposes.
We are misunderstanding each other.
I think we are at cross purposes.
questions.explanation: In "We are talking at cross purposes.", "at cross purposes" means each person is talking about something different without realizing it. This is why they misunderstand each other.

questions.prompt: Say something would set a bad precedent.
acceptableAnswers: That would set an unfortunate precedent.
That would set a bad precedent.
It would establish an unwelcome precedent.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That would set an unfortunate precedent." "Set a precedent" means create an example others will follow, and "unfortunate" is a politer word than "bad".

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance 3
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Extend someone good faith despite doubts.
acceptableAnswers: I am inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt.
I'd give them the benefit of the doubt.
I am willing to assume good faith.
questions.explanation: In "I am inclined to give them the benefit of the doubt.", the idiom means you choose to trust someone even though you cannot be sure. "I am inclined to" keeps the tone formal and hedged.

questions.prompt: Say a proposal is ambitious, understating it.
acceptableAnswers: The proposal is ambitious, to put it mildly.
To say the proposal is ambitious is an understatement.
The proposal is, to put it mildly, ambitious.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "The proposal is ambitious, to put it mildly." "To put it mildly" signals that the real situation is far more extreme than the word used.

questions.prompt: Warn against discarding the good with the bad.
acceptableAnswers: We should not throw the baby out with the bathwater.
Let us not discard what works along with what does not.
We should not discard the good along with the bad.
questions.explanation: "We should not throw the baby out with the bathwater." is an idiom warning against getting rid of something valuable while getting rid of what is unwanted.

questions.prompt: Say a distinction makes no real difference.
acceptableAnswers: That is a distinction without a difference.
That distinction makes no real difference.
There is no practical difference there.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That is a distinction without a difference." This set phrase means two things are labeled differently but are the same in practice.

questions.prompt: Say you would go so far as to call it reckless.
acceptableAnswers: I would go so far as to call it reckless.
I'd even call it reckless.
I would describe it as reckless.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would go so far as to call it reckless." "Go so far as to" shows you are choosing a strong word on purpose, while "I'd even call it reckless" says the same thing more casually.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance 4
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say findings are suggestive rather than conclusive.
acceptableAnswers: The findings are suggestive rather than conclusive.
The evidence suggests but does not prove.
These findings are indicative, but they do not settle the matter.
questions.explanation: "The findings are suggestive rather than conclusive." contrasts evidence that only hints at a conclusion with evidence that proves it, a typical cautious academic phrasing.

questions.prompt: Say it is about priorities, not resources.
acceptableAnswers: It is a question of priorities, not resources.
This is about priorities rather than resources.
The issue is priorities, not resources.
questions.explanation: "It is a question of priorities, not resources." uses the pattern "a question of X, not Y" to say the real issue is X and to rule out Y.

questions.prompt: Say you have left yourselves no options.
acceptableAnswers: We have painted ourselves into a corner.
We have left ourselves no room to move.
We have left ourselves no options.
questions.explanation: "We have painted ourselves into a corner." is an idiom for getting into a position with no way out through your own actions.

questions.prompt: Say an interpretation seems like a stretch.
acceptableAnswers: That interpretation strikes me as a stretch.
That reading seems like a stretch.
I find that interpretation strained.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "That interpretation strikes me as a stretch." "Strikes me as" is a polished way to give your own judgment, and "a stretch" means the reading goes further than the evidence supports.

questions.prompt: Urge people not to lose sight of the original aim.
acceptableAnswers: Let us not lose sight of the original aim.
We should keep the original aim in view.
Let's remember what we set out to do.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Let us not lose sight of the original aim." "Let us not" is a formal way to urge a group, and "lose sight of" means to stop paying attention to something important.

lessons.title: Say It Your Way: Register and Nuance 5
lessons.subtitle: Write the idea in English

questions.prompt: Say the tone of a letter was unmistakable.
acceptableAnswers: The tone of the letter was unmistakable.
There was no mistaking the tone of the letter.
The letter's tone was perfectly clear.
questions.explanation: "The tone of the letter was unmistakable." uses "unmistakable" to mean so clear that nobody could misread it.

questions.prompt: Say you would put something more carefully.
acceptableAnswers: I would put it more carefully than that.
I'd phrase that more carefully.
I would be more careful in how I said that.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "I would put it more carefully than that." Here "put" means "express", so this is a tactful way to say someone's wording was too blunt.

questions.prompt: Say this is where an argument starts to fall apart.
acceptableAnswers: This is where the argument starts to unravel.
The argument begins to break down here.
Here is where it falls apart.
questions.explanation: "This is where the argument starts to unravel." uses "unravel", a figurative verb for something coming apart thread by thread, which suits an argument losing its logic.

questions.prompt: Say you and your team are effectively back where you started.
acceptableAnswers: We are effectively back where we started.
We have come full circle.
We are essentially back at the beginning.
questions.explanation: "We are effectively back where we started." uses "effectively" to mean in practice, even if some things have formally changed.

questions.prompt: Say it bears repeating that nothing was agreed.
acceptableAnswers: It bears repeating that nothing was agreed.
It is worth saying again that nothing was agreed.
Let me repeat that nothing was agreed.
questions.explanation: "It bears repeating that nothing was agreed." uses the formal phrase "it bears repeating" to stress a point worth saying again.
